title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
1. Target function and dataset
We use the example from the Lecture Notes, \[g(x) = x^2\sin(\pi x) - \frac{1}{2+\cos x}, \qquad x\in[-2, 2],\] and a training set \(\mathcal D = \{(x_k, g(x_k))\}_{k=1}^{K}\) of \(K=100\) points \(x_k\) drawn at random (uniformly) from the interval. We deliberately do not use an equally spaced grid: in real experiments and simulations the sampling points are rarely regular, and a fit should be judged on how well it reproduces \(g\) between the sampling points. For this reason all fits are plotted on a separate dense grid x_plot.
The size \(K = 100\) follows from the size of the networks below. They have a few tens of parameters (30 for \(N = 10\)), and the number of data points should be several times larger than the number of parameters, otherwise the data do not determine the fit; any \(K\) of order 100 serves the purpose. The seed 2026 of the random generator fixes the points, so that every run of the notebook gives the same numbers; its value is arbitrary, as are all other seeds in this notebook.


Code
def g(x):
    """Target function from the Lecture Notes (Chapter 2)."""
    return x**2 * np.sin(np.pi * x) - 1.0 / (2.0 + np.cos(x))

K = 100
rng_data = np.random.default_rng(2026)
x_train = np.sort(rng_data.uniform(-2, 2, K))     # random, non-equidistant sampling points (sorted for convenience)
y_train = g(x_train)
x_plot = np.linspace(-2, 2, 1000)                 # dense grid, used only for plotting and for judging fits

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
ax.plot(x_train, y_train, "o", color="C3", ms=4, label=f"{K} random sampling points")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
2. Building blocks

2.1 One neuron
Before fitting anything, we look at the pieces from which the network is assembled. A single hidden neuron contributes \(W^{(2)}\tanh(W^{(1)}x + b)\), a smooth step. The weight \(W^{(1)}\) sets its steepness, the ratio \(-b/W^{(1)}\) sets the position of the step, and \(W^{(2)}\) sets its height. The figure below varies \(W^{(1)}\) and \(b\) separately, so that each effect can be seen on its own.
The labels in the plotting code are f-strings that contain LaTeX. Inside an f-string single braces {w} insert the value of a variable, so a literal brace, needed for the LaTeX superscript W^{(1)}, is written twice: f"$W^{{(1)}} = {w}$" produces the text $W^{(1)} = 0.5$.


Code
x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for w in [0.5, 1, 3, 10]:
    axes[0].plot(x, np.tanh(w * x), label=f"$W^{{(1)}} = {w}$")
for b in [-2, 0, 2]:
    axes[1].plot(x, np.tanh(3 * x + b), label=f"$b = {b}$  (step at $x = {-b/3:.2f}$)")
axes[0].set_title(r"$\tanh(W^{(1)} x)$: steepness"); axes[1].set_title(r"$\tanh(3x + b)$: position")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()







2.2 A bump from two neurons
Two neurons are already enough to make a localised feature. The difference of two shifted steps is a bump, \(\tfrac12\big[\tanh(s(x - a)) - \tanh(s(x - c))\big] \approx 1\) for \(a < x < c\) and \(\approx 0\) elsewhere. Each \(\tanh\) goes from \(-1\) to \(+1\), i.e. changes by 2 across its step; the difference of two steps therefore has height 2, and the factor \(\tfrac12\) normalises the bump to height 1. A sum of such bumps with suitable heights can follow any continuous curve, and this is the intuition behind the UAT. The values \(s = 8\), \(a = -0.5\), \(c = 1\) used below are arbitrary illustration values.


Code
s, a, c = 8.0, -0.5, 1.0
step1, step2 = np.tanh(s * (x - a)), np.tanh(s * (x - c))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.plot(x, step1, "--", label=r"$\tanh(s(x-a))$")
ax.plot(x, -step2, "--", label=r"$-\tanh(s(x-c))$")
ax.plot(x, 0.5 * (step1 - step2), "k", lw=2.5, label="half of the sum: a bump on $[a, c]$")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
3. A constructive approximation
The bump picture can be turned directly into an approximation of \(g\), with all parameters written down explicitly and no optimisation at all. Divide \([-2,2]\) into \(N\) intervals with nodes \(x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_N\). A staircase that jumps by \(g(x_j) - g(x_{j-1})\) at the midpoint \(m_j\) of each interval is \[f_N(x) = g(x_0) + \sum_{j=1}^{N}\big[g(x_j) - g(x_{j-1})\big]\;\frac{1 + \tanh\big(s\,(x - m_j)\big)}{2}.\] The function \(\tfrac12\big(1+\tanh(s(x-m_j))\big)\) is a smooth step that goes from 0 (for \(x \ll m_j\)) to 1 (for \(x \gg m_j\)), so each term adds the jump \(g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})\) once \(x\) has passed \(m_j\).
This is a one-hidden-layer network with \(N\) neurons (plus a constant), whose parameters we chose explicitly: \(W^{(1)}_j = s\), \(b_j = -s m_j\), \(W^{(2)}_j = [g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})]/2\). The factor \(\tfrac12\) in \(W^{(2)}_j\) comes from \(\tfrac12(1+\tanh z) = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\tanh z\): each term is half a jump times \(\tanh\), plus half a jump as a constant. All these constants add up to the constant of the network, \(g(x_0) + \tfrac12\sum_j[g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})] = \tfrac12[g(x_0)+g(x_N)]\). As \(N\to\infty\) (with \(s\) growing so that the steps stay sharp) the error goes to zero, which is a constructive version of the theorem.
Two details of the code deserve a comment. The first is the steepness. The intervals have width \(h = 4/N\), and we take \(s = 4N\), so that \(s\,h = 16\): each step rises from 0 to 1 within a small fraction of its interval, and the network is a genuine staircase. The factor 4 is arbitrary. Smaller factors make neighbouring steps overlap; the sum then becomes a smoother interpolation and is in fact somewhat more accurate (with factor 1 the error for \(N \ge 64\) is about 2.5 times smaller), but the sharp version shows the construction better.
The second is broadcasting. Indexing with None adds an axis of length 1: x[:, None] is a column of shape \((K, 1)\) and mids[None, :] a row of shape \((1, N)\). Their difference is broadcast to a \((K, N)\) table whose entry \((k, j)\) is \(x_k - m_j\), i.e. neuron \(j\) evaluated at point \(k\). The product hidden @ jumps then sums over the neurons.
The figure shows the staircase for several \(N\) (left) and the maximal error on the dense grid as a function of \(N\) (right).


Code
def staircase(x, N, steepness_factor=4.0):
    """Hand-built one-hidden-layer tanh network approximating g with N neurons."""
    nodes = np.linspace(-2, 2, N + 1)
    mids = 0.5 * (nodes[1:] + nodes[:-1])
    jumps = g(nodes[1:]) - g(nodes[:-1])
    s = steepness_factor * N                       # steps get sharper as intervals shrink
    hidden = 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(s * (x[:, None] - mids[None, :])))   # shape (len(x), N)
    return g(nodes[0]) + hidden @ jumps

x_fine = np.linspace(-2, 2, 2000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
axes[0].plot(x_fine, g(x_fine), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
for N in [5, 10, 40]:
    axes[0].plot(x_fine, staircase(x_fine, N), label=f"$N = {N}$")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[0].legend()

Ns = np.array([4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512])
sup_err = [np.max(np.abs(staircase(x_fine, N) - g(x_fine))) for N in Ns]
axes[1].loglog(Ns, sup_err, "o-", label=r"$\max_x |f_N(x) - g(x)|$")
axes[1].loglog(Ns, 20 / Ns, "k--", label=r"$\propto 1/N$")   # guide line; the prefactor 20 only places it near the points
axes[1].set_xlabel("number of neurons $N$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("sup error"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The construction works but is inefficient: the error decreases only like \(1/N\), and it needs \(g\) at equally spaced nodes of our choice. The \(1/N\) law follows from the shape of a staircase. Within one interval the staircase is (nearly) constant, while \(g\) changes by up to \(|g'|_{\max}\,h\) with \(h = 4/N\). The error is therefore at most about half of such a change, \(\tfrac12|g'|_{\max}\cdot 4/N \approx 26/N\) for \(|g'|_{\max}\approx 12.9\) on \([-2,2]\); the measured error is about \(18/N\) for large \(N\). In practice the sampling points are given, and a minimiser has to choose all \(3N\) parameters, including the positions of the steps. Section 7 shows that an optimised network with \(N \approx 8\) neurons is more accurate than the staircase with \(N = 512\). The rest of the notebook is therefore about minimisation.

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
section: 4. The loss function as a function of a parameter vector
text:
4. The loss function as a function of a parameter vector
Most minimisers (in particular scipy.optimize.minimize) work with a flat vector of parameters \(\vec\theta\in\mathbb R^{3N}\). We store \(\vec\theta = (W^{(1)}_1,\dots,W^{(1)}_N,\; b_1,\dots,b_N,\; W^{(2)}_1,\dots,W^{(2)}_N)\) and unpack it inside the model.
The model itself is a few lines of NumPy. np.outer(x, W1) is the \(K\times N\) matrix with entries \(x_k W^{(1)}_i\). Adding the length-\(N\) vector b adds \(b_i\) to every entry of column \(i\) (broadcasting), so entry \((k, i)\) of the table is the argument of neuron \(i\) at point \(k\). Multiplying by W2 with @ sums the neurons with their output weights.
The random initial parameters are arbitrary, but their order of magnitude is not. We draw \(W^{(1)}_i, b_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 2^2)\). With \(x\in[-2,2]\) a neuron \(\tanh(W^{(1)}x+b)\) is a step at \(x = -b/W^{(1)}\) of width about \(1/|W^{(1)}|\). Values of order 2 give steps that are narrower than the interval and positions \(-b/W^{(1)}\) of order 1, i.e. mostly inside the interval. Much smaller values would give nearly linear neurons, much larger values very sharp steps with vanishing slope almost everywhere. The output weights are drawn as \(W^{(2)}_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/N)\). The output is a sum of \(N\) terms of random sign, so its variance is \(N\cdot\mathrm{Var}(W^{(2)})\) times a number of order 1. With \(\mathrm{Var}(W^{(2)}) = 1/N\) the initial \(f(x)\) is of order 1, comparable to \(g\), for every \(N\) (the standard deviation of \(W^{(2)}\) scales as \(1/\sqrt N\)).
We use \(N = 10\) (30 parameters): small enough for the gradient-free methods and the finite-difference gradients below to finish in seconds, and large enough for a good fit. The cell prints the number of parameters and the loss at the random starting point \(\vec\theta_0\), about 1.04.


Code
def unpack(theta):
    """Split the flat parameter vector into (W1, b, W2), each of length N."""
    N = theta.size // 3                         # // is integer division: 30 // 3 = 10 (an integer, usable as an index)
    return theta[:N], theta[N:2 * N], theta[2 * N:]

def model(theta, x):
    """f(x; theta) = sum_i W2_i tanh(W1_i x + b_i), evaluated for all x at once."""
    W1, b, W2 = unpack(theta)
    hidden = np.tanh(np.outer(x, W1) + b)       # shape (K, N): neuron i evaluated at point k
    return hidden @ W2                          # shape (K,)

def loss(theta, x=x_train, y=y_train):
    """Mean squared error on the training set."""
    return np.mean((model(theta, x) - y)**2)

def init_theta(N, seed):
    """Random initial parameters: input weights and biases ~ N(0, 2^2), output weights ~ N(0, 1/N)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # np.concatenate joins the three length-N arrays into one flat vector of length 3N
    return np.concatenate([rng.normal(0, 2, N), rng.normal(0, 2, N), rng.normal(0, 1, N) / np.sqrt(N)])

N = 10
theta0 = init_theta(N, seed=0)        # ONE common starting point for all minimisers below
print("number of parameters:", theta0.size, "  initial loss:", loss(theta0))


number of parameters: 30   initial loss: 1.0398383815103345



4.1 Backpropagation for one hidden layer
Gradient-based minimisers need \(\nabla_{\vec\theta}\mathcal L\), and for one hidden layer it can be derived analytically in a few lines. With \(a_{ki} = W^{(1)}_i x_k + b_i\), \(h_{ki} = \tanh a_{ki}\), \(f_k = \sum_i W^{(2)}_i h_{ki}\) and residuals \(r_k = f_k - y_k\), \[\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W^{(2)}_i} = \frac{2}{K}\sum_k r_k\,h_{ki},\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial b_i} = \frac{2}{K}\sum_k r_k\,W^{(2)}_i\,(1 - h_{ki}^2),\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W^{(1)}_i} = \frac{2}{K}\sum_k r_k\,W^{(2)}_i\,(1 - h_{ki}^2)\,x_k .\] The factors come from the chain rule: \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial f_k = 2r_k/K\); then \(\partial f_k/\partial W^{(2)}_i = h_{ki}\), \(\partial f_k/\partial h_{ki} = W^{(2)}_i\), \(\partial h_{ki}/\partial a_{ki} = 1-h_{ki}^2\) (we used \(\tanh' = 1 - \tanh^2\)), and \(\partial a_{ki}/\partial b_i = 1\), \(\partial a_{ki}/\partial W^{(1)}_i = x_k\). Each parameter affects \(\mathcal L\) through all \(K\) points, hence the sums over \(k\). This is the chain rule applied backwards through the network, i.e. backpropagation; autograd performs the same computation automatically.
An analytic gradient is easy to get wrong, so we compare it with the central difference \([\mathcal L(\vec\theta+\delta\vec e) - \mathcal L(\vec\theta-\delta\vec e)]/(2\delta)\) for every unit vector \(\vec e\), with step \(\delta\) (eps in the code). Its truncation error is of order \(\delta^2\) and its round-off error of order \(10^{-16}/\delta\), so \(\delta\) between about \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-7}\) gives differences of \(10^{-9}\) or smaller; we take \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). The gradient components here are of order 1, so a mistake in one of the formulas would show up as a difference of order 1. The largest difference printed below is \(2\cdot10^{-10}\), so the formulas are correct.


Code
def grad(theta, x=x_train, y=y_train):
    """Analytic gradient of the MSE loss with respect to theta = (W1, b, W2)."""
    W1, b, W2 = unpack(theta)
    K = x.size
    h = np.tanh(np.outer(x, W1) + b)            # (K, N) hidden activations
    r = h @ W2 - y                              # (K,)   residuals
    dW2 = 2 / K * h.T @ r                       # (N,)   (2/K) sum_k r_k h_ki
    delta = 2 / K * r[:, None] * W2[None, :] * (1 - h**2)   # (K, N) dL/da_ki
    db = delta.sum(axis=0)                      # (N,)   sum over the points k
    dW1 = delta.T @ x                           # (N,)   sum_k delta_ki x_k
    return np.concatenate([dW1, db, dW2])

# Always check a hand-written gradient against finite differences before using it.
# The rows of np.eye(n) are the unit vectors e; each one perturbs a single parameter.
eps = 1e-6
fd = np.array([(loss(theta0 + eps * e) - loss(theta0 - eps * e)) / (2 * eps) for e in np.eye(theta0.size)])
print("max |analytic - finite difference| =", np.max(np.abs(grad(theta0) - fd)))


max |analytic - finite difference| = 2.181130831502287e-10

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
5. Minimisers in SciPy
With the loss and its gradient in hand we can compare minimisers. scipy.optimize.minimize(fun, x0, method=..., jac=...) gives access to many classical algorithms, and we compare two families: methods that use only the values of \(\mathcal L\), and methods that also use the gradient \(\nabla\mathcal L\).








method
uses
idea




Nelder–Mead
only \(\mathcal L\)
moves a simplex of \(3N+1\) points by reflections/contractions


Powell
only \(\mathcal L\)
successive 1D line minimisations along a set of directions


CG (conjugate gradient)
\(\mathcal L\), \(\nabla\mathcal L\)
line searches along conjugate-gradient directions: each new direction is the gradient corrected so that it does not undo the progress along the previous directions


BFGS (Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno)
\(\mathcal L\), \(\nabla\mathcal L\)
quasi-Newton: builds an approximation of the inverse Hessian from gradient history


L-BFGS-B (limited-memory BFGS with bounds)
\(\mathcal L\), \(\nabla\mathcal L\)
BFGS with limited memory (stores the last few differences of parameters and gradients), usable for many parameters; “-B”: optional bounds on the parameters, not used here



Two terms in the table need a definition. A simplex in \(n\) dimensions is a set of \(n+1\) points (a triangle for \(n = 2\), a tetrahedron for \(n = 3\)); Nelder–Mead compares \(\mathcal L\) at its corners and moves the worst corner. A line search (line minimisation) is a one-dimensional minimisation of \(\mathcal L(\vec\theta + \alpha\vec d)\) over the step length \(\alpha\) along a chosen direction \(\vec d\).
To follow the progress we pass a callback, which SciPy calls after every iteration with the current \(\vec\theta\). We also count how many times \(\mathcal L\) was evaluated (nfev) and, for the methods that use it, how many times the gradient was evaluated (njev); with the analytic gradient one gradient costs about as much as a few evaluations of \(\mathcal L\). The field message reports why the minimiser stopped.
A few details of the code below are worth knowing. minimize returns an OptimizeResult object: res.x is the parameter vector at the end of the run, res.fun the loss there, and res.nfev, res.njev the numbers of loss and gradient evaluations. Results of the gradient-free methods have no attribute njev; getattr(obj, "name", default) returns the attribute if it exists and default otherwise, so the same code works for all methods. All methods get the common limit maxiter = 5000, because the default limits differ between methods; with this limit every method can stop on its own convergence criterion, except Nelder–Mead, which reaches the limit (with 20000 iterations it gets to \(5\cdot10^{-2}\), still far from the other methods, at four times the cost). Each method has its own default stopping tolerance, so the final losses are not compared at equal accuracy; they show what each method delivers with its standard settings. One extra run uses BFGS without the analytic gradient, so that SciPy estimates the gradient by finite differences.


Code
def run_scipy(method, use_grad, theta_start=theta0, maxiter=5000):
    """Minimise the loss with scipy; return a dict with the history and statistics."""
    history = [loss(theta_start)]
    callback = lambda th: history.append(loss(th))       # record loss after each iteration
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    res = minimize(loss, theta_start, method=method,
                   jac=grad if use_grad else None,       # None -> scipy uses finite differences (if it needs a gradient)
                   callback=callback,
                   options={"maxiter": maxiter})
    return dict(theta=res.x, history=history, final_loss=res.fun, nfev=res.nfev,
                njev=getattr(res, "njev", 0), message=res.message, time=time.perf_counter() - t0)

scipy_runs = {
    "Nelder-Mead":           run_scipy("Nelder-Mead", use_grad=False),
    "Powell":                run_scipy("Powell", use_grad=False),
    "CG":                    run_scipy("CG", use_grad=True),
    "BFGS":                  run_scipy("BFGS", use_grad=True),
    "BFGS (finite-diff grad)": run_scipy("BFGS", use_grad=False),
    "L-BFGS-B":              run_scipy("L-BFGS-B", use_grad=True),
}
for name, r in scipy_runs.items():
    print(f"{name:25s} loss = {r['final_loss']:.2e}   nfev = {r['nfev']:6d}   njev = {r['njev']:5d}   time = {r['time']:.2f} s   ({r['message']})")


Nelder-Mead               loss = 8.06e-02   nfev =   5986   njev =     0   time = 0.32 s   (Maximum number of iterations has been exceeded.)
Powell                    loss = 4.95e-03   nfev =  28849   njev =     0   time = 0.80 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
CG                        loss = 2.69e-06   nfev =   3107   njev =  3107   time = 0.35 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
BFGS                      loss = 1.11e-06   nfev =    592   njev =   592   time = 0.09 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
BFGS (finite-diff grad)   loss = 2.19e-06   nfev =  16089   njev =   519   time = 0.48 s   (Optimization terminated successfully.)
L-BFGS-B                  loss = 1.34e-05   nfev =    703   njev =   703   time = 0.06 s   (CONVERGENCE: RELATIVE REDUCTION OF F <= FACTR*EPSMCH)


The table shows a clear hierarchy. BFGS reaches a loss of about \(10^{-6}\) with about 600 evaluations, while Powell needs almost \(3\cdot10^4\) evaluations and stops at a loss several thousand times larger, and Nelder–Mead stops at the iteration limit with a loss of about 0.08. The line BFGS (finite-diff grad) reaches a similar loss, but needs many more function evaluations, because every gradient costs \(3N+1\) evaluations of \(\mathcal L\). With \(10^6\) parameters this is not feasible, and deep learning therefore relies on backpropagation.

5.1 Plain gradient descent
The simplest gradient-based method uses the analytic gradient of Section 4.1 directly: \(\vec\theta_{t+1} = \vec\theta_t - \eta\,\nabla\mathcal L(\vec\theta_t)\) with a fixed learning rate \(\eta\).
The learning rate cannot be arbitrarily large. Near a minimum \(\mathcal L\) is approximately quadratic, and along the eigenvector of the Hessian with the largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_{\max}\) one step multiplies the distance to the minimum by \((1-\eta\lambda_{\max})\). The iteration is stable only if \(|1-\eta\lambda_{\max}|<1\), i.e. \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\); otherwise the parameters oscillate with growing amplitude. For our start \(\lambda_{\max}\approx 9\), so the limit is \(\eta\approx 0.2\). In measurements, \(\eta = 0.5\) diverges within 10 steps, while \(\eta\) up to \(0.3\) does not diverge in 20000 steps: the parameters drift into a region where the landscape is flatter (at the end of the run with \(\eta = 0.3\), \(\lambda_{\max}\approx 6.7 \approx 2/0.3\)), so the estimate from the starting point is only a rough guide. The value \(\eta = 0.05\) used below is a safe choice well below the limit, not an optimal one (\(\eta = 0.1\) reaches a loss about 3 times lower here); Exercise 3 scans \(\eta\) systematically. Because each step is small, the loss decreases slowly along the flat directions of the landscape, hence the large number of steps. After 20000 steps the loss is \(3.7\cdot10^{-3}\), far above the BFGS result.


Code
eta, n_steps = 0.05, 20000
theta = theta0.copy()
gd_history = [loss(theta)]
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for t in range(n_steps):
    theta = theta - eta * grad(theta)
    gd_history.append(loss(theta))
gd_run = dict(theta=theta, history=gd_history, final_loss=gd_history[-1], nfev=n_steps, time=time.perf_counter() - t0)
print(f"gradient descent: loss = {gd_run['final_loss']:.2e} after {n_steps} steps")


gradient descent: loss = 3.70e-03 after 20000 steps




5.2 Convergence of the SciPy minimisers
The figure shows the loss versus iteration (left) and the resulting fits (right). An “iteration” means different things for different methods (one simplex move, one line search, one gradient step), so the table of function and gradient evaluations above should be read together with the left panel. On the left, Powell decreases fastest during the first iterations, but each of its iterations costs many evaluations of \(\mathcal L\). BFGS (with analytic or finite-difference gradient) and CG reach the lowest losses (about \(10^{-6}\)), while L-BFGS-B stops about ten times higher with its default tolerance; gradient descent decreases slowly over \(2\cdot10^4\) steps, and Nelder–Mead hardly moves during the first few hundred iterations. On the right, most fits lie on top of \(g\); the Nelder–Mead fit is visibly wrong near the ends of the interval and around \(x = 0\).


Code
all_np = {**scipy_runs, "gradient descent": gd_run}     # new dict: all entries of scipy_runs plus one more
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8))
for i, (name, r) in enumerate(all_np.items()):
    axes[0].loglog(np.arange(1, len(r["history"]) + 1), r["history"], color=f"C{i}", label=name)
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, model(r["theta"], x_plot), color=f"C{i}", lw=1.2)
axes[1].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label="$g(x)$")
axes[1].plot(x_train, y_train, "k.", ms=4, label="sampling points")
axes[0].set_xlabel("iteration"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\mathcal{L}$"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
6. Optimisers in PyTorch
In deep learning nobody derives gradients analytically: autograd computes them, and the optimisers of torch.optim use them. We now solve the same problem in this way and compare the optimisers used in deep learning (see The Zoo of Optimization Algorithms in the Lecture Notes): stochastic gradient descent (SGD), SGD with momentum, RMSprop (root-mean-square propagation), Adam (adaptive moment estimation) and L-BFGS. All runs start from the same \(\vec\theta_0\) as before. L-BFGS in PyTorch needs a closure, a function that recomputes the loss and the gradient, because it evaluates them several times per step (line search).
Three details of the code are new. getattr(torch.optim, "Adam") is the same object as torch.optim.Adam, so the optimiser class is selected from its name given as a string, and one function run_torch serves all optimisers. **opt_kwargs in the definition of a function collects all extra keyword arguments into a dictionary, and **kw in a call unpacks a dictionary into keyword arguments, so run_torch("SGD", 2000, **dict(lr=0.05)) is the same as run_torch("SGD", 2000, lr=0.05). Finally, opt.step(closure) returns the loss computed by the (first) call of the closure, i.e. the loss before the update of this step, and .item() turns the one-element tensor into a Python number, so the list history does not keep the computational graph in memory.
The learning rates differ between optimisers for a reason. With momentum \(\beta = 0.9\) the steps accumulate along a steady slope to about \(\mathrm{lr}/(1-\beta) = 10\,\mathrm{lr}\), so momentum needs a smaller lr than plain SGD. RMSprop and Adam divide the gradient by a running average of its size, so for them lr is roughly the step length in parameter units, independent of the size of the gradient. All these values were tuned manually to give stable runs; they are typical, not optimal (Exercise 3 scans the learning rate).
L-BFGS has its own settings. max_iter = 20 is the number of inner quasi-Newton iterations per call of step, so 50 outer steps allow up to 1000 iterations (each with several evaluations of the loss in the line search), comparable in cost to the 2000 steps of the first-order methods. The numbers of steps are kept small so that the cell runs in a few seconds; with 5000 steps the first-order methods reach lower losses (Adam \(9\cdot10^{-5}\), momentum \(4\cdot10^{-3}\), RMSprop \(10^{-2}\), SGD \(6\cdot10^{-2}\)). The learning rate lr = 1 is the natural step length for L-BFGS, because a quasi-Newton direction already has the scale of a Newton step. Without a line search PyTorch takes this fixed step, which can increase the loss; with line_search_fn="strong_wolfe" the step length is adjusted at every iteration so that the loss decreases sufficiently (the Wolfe conditions).


Code
xt, yt = torch.tensor(x_train), torch.tensor(y_train)

def model_torch(theta, x):
    """Same network as `model`, written with torch operations."""
    N = theta.numel() // 3
    W1, b, W2 = theta[:N], theta[N:2 * N], theta[2 * N:]
    return torch.tanh(x[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2

def run_torch(opt_name, n_steps, **opt_kwargs):
    theta = torch.tensor(theta0, requires_grad=True)          # fresh copy of the common start
    opt = getattr(torch.optim, opt_name)([theta], **opt_kwargs)
    history = []

    def closure():                                            # forward + backward; used by every optimiser
        opt.zero_grad()
        L = torch.mean((model_torch(theta, xt) - yt)**2)
        L.backward()
        return L

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        L = opt.step(closure)                                 # SGD/Adam call closure once, LBFGS several times
        history.append(L.item())
    return dict(theta=theta.detach().numpy(), history=history, final_loss=history[-1],
                time=time.perf_counter() - t0)

torch_setups = {
    "SGD":             ("SGD",     2000, dict(lr=0.05)),
    "SGD + momentum":  ("SGD",     2000, dict(lr=0.02, momentum=0.9)),
    "RMSprop":         ("RMSprop", 2000, dict(lr=3e-3)),
    "Adam":            ("Adam",    2000, dict(lr=1e-2)),
    "L-BFGS (torch)":  ("LBFGS",     50, dict(lr=1, max_iter=20, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")),
}
torch_runs = {name: run_torch(opt, n, **kw) for name, (opt, n, kw) in torch_setups.items()}
for name, r in torch_runs.items():
    print(f"{name:16s} loss = {r['final_loss']:.2e}   time = {r['time']:.2f} s")


SGD              loss = 1.12e-01   time = 0.53 s
SGD + momentum   loss = 2.43e-02   time = 0.51 s
RMSprop          loss = 3.54e-02   time = 0.54 s
Adam             loss = 4.29e-03   time = 0.58 s
L-BFGS (torch)   loss = 6.82e-06   time = 1.09 s


After 2000 steps the first-order optimisers are far behind: Adam reaches \(4.3\cdot10^{-3}\) and SGD only \(0.11\), while L-BFGS reaches \(6.8\cdot10^{-6}\). The figure shows the loss versus optimiser step (left) and the error \(f(x) - g(x)\) of the final fits on the dense grid (right). A perfect fit would give the horizontal line at zero in the right panel. L-BFGS is close to this line everywhere. Adam has errors of a few tenths, SGD, momentum and RMSprop of order 1 even inside the interval, and the largest errors (up to almost 2 for SGD) are at the ends \(x = \pm 2\), where the data constrain the fit only from one side.

    axes[1].plot(x_plot, model(r["theta"], x_plot) - g(x_plot), color=f"C{i}", lw=1.2, label=name)

axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"error $f(x;\theta) - g(x)$ on the dense grid"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The exact numbers depend on the random start and on the hyperparameters, but the ranking reflects general properties of the methods. The gradient-free methods (Nelder–Mead, Powell) need many function evaluations already for 30 parameters, and Nelder–Mead stopped at the iteration limit without converging (see its message above). The methods that use curvature information, either by building an approximation of the Hessian from the history of gradients (BFGS, L-BFGS) or through conjugate directions (CG), are the most accurate for this small, smooth, full-batch problem. The first-order methods (SGD, momentum, RMSprop, Adam) converge more slowly here, but they are the only ones that remain practical for millions of parameters and mini-batches of data (at every step the gradient is computed from a random subset of the data, which makes it noisy), which is the situation in deep learning. Every method has hyperparameters (learning rate, momentum, number of steps), and with other values the ranking can change (Exercise 3).

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
section: 7. Loss and the number of neurons
text:
7. Loss and the number of neurons
With BFGS as a reliable minimiser we can now test the UAT numerically: if the theorem is at work, the best achievable loss should fall rapidly as \(N\) grows. For each \(N\) we run BFGS from a few random starting points and keep the best result.
Restarts are needed because the landscape is non-convex (Section 9), so a single run can end in a poor minimum. Three starts per \(N\) (seeds 0, 1, 2) are a compromise between cost and the chance of missing a good minimum; any small number (3–10) is reasonable. The stopping criterion also matters. BFGS stops when the largest component of the gradient falls below gtol (default \(10^{-5}\)), or after maxiter iterations. With the default, the run for \(N = 8\) stops at a loss of about \(10^{-6}\), although much lower losses exist: near such a small minimum the gradient is already tiny. We therefore set gtol = 1e-8. To keep the cell fast we allow at most 1000 iterations, and for \(N \ge 6\) the runs stop at this limit. The losses for \(N \ge 6\) (of order \(10^{-7}\)) are therefore set by the iteration budget, not by \(N\). With max_iter = 5000 (about four times longer) the losses are \(1.6\cdot10^{-9}\) for \(N = 8\) and \(10^{-10}\) for \(N = 12\).


Code
Ns = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12]
max_iter = 1000          # kept small so that the cell runs in a few seconds; 5000 gives lower losses for N >= 6
best_loss, best_theta = {}, {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for N in Ns:
    results = [minimize(loss, init_theta(N, seed), jac=grad, method="BFGS",
                        options={"maxiter": max_iter, "gtol": 1e-8}) for seed in range(3)]
    best = min(results, key=lambda r: r.fun)      # the result with the smallest r.fun (final loss)
    best_loss[N], best_theta[N] = best.fun, best.x
    print(f"N = {N:2d}   ({3*N:2d} parameters)   best loss = {best.fun:.2e}")
print(f"total time {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))
axes[0].semilogy(Ns, [best_loss[N] for N in Ns], "o-")
axes[0].set_xlabel("number of hidden neurons $N$"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"best $\mathcal{L}$")

    axes[1].plot(x_plot, model(best_theta[N], x_plot), "--", lw=2, label=f"$N = {N}$")

fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Compare with Fig. 2.3 of the Lecture Notes (\(N = 2, 3, 4\)). Already \(N = 6\) to \(8\) neurons give a mean squared error below \(10^{-6}\) on the training points (and of order \(10^{-9}\) with more iterations); the small rise from \(N = 6\) to \(N = 8\) is due to the iteration limit. The training loss measures the error only at the sampling points. The UAT, however, bounds the maximal error, so we also compute \(\max|f-g|\) on the dense grid and compare the optimised network with the constructive staircase of Section 3.


Code
sup_net = np.max(np.abs(model(best_theta[8], x_plot) - g(x_plot)))
sup_stair = np.max(np.abs(staircase(x_plot, 512) - g(x_plot)))
print(f"max |f - g| on the dense grid:  optimised network N = 8: {sup_net:.1e},   staircase N = 512: {sup_stair:.1e}")


max |f - g| on the dense grid:  optimised network N = 8: 8.0e-03,   staircase N = 512: 3.4e-02


The optimised network with 8 neurons has a maximal error of \(8\cdot10^{-3}\), about four times smaller than the staircase with 512 neurons (\(3.4\cdot10^{-2}\)): optimising the positions of the steps is far more efficient than placing them on a fixed grid.

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
8. Building approximators for other functions
We now collect everything into one tool that builds the approximator \[f(x;\vec W^{(1)},\vec b,\vec W^{(2)}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_i\,\sigma\big(W^{(1)}_i x + b_i\big) + c\] for any target \(g(x)\) on an interval \([x_\min, x_\max]\), with a chosen number of hidden nodes \(N\) (we use ‘node’ and ‘neuron’ interchangeably), activation \(\sigma\), number of sampling points \(K\) and minimiser. We add an output bias \(c\): for activations that are not odd, i.e. do not satisfy \(\sigma(-z) = -\sigma(z)\) (sigmoid, ReLU, …), it is needed to shift the output; for \(\tanh\) it changes little.
The function fit_uat follows the procedure from the lecture. It samples \(K\) points \(x_k\) in the interval and computes \(y_k = g(x_k)\); it initialises the parameters \(\vec\theta = (\vec W^{(1)}, \vec b, \vec W^{(2)}, c)\) randomly; it defines the loss \(\mathcal L(\vec\theta) = \frac1K\sum_k \big(y_k - f(x_k;\vec\theta)\big)^2\); and it minimises by repeating three operations: compute \(\mathcal L\), compute \(\nabla_{\vec\theta}\mathcal L\) by autograd, update \(\vec\theta\). Since the landscape is non-convex, it can optionally repeat the whole minimisation from a few random starts (n_restarts) and keep the best result.
Several choices inside fit_uat need a justification. The input \(x\) is first mapped linearly to \([-1, 1]\). The random initial steps have positions \(-b_i/W^{(1)}_i\) of order 1 and widths \(1/|W^{(1)}_i|\) of order \(1/3\), so they cover \([-1,1]\) well. On an interval far from this scale the same initialisation fails: for \(g\) shifted to \([100, 104]\) (8 nodes) the loss stays at 1.4, which is the variance of the data (no fit at all, every \(\tanh\) is saturated), while with rescaling it reaches \(3\cdot10^{-6}\); on \([-0.02, 0.02]\) the numbers are 0.13 and \(2\cdot10^{-5}\). For the intervals used below, all of width 2–6 around 0, rescaling makes little difference, but it costs nothing. The output \(y\) is not rescaled, since the targets below are of order 1.
The initial weights are drawn as \(W^{(1)}_i, b_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 3^2)\) and \(W^{(2)}_i\sim\mathcal N(0, 1/N)\) (Section 4). The value 3 is arbitrary: standard deviations 1, 3, 5 and 10 tested with 8 nodes all give small final losses for the smooth targets, with no systematic trend; for the sawtooth the final loss ranges from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-1}\) and depends mainly on which minimum the run happens to reach (Section 9), not on this value. The output bias \(c\) starts at the mean of the data, so the nodes only have to represent the deviations from the mean; starting from \(c = 0\) also works.
The default numbers of steps and learning rates follow Section 6: L-BFGS needs some tens of outer steps with lr \(= 1\), while the first-order methods need thousands of steps with a small lr. The defaults (30 L-BFGS steps of up to 20 inner iterations each, 2000 Adam/SGD steps, a single start) are kept small so that every figure below takes only a few seconds; larger values (e.g. n_steps=100, n_restarts=5) give lower losses for the larger \(N\), at a correspondingly higher cost.


Code
import torch.nn.functional as F    # PyTorch module with activation functions written as plain functions, e.g. F.elu(z)

# Activation functions from the lecture slide
ACTIVATIONS = {
    "sigmoid":   torch.sigmoid,
    "tanh":      torch.tanh,
    "ReLU":      torch.relu,
    "LeakyReLU": lambda z: F.leaky_relu(z, negative_slope=0.1),
    "ELU":       F.elu,
}

def fit_uat(g, x_range, N, K=30, activation="tanh", optimizer="LBFGS",
            n_steps=None, lr=None, n_restarts=1, sampling="random", seed=0):
    """
    Fit f(x) = sum_i W2_i * sigma(W1_i * x + b_i) + c  to the function g on the interval x_range.

    g          : function of a NumPy array (the target)
    x_range    : (x_min, x_max)
    N          : number of nodes in the single hidden layer
    K          : number of sampling (training) points
    activation : key of ACTIVATIONS
    optimizer  : "LBFGS", "Adam" or "SGD"
    n_restarts : number of random initialisations; the best one is returned
    sampling   : "random" (uniformly random points) or "grid" (equally spaced points)
    Returns a dict with the fitted predictor, the data, the final loss and the loss history.
    """
    sigma = ACTIVATIONS[activation]
    x_min, x_max = x_range
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # ---- 1. data -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    if sampling == "random":
        x_data = np.sort(rng.uniform(x_min, x_max, K))
    else:
        x_data = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, K)
    y_data = g(x_data)
    to_unit = lambda x: 2 * (x - x_min) / (x_max - x_min) - 1      # rescale input to [-1, 1]
    xt, yt = torch.tensor(to_unit(x_data)), torch.tensor(y_data)

    # default number of steps and learning rate for each optimiser
    defaults = {"LBFGS": (30, 1.0), "Adam": (2000, 1e-2), "SGD": (2000, 1e-2)}
    # `a or b` gives b when a is None (or 0): the default is used only when no value was passed
    n_steps = n_steps or defaults[optimizer][0]
    lr = lr or defaults[optimizer][1]

    best = None
    for restart in range(n_restarts):
        torch.manual_seed(seed + restart)
        # ---- 2. model parameters (random initialisation) -----------------------------
        W1 = (3 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()               # steepness of each node
        b = (3 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()                # position of each node
        W2 = (torch.randn(N) / np.sqrt(N)).requires_grad_()      # height of each node
        c = torch.tensor([float(y_data.mean())], requires_grad=True)  # output bias
        params = [W1, b, W2, c]

        def f(x):                                                # the approximator f(x; theta)
            return sigma(x[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c

        # ---- 3. loss -----------------------------------------------------------------
        # closure uses opt, which is created only further down: Python looks up the name opt when closure is CALLED
        # (inside opt.step), not when it is defined, and by then opt exists.
        def closure():
            opt.zero_grad()
            L = torch.mean((yt - f(xt))**2)
            L.backward()                                         # gradient by autograd
            return L

        # ---- 4. minimisation ---------------------------------------------------------
        if optimizer == "LBFGS":
            opt = torch.optim.LBFGS(params, lr=lr, max_iter=20, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")
        else:
            opt = getattr(torch.optim, optimizer)(params, lr=lr)
        history = []
        for step in range(n_steps):
            L = opt.step(closure)
            history.append(L.item())
            if not np.isfinite(history[-1]):                     # stop a diverging run
                break

        # ---- 5. keep the best restart ------------------------------------------------
        # keep this restart if it is the first one, if the best so far diverged (nan), or if it is better
        if best is None or not np.isfinite(best["loss"]) or history[-1] < best["loss"]:
            # detach().clone(): an independent copy outside the autograd graph, not changed by later restarts.
            # The default argument frozen=frozen is evaluated when predict is defined, so predict keeps the
            # parameters of THIS restart (a direct reference to W1, b, ... would see the names of the last restart).
            frozen = [p.detach().clone() for p in params]
            def predict(x, frozen=frozen):
                W1_, b_, W2_, c_ = frozen
                return (sigma(torch.tensor(to_unit(np.asarray(x)))[:, None] * W1_ + b_) @ W2_ + c_).numpy()
            best = dict(predict=predict, loss=history[-1], history=history,
                        x_data=x_data, y_data=y_data, N=N, activation=activation)
    return best


A plotting function then reproduces the figure from the lecture slide: the target \(g(x)\), the sampling points and the approximations for several \(N\) on the left, and the loss during minimisation on the right. We apply it first to the function \(g\) of Section 1.


Code
def plot_approximations(g, x_range, N_list, title="", **fit_kwargs):
    """Fit and plot f(x) for every N in N_list (as on the lecture slide), plus the loss curves."""
    x_plot = np.linspace(*x_range, 600)          # *x_range unpacks the pair: same as np.linspace(x_range[0], x_range[1], 600)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]})   # left panel 1.6 times wider
    axes[0].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
    for i, N in enumerate(N_list):
        res = fit_uat(g, x_range, N, **fit_kwargs)
        axes[0].plot(x_plot, res["predict"](x_plot), "--", lw=2, color=f"C{i}",
                     label=f"$f(x)$, $N = {N}$")
        axes[1].semilogy(res["history"], color=f"C{i}", label=f"$N = {N}$: final $\\mathcal{{L}}$ = {res['loss']:.1e}")
    axes[0].plot(res["x_data"], res["y_data"], "o", color="k", ms=6, label="sampling points of $g(x)$")
    # limit the vertical range: between sampling points a fit can make very large excursions, which would hide everything else
    g_min, g_max = g(x_plot).min(), g(x_plot).max()
    span = g_max - g_min
    axes[0].set_ylim(g_min - 0.5 * span, g_max + 0.5 * span)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("$g(x)$"); axes[0].set_title(title)
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("optimiser step"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\mathcal{L}$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# The example from the slide: g(x) on [-2, 2], K = 30 random sampling points, N = 2, 3, 4
plot_approximations(g, (-2, 2), N_list=[2, 3, 4], K=30, title="lecture example")





This is the situation of the lecture slide. With \(N = 2\) and \(N = 3\) the fits are made of a few steep steps, and their loss curves become flat after a few steps: the minimiser has stopped in a minimum and more steps do not help (with n_steps=100 the final losses for this seed are unchanged). The result depends on the starting point: for \(N = 3\) the seeds 0–5 give final losses between \(9\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(5\cdot10^{-1}\). With \(N = 4\) the fit follows \(g\) closely.

8.1 A gallery of harder targets
Some functions are harder to approximate than others. The number of nodes needed depends on how many features (bumps, kinks, steps) the function has on the interval, and on how sharp they are. To see this, the dictionary TARGETS collects, besides \(g\), six targets, each chosen for one particular difficulty. The Gaussian wave packet \(e^{-x^2}\cos(8x)\) has many oscillations; \(|x|\) has a kink, being not differentiable at 0; the smoothed step \(\tanh(30x)\) is very steep; and the sawtooth has several jumps. Two targets come from physics. The Lennard-Jones potential \(4(r^{-12} - r^{-6})\) combines a steep wall with a shallow minimum (in its panel the horizontal axis is the distance \(r\)). The ground state of the double well \(V = \tfrac12x^2 + \kappa e^{-x^2/2}\) (\(\kappa = 6\), units \(\hbar = m = 1\)) is computed by discretising \(H = -\tfrac12\, d^2/dx^2 + V\) with the three-point stencil on 400 equally spaced points in \([-6, 6]\) and diagonalising the resulting matrix. The cells below fit the wave packet, \(|x|\), the sawtooth and the Lennard-Jones potential with \(K = 60\) sampling points (the harder targets need more points than the 30 used for \(g\)); the steep step and the double-well ground state can be selected in Section 8.2.


Code
def double_well_ground_state(x, kappa=6.0):
    """Ground-state wavefunction of V = x^2/2 + kappa exp(-x^2/2), interpolated onto x."""
    grid = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400); dx = grid[1] - grid[0]
    H = (-0.5 / dx**2 * (np.diag(np.ones(399), 1) - 2 * np.eye(400) + np.diag(np.ones(399), -1))
         + np.diag(0.5 * grid**2 + kappa * np.exp(-grid**2 / 2)))
    psi0 = np.linalg.eigh(H)[1][:, 0]
    # eigh normalises sum(psi0**2) = 1; dividing by sqrt(dx) gives sum(psi0**2) * dx = 1, the discrete form of
    # the integral normalisation. abs() removes the arbitrary overall sign (the ground state has no nodes).
    psi0 = np.abs(psi0) / np.sqrt(dx)
    return np.interp(x, grid, psi0)          # linear interpolation of the grid values psi0 at the points x

TARGETS = {
    # name: (function, interval)
    "lecture g(x)":            (g, (-2, 2)),
    "wave packet":             (lambda x: np.exp(-x**2) * np.cos(8 * x), (-3, 3)),
    "|x|":                     (np.abs, (-1, 1)),
    "steep step tanh(30x)":    (lambda x: np.tanh(30 * x), (-1, 1)),
    "sawtooth":                (lambda x: 2 * (x - np.floor(x + 0.5)), (-2, 2)),   # x - floor(x + 1/2): signed distance to the nearest integer, in [-1/2, 1/2)
    "Lennard-Jones":           (lambda r: 4 * (r**-12 - r**-6), (0.95, 3.0)),
    "double-well ground state": (double_well_ground_state, (-4, 4)),
}

# K = 60 sampling points (instead of 30): the harder targets need more points to resolve their oscillations and jumps.
# For N = 16 the network has 49 parameters (3N + 1 with the output bias c), comparable to K; experiment 3 of Section 8.2
# shows what happens when K is smaller than the number of parameters.
# The intervals contain the region where each function has its features; their exact limits are arbitrary.
for name in ["wave packet", "|x|"]:
    func, interval = TARGETS[name]
    plot_approximations(func, interval, N_list=[2, 4, 8, 16], K=60, title=name)








The sawtooth and the Lennard-Jones potential are fitted with the same settings.


Code
for name in ["sawtooth", "Lennard-Jones"]:
    func, interval = TARGETS[name]
    plot_approximations(func, interval, N_list=[2, 4, 8, 16], K=60, title=name)








Each target behaves according to its difficulty. The wave packet has 9 maxima and minima of visible size; \(N = 8\) still misses several of them, while \(N = 16\) (about two nodes per extremum) follows all of them. For \(|x|\) a network with rectified linear units (ReLU) would need only two nodes, since \(|x| = \mathrm{ReLU}(x) + \mathrm{ReLU}(-x)\), while \(\tanh\) needs several, so the choice of \(\sigma\) matters. The jumps of the sawtooth are approximated by very steep \(\tanh\) nodes, and between the sampling points the fit can do anything. For \(N = 16\) the loss is still decreasing after the 30 default L-BFGS steps, and n_steps=100 gives a much better fit. On \([0.95, 3]\) the Lennard-Jones potential varies only between \(-1\) and \(2\) and is fitted well already with a few nodes; closer to \(r = 0.9\) the wall would grow much faster and the fit would become harder.


8.2 Experiments with the settings
The cell below lets you repeat these fits with your own settings. Change the settings and run it. In Colab the comments # @param turn into a form with drop-down lists and sliders on the right side of the cell; outside Colab they are ordinary comments and the values are changed by editing the lines.
Suggested experiments: 1. For each target find the smallest \(N\) for which the fit looks good. How does it depend on the target? 2. Compare tanh with ReLU for |x| and for the wave packet. 3. Take K = 8 sampling points and N = 16 nodes. Does a small loss mean a good approximation of \(g\) between the points? 4. Switch the optimiser to SGD or Adam and compare the loss curves with LBFGS. 5. Add a new target function to the TARGETS dictionary, e.g. in a new cell TARGETS["my function"] = (lambda x: x * np.sin(3 * x), (-2, 2)), and set target_name = "my function" by editing the line (the drop-down list shows only the names listed in the # @param comment).


Code

N1 = 4                        # @param {type:"slider", min:1, max:64, step:1}

K = 40                        # @param {type:"slider", min:4, max:200, step:1}

plot_approximations(func, interval, N_list=[N1, N2, N3], K=K, activation=activation,
                    optimizer=optimizer, sampling=sampling, seed=seed,

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
9. Non-convex loss landscape
Sections 7 and 8 already showed that the final loss depends on the starting point. The reason is that \(\mathcal L(\vec\theta)\) is not convex: running the same minimiser (BFGS) from 10 random starting points gives a whole distribution of final losses. We use \(N = 6\), small enough for 10 BFGS runs (at most 1000 iterations each) to take only seconds, and large enough for the final losses to spread over several orders of magnitude (from about \(10^{-6}\) to \(3\cdot10^{-3}\) here).


Code
N = 6
finals, thetas = [], []
for seed in range(10):       # 10 starts keep the cell fast; 30 or more give a smoother histogram
    # seeds 100..109: starting points different from those of Section 7 (the value 100 is arbitrary)
    r = minimize(loss, init_theta(N, seed=100 + seed), jac=grad, method="BFGS", options={"maxiter": 1000, "gtol": 1e-8})
    finals.append(r.fun); thetas.append(r.x)
finals = np.array(finals)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.hist(np.log10(finals), bins=10)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\log_{10}$ of final loss"); ax.set_ylabel("number of runs")
ax.set_title(f"BFGS from {len(finals)} random starts, N = {N}")
plt.show()





Different final losses alone do not yet prove that the minima are separated by barriers. To see a barrier directly, we take the best solution \(\vec\theta_A\) and a worse one \(\vec\theta_B\), and evaluate the loss along the straight line between them, \(\mathcal L\big((1-t)\vec\theta_A + t\vec\theta_B\big)\). If the landscape were convex, this curve could not have a maximum between the two minima.


Code
order = np.argsort(finals)
theta_A, theta_B = thetas[order[0]], thetas[order[len(order) // 2]]   # best and median run
ts = np.linspace(-0.2, 1.2, 281)          # step 0.005: the grid contains t = 0 and t = 1 exactly
# t < 0 and t > 1 are included to show that the loss also rises on the outer side of each minimum
path_loss = [loss((1 - t) * theta_A + t * theta_B) for t in ts]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.semilogy(ts, path_loss)
ax.axvline(0, color="C2", ls=":", label=r"$\theta_A$ (best)")
ax.axvline(1, color="C3", ls=":", label=r"$\theta_B$ (median)")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\mathcal{L}((1-t)\theta_A + t\theta_B)$"); ax.legend()
plt.show()





There is a barrier between the two minima. The valleys around the minima are very narrow (the parameters have large values, so a small relative change of \(\vec\theta\) changes \(f\) strongly); this is why the curve must be evaluated exactly at \(t=0\) and \(t=1\) to show the minimal losses. Part of the multiplicity of minima is trivial: permuting the \(N\) neurons, or flipping the signs \((W^{(1)}_i, b_i, W^{(2)}_i)\to(-W^{(1)}_i, -b_i, -W^{(2)}_i)\) (since \(\tanh\) is odd), does not change \(f\). A generic minimum therefore has \(N!\,2^N\) equivalent copies (\(N!\) orderings of the neurons times two signs for each of them), fewer if some neurons are identical.

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
10. Extrapolation outside the training interval
The UAT and all our fits concern the interval \([-2, 2]\) on which the network was trained. We now evaluate the network fitted there on the wider interval \([-4, 4]\) and compare it with \(g\).


Code
x_wide = np.linspace(-4, 4, 800)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(x_wide, g(x_wide), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
for N in [4, 8, 12]:
    ax.plot(x_wide, model(best_theta[N], x_wide), label=f"network, $N = {N}$")
ax.axvspan(-2, 2, color="gray", alpha=0.15, label="training interval")
ax.set_ylim(-20, 20); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$g(x)$, $f(x)$"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.show()





Outside the training interval the network continues the trend of its outermost neurons and, far away, tends to a constant once all \(\tanh\) saturate; it has no information about the oscillations of \(g\). The UAT is a statement about a compact set, and the network has learned the data, not the formula for \(g(x)\): it interpolates, but it does not extrapolate. The same limitation applies whenever a network is applied to physical parameters outside its training range.

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
11. Summary
A network with one hidden layer is a weighted sum of shifted and stretched \(\tanh\) steps; pairs of steps make bumps, and sums of bumps approximate any continuous function. The UAT guarantees that good parameters exist, but finding them is a non-convex minimisation of \(\mathcal L(\vec\theta)\), and different initialisations lead to different minima.
The minimisers differ in what they need and how they scale. Gradient-free methods need no derivatives but scale badly. Finite-difference gradients cost \(\mathcal O(\dim\vec\theta)\) evaluations, a number proportional to the number of parameters, while backpropagation (autograd) gives the exact gradient at the cost of a few evaluations of \(\mathcal L\), independently of \(\dim\vec\theta\). For small smooth problems quasi-Newton methods (BFGS, L-BFGS) are very effective; for large networks and mini-batches, first-order methods (SGD, Adam) are used.
Finally, a fitted network interpolates between its training points; it does not extrapolate beyond them.

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
12. Exercises

Exercise 1 — Activation functions
Repeat the experiment of Section 7, with an additional output bias \(c\), for three activations: \(\tanh\), the sigmoid \(1/(1+e^{-z})\) and the rectified linear unit ReLU \(\max(0,z)\). Use PyTorch with Adam (lr=1e-2, 1000 steps; more steps give lower losses but take longer), \(N\in\{4, 8, 16\}\), and plot the final loss vs. \(N\) for each activation. Plot the ReLU fit for \(N = 8\) and describe what kind of function it is.

Solution


Code
activations = {name: ACTIVATIONS[name] for name in ["tanh", "sigmoid", "ReLU"]}   # from Section 8

def fit_adam(N, act, n_steps=1000, lr=1e-2, seed=0):
    """Fit f(x) = sum_i W2_i act(W1_i x + b_i) + c with Adam; return the final loss and the parameters."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    # the initialisation of Section 4 (input x in [-2, 2], not rescaled as in fit_uat)
    W1 = (2 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()
    b = (2 * torch.randn(N)).requires_grad_()
    W2 = (torch.randn(N) / N**0.5).requires_grad_()
    c = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)          # output bias: sigmoid and ReLU are not odd, a shift helps
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([W1, b, W2, c], lr=lr)
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        pred = act(xt[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c
        L = torch.mean((pred - yt)**2)
        L.backward()
        opt.step()
    return L.item(), (W1, b, W2, c)

Ns_act = [4, 8, 16]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
for name, act in activations.items():
    losses = [fit_adam(N, act)[0] for N in Ns_act]
    print(f"{name:8s} final losses for N = {Ns_act}: " + ", ".join(f"{L:.1e}" for L in losses))
    axes[0].semilogy(Ns_act, losses, "o-", label=name)
axes[0].set_xlabel("$N$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("final loss"); axes[0].legend()

# the ReLU network is piecewise linear: N kinks at x = -b_i / W1_i
_, (W1, b, W2, c) = fit_adam(8, torch.relu)
with torch.no_grad():
    xp = torch.tensor(x_plot)
    f_relu = (torch.relu(xp[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c).numpy()      # ReLU network on the dense grid
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=3, alpha=0.4, label="$g(x)$")
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, f_relu, label="ReLU network, N = 8")
    kinks = (-b / W1).numpy()
    kinks = kinks[(kinks > -2) & (kinks < 2)]
    axes[1].plot(kinks, np.interp(kinks, x_plot, f_relu),
                 "rx", ms=10, label="kinks $x = -b_i/W^{(1)}_i$")
axes[1].legend(); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# tanh gives the lowest loss for every N. All losses (printed above) are of order 1e-2 to 1e-1, far above the BFGS
# results of Section 7: 1000 Adam steps are not enough to converge, which is also why the loss does not always
# decrease with N (tanh, N = 8 vs N = 4). The ReLU fit is piecewise linear: straight segments joined at the kinks.


tanh     final losses for N = [4, 8, 16]: 6.5e-02, 7.2e-02, 3.1e-02


sigmoid  final losses for N = [4, 8, 16]: 1.2e-01, 1.1e-01, 4.6e-02


ReLU     final losses for N = [4, 8, 16]: 2.2e-01, 1.0e-01, 5.4e-02








Exercise 2 — Noisy data and overfitting
Real data are noisy and scarce. Generate \(K=20\) training points \(y_k = g(x_k) + \xi_k\), \(\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0, \sigma_\xi^2)\) with noise standard deviation \(\sigma_\xi = 0.3\), with \(x_k\) uniformly random in \([-2,2]\), and a separate validation set of 200 noisy points. 1. Fit networks with \(N \in\{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}\) using BFGS (with the functions loss and grad, passing the data through args=). minimize calls loss(theta, *args) and grad(theta, *args); so far args was not given and the default arguments x=x_train, y=y_train were used. 2. Plot the training and the validation loss vs. \(N\). 3. Plot the fits for a small and for the largest \(N\) and explain the result. (This is the starting point of the next lecture: regularisation.)

Solution


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
noise = 0.3
x_tr = np.sort(rng.uniform(-2, 2, 20)); y_tr = g(x_tr) + noise * rng.normal(size=20)
x_val = rng.uniform(-2, 2, 200);        y_val = g(x_val) + noise * rng.normal(size=200)

Ns_of = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]
train_loss, val_loss, fits = [], [], {}
for N in Ns_of:
    # best of 3 starts, judged on the TRAINING loss (the validation set must not be used for fitting).
    # At most 2000 iterations per run (for speed). The networks with N >= 16 nevertheless pass through
    # all 20 points: their training losses are of order 1e-12 or smaller.
    runs = [minimize(loss, init_theta(N, s), args=(x_tr, y_tr), jac=grad, method="BFGS",
                     options={"maxiter": 2000}) for s in range(3)]
    best = min(runs, key=lambda r: r.fun)
    fits[N] = best.x
    train_loss.append(best.fun)
    val_loss.append(loss(best.x, x_val, y_val))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.2))
axes[0].loglog(Ns_of, train_loss, "o-", label="training loss")
axes[0].loglog(Ns_of, val_loss, "s-", label="validation loss")
axes[0].axhline(noise**2, color="gray", ls=":", label=r"noise variance $0.3^2$")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$N$"); axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=2, alpha=0.4, label="$g(x)$ (unknown in practice)")
axes[1].plot(x_tr, y_tr, "o", color="k", label="training data")
for N in [4, 64]:
    axes[1].plot(x_plot, model(fits[N], x_plot), label=f"N = {N}")
axes[1].set_ylim(-6, 6); axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for N, tr, va in zip(Ns_of, train_loss, val_loss):
    print(f"N = {N:3d}:  training loss = {tr:.1e},  validation loss = {va:.1e}")
print("smallest validation loss at N =", Ns_of[int(np.argmin(val_loss))])
# The training loss decreases with N and drops far below the noise variance 0.3^2 = 0.09: a large network
# passes through the 20 noisy points and oscillates strongly between them. The validation loss is smallest for a
# small network (printed above) and becomes orders of magnitude larger for large N: overfitting.
# The validation loss is not monotonic in N: it peaks at N = 8 (5.4e+03) and is lower again for N = 16, 32 (about 2e+02).
# Even its smallest value (0.8 at N = 2) is well above the noise variance 0.09, so none of these fits reproduces g closely.

N =   4:  training loss = 4.4e-02,  validation loss = 8.3e-01
N =   8:  training loss = 8.1e-03,  validation loss = 5.4e+03
N =  16:  training loss = 5.6e-13,  validation loss = 2.3e+02
N =  32:  training loss = 3.4e-12,  validation loss = 2.1e+02

Exercise 3 — Learning-rate scan
For \(N=10\) and the common start \(\vec\theta_0\), run SGD and Adam for 1000 steps with learning rates \(\eta\in\{10^{-4}, 10^{-3}, \dots, 1\}\) (use np.logspace(-4, 0, 5); a finer scan with np.logspace(-4, 0, 9) and 2000 steps takes about 3.5 times longer) and plot the final loss vs. \(\eta\) (log-log). Mark runs that diverged (nan or inf). Determine which optimiser is less sensitive to the choice of \(\eta\).

Solution


Code
lrs = np.logspace(-4, 0, 5)          # 5 values and 1000 steps keep the cell fast; 9 values and 2000 steps give a finer picture
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for i, opt_name in enumerate(["SGD", "Adam"]):
    finals = np.array([run_torch(opt_name, 1000, lr=lr)["final_loss"] for lr in lrs])
    ok = np.isfinite(finals) & (finals < 1e3)           # diverged: nan/inf, or far above the initial loss of about 1
    # ~ok is the element-wise NOT of the boolean array: True for the diverged runs; np.full(n, 1e1) is an array of n values 10
    ax.loglog(lrs[ok], finals[ok], "o-", color=f"C{i}", label=opt_name)
    ax.loglog(lrs[~ok], np.full((~ok).sum(), 1e1), "x", color=f"C{i}", ms=12)   # crosses at an arbitrary height 10
ax.set_xlabel(r"learning rate $\eta$"); ax.set_ylabel("final loss (x = diverged)")
ax.legend(); plt.show()
# SGD converges slowly for small eta and diverges once eta exceeds a threshold (the crosses).
# Adam divides each step by the square root of a running average of the squared gradient, so its step length is
# about eta independently of the size of the gradient; it does not diverge in the scanned range and reaches much
# lower losses, with an optimum at an intermediate eta.








Exercise 4 — A network as a surrogate for a quantum calculation
The ground-state energy \(E_0(\kappa)\) of the double well \(V = \tfrac12x^2 + \kappa e^{-x^2/2}\) can be computed by exact diagonalisation of the finite-difference Hamiltonian. Suppose each diagonalisation were expensive and we could afford only 12 of them. 1. Compute \(E_0(\kappa_j)\) for 12 randomly chosen \(\kappa_j\in[0, 12]\) (the first lines of the solution build the data; you may copy them). 2. Fit a one-hidden-layer network (\(N=8\), \(\tanh\), with output bias) to these 12 points, in PyTorch with L-BFGS. Rescale the input to \([-1,1]\) first. 3. Compare the network with the exact \(E_0(\kappa)\) on a fine grid of 100 points. 4. Use autograd on the network to get \(dE_0/d\kappa\) and compare with the exact derivative (Hellmann–Feynman). Is the derivative of a good fit also a good approximation of the derivative?

Solution


Code
xg = np.linspace(-6, 6, 300); dxg = xg[1] - xg[0]
H_kin = -0.5 / dxg**2 * (np.diag(np.ones(299), 1) - 2 * np.eye(300) + np.diag(np.ones(299), -1))
def E0_and_dE0(kappa):
    """Exact ground-state energy and its derivative (Hellmann-Feynman) for barrier height kappa."""
    E, psi = np.linalg.eigh(H_kin + np.diag(0.5 * xg**2 + kappa * np.exp(-xg**2 / 2)))
    # Hellmann-Feynman: dE0/dkappa = <psi0| dH/dkappa |psi0> with dH/dkappa = exp(-x^2/2).
    # eigh normalises sum(psi**2) = 1, so the expectation value is a plain sum (no factor dx).
    return E[0], np.sum(psi[:, 0]**2 * np.exp(-xg**2 / 2))

# 1) the 12 "expensive" data points and a fine reference grid
k_train = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(3).uniform(0, 12, 12))     # 12 random, non-equidistant points
E_train = np.array([E0_and_dE0(k)[0] for k in k_train])
k_fine = np.linspace(0, 12, 100)
# the list of 100 pairs (E0, dE0) becomes an array of shape (100, 2); .T gives shape (2, 100), whose two rows are unpacked
E_fine, dE_fine = np.array([E0_and_dE0(k) for k in k_fine]).T

# 2) network with output bias; input rescaled from [0, 12] to [-1, 1]
to_unit = lambda k: (k - 6.0) / 6.0
torch.manual_seed(0)
N = 8
# standard deviation 1 (an arbitrary choice): on the rescaled input [-1, 1] it already places the steps inside the interval
W1, b, W2 = torch.randn(N, requires_grad=True), torch.randn(N, requires_grad=True), torch.randn(N, requires_grad=True)
c = torch.tensor([E_train.mean()], requires_grad=True)
net = lambda k: torch.tanh(to_unit(k)[:, None] * W1 + b) @ W2 + c

kt, Et = torch.tensor(k_train), torch.tensor(E_train)
opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([W1, b, W2, c], lr=1, max_iter=50, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")
def closure():
    opt.zero_grad()
    L = torch.mean((net(kt) - Et)**2)
    L.backward()
    return L
for _ in range(10):          # with 25 parameters and 12 points the loss stops changing after 5 outer steps
    L = opt.step(closure)
print(f"training loss: {L.item():.2e}")

# 3) and 4) prediction and its derivative on the fine grid (autograd w.r.t. the INPUT kappa)
kf = torch.tensor(k_fine, requires_grad=True)
E_pred = net(kf)
# E_pred[j] depends only on kf[j], so the gradient of the SUM w.r.t. kf is the vector of derivatives dE_pred[j]/dkappa_j.
# torch.autograd.grad returns a tuple (one entry per input); (dE_pred,) = ... unpacks its single element.
(dE_pred,) = torch.autograd.grad(E_pred.sum(), kf)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
axes[0].plot(k_fine, E_fine, "k", lw=2, label="exact")
axes[0].plot(k_fine, E_pred.detach(), "--", label="network")
axes[0].plot(k_train, E_train, "o", color="C3", label="12 training points")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$E_0(\kappa)$"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].semilogy(k_fine, np.abs(E_pred.detach().numpy() - E_fine))
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$|E_0^{\rm net} - E_0^{\rm exact}|$")
axes[2].plot(k_fine, dE_fine, "k", lw=2, label="exact (Hellmann-Feynman)")
axes[2].plot(k_fine, dE_pred, "--", label="autograd of the network")
axes[2].set_ylabel(r"$dE_0/d\kappa$"); axes[2].legend()
for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel(r"$\kappa$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
inside = (k_fine >= k_train.min()) & (k_fine <= k_train.max())     # between the smallest and largest training kappa
err_E, err_dE = np.abs(E_pred.detach().numpy() - E_fine), np.abs(dE_pred.numpy() - dE_fine)
print(f"training kappa from {k_train.min():.2f} to {k_train.max():.2f}")
print(f"max error of E0 :  inside {err_E[inside].max():.1e},  outside {err_E[~inside].max():.1e}")
print(f"max error of dE0:  inside {err_dE[inside].max():.1e},  outside {err_dE[~inside].max():.1e}")
# Between the smallest and largest training kappa (interpolation) the errors are much smaller than outside the
# sampled range (extrapolation, see Section 10). Inside, the derivative is less accurate than the energy itself:
# the loss contains only values of E0, nothing constrains the slope directly. The network has 25 parameters
# for 12 data points, so it can pass through all of them; the fit is nevertheless smooth here because E0(kappa)
# itself is smooth. (Adding the Hellmann-Feynman derivatives to the loss is known as Sobolev training.)


training loss: 6.09e-07





training kappa from 1.03 to 9.62
max error of E0 :  inside 2.1e-03,  outside 7.8e-02
max error of dE0:  inside 1.5e-02,  outside 1.5e-01





Exercise 5 (advanced) — Two dimensions
The UAT holds in any dimension. Fit \(g(x,y) = \sin(2x)\cos(y) e^{-(x^2+y^2)/4}\) on \([-3,3]^2\) (a \(30\times30\) grid of training points) with nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, N), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(N, 1)) for \(N = 8, 32, 128\), using Adam (lr=1e-2, 1500 steps; kept small for speed, 3000 or more steps give smaller errors). Here nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) is the affine map \(\mathbf W\mathbf x + \mathbf b\) from \(n_{\rm in}\) to \(n_{\rm out}\) components (with trainable \(\mathbf W\) and \(\mathbf b\)), and nn.Sequential chains the layers, applying them one after another. Show the target, the fit and the error as images (imshow), one row per \(N\). The first lines of the solution build the data (you may copy them): torch.meshgrid(xs, xs, indexing="xy") returns two \(30\times30\) arrays X, Y with the \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates of all grid points (with "xy" the rows correspond to \(y\), the layout that imshow expects), and reshape(-1) flattens them into lists of 900 points.

Solution


Code
import torch.nn as nn
n_grid = 30
xs = torch.linspace(-3, 3, n_grid)
X, Y = torch.meshgrid(xs, xs, indexing="xy")
G = torch.sin(2 * X) * torch.cos(Y) * torch.exp(-(X**2 + Y**2) / 4)
inputs = torch.stack([X.reshape(-1), Y.reshape(-1)], dim=1)   # shape (900, 2): each row is a point (x, y)
targets = G.reshape(-1, 1)                                    # shape (900, 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(12, 11))
for row, N in enumerate([8, 32, 128]):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    # nn.Linear creates its weights and biases with PyTorch's default random initialisation (scaled by 1/sqrt(n_in))
    net2d = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, N), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(N, 1))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net2d.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    for _ in range(1500):
        opt.zero_grad()
        L = torch.mean((net2d(inputs) - targets)**2)
        L.backward()
        opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        F_net = net2d(inputs).reshape(n_grid, n_grid)
    for ax, img, title in zip(axes[row], [G, F_net, F_net - G],
                              ["target", f"network N = {N}", f"error, MSE = {L.item():.1e}"]):
        im = ax.imshow(img, origin="lower", extent=[-3, 3, -3, 3], cmap="RdBu_r")
        fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
        ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# The error decreases from N = 8 to N = 32; beyond that the result is limited by the 1500 Adam steps, not by N
# (N = 32 and N = 128 give the same MSE).

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
section: 1. Notation: a network as a composition of layers
text:
1. Notation: a network as a composition of layers
A fully connected (dense) network with layer sizes \(n_0, n_1, \dots, n_L\) maps an input \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}\) to an output in \(\mathbb R^{n_L}\) through \[\mathbf h^{(0)} = \mathbf x,\qquad \mathbf h^{(l)} = \sigma\big(\mathbf W^{(l)}\mathbf h^{(l-1)} + \mathbf b^{(l)}\big),\quad l = 1,\dots,L-1,\qquad
f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf W^{(L)}\mathbf h^{(L-1)} + \mathbf b^{(L)} .\] Here \(\mathbf W^{(l)}\) is a matrix of shape \(n_l\times n_{l-1}\) and \(\mathbf b^{(l)}\) a vector of length \(n_l\), so layer \(l\) has \(n_l(n_{l-1}+1)\) parameters. The activation \(\sigma\) is applied element-wise in the hidden layers. The last layer usually has no activation (regression), or one adapted to the task, e.g. softmax for classification, which in PyTorch is usually applied inside the loss function rather than as a layer (see Section 14.2).
In PyTorch one layer \(\mathbf h \mapsto \mathbf W\mathbf h + \mathbf b\) is nn.Linear(n_in, n_out); it stores weight with shape (n_out, n_in) and bias with shape (n_out,). Data are processed in batches: an input tensor has shape (B, n_0), one row per sample, and the output has shape (B, n_L). For a batch the layer computes H_out = H_in @ W.T + b. The transpose appears because every sample is a row of H_in: the row form of \(\mathbf h_{\rm out} = \mathbf W\mathbf h_{\rm in} + \mathbf b\) is \(\mathbf h_{\rm out}^T = \mathbf h_{\rm in}^T\mathbf W^T + \mathbf b^T\), applied to all rows at once.
The list \([n_0, n_1, \dots, n_L]\) together with the choice of \(\sigma\) is the architecture of the network.

title: Lab 007: Building and training neural networks
text:
2. Drawing a network
Every architecture in this notebook is drawn with the functions below. A drawing helps only if we know how it is made, so the code is short and commented, and it is worth reading and changing. A dense network is fixed by its list of layer sizes \([n_0, n_1, \dots, n_L]\). Each layer becomes a vertical column of circles, one circle per node (neuron), with neighbouring circles one unit apart, and layer \(l\) is placed at the horizontal position \(l\,\Delta x\). The weights of the Linear layer between two columns become thin, semi-transparent grey lines, one from every node of the first column to every node of the second, so that between columns of \(n_{l-1}\) and \(n_l\) circles there are \(n_{l-1}n_l\) lines, as many as weights. The biases are not drawn.
Wide layers cannot be drawn node by node, since 784 circles do not fit on a page. Up to max_nodes nodes (8 by default) every node is drawn. A wider layer gets max_nodes circles plus growth \(=1.5\) circles for every doubling of its width; three dots in the middle of the column stand for the omitted nodes, and the true width is written under the column. The height of a column therefore still grows with the width of the layer, logarithmically: a layer of 16 nodes is drawn with 10 circles, 64 with 12, 256 with 16 and 784 with 18. A network whose layers become narrower, such as the image classifier of Example D, also looks narrower in the drawing.
The first cell contains the building blocks. nodes_shown decides how many circles a layer gets, draw_layer draws one column and returns the heights of its circles, connect draws the lines between two columns (every pair of nodes for a dense layer, only the pairs \(j\to j\) for an element-wise operation), bracket marks a group of layers, and finish sets equal scales on both axes, so that circles stay round, and a figure size proportional to the drawing.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Rectangle
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection

SCALE = 0.42          # inches of figure per drawing unit; neighbouring nodes of a layer are 1 unit apart
NODE_COLORS = {"input": "#8A929E", "hidden": "#005CA7", "latent": "#D35A05", "output": "#002B5C",
               "cond": "#2E8B57", "noise": "#F2B28A"}


def text_height(fontsize, lines=1):
    """Height of `lines` lines of text of the given font size, in drawing units (used to place labels)."""
    return lines * 1.25 * fontsize / 72 / SCALE


def nodes_shown(n, max_nodes=8, growth=1.5):
    """Number of circles drawn for a layer of width n.
    Up to max_nodes every node is drawn. A wider layer gets max_nodes circles plus `growth` circles for every
    doubling of its width, so the column height still grows with the width: with the defaults a layer of
    16 nodes is drawn with 10 circles, 64 with 12, 256 with 16 and 784 with 18."""
    if n <= max_nodes:
        return n
    return max_nodes + int(round(growth * np.log2(n / max_nodes)))


def draw_layer(ax, x, n, y0=0.0, color=NODE_COLORS["hidden"], max_nodes=8, growth=1.5, r=0.32,
               top=None, bottom=None, show_width=True, fontsize=12):
    """Draw one layer of width n as a vertical column of circles at horizontal position x, centred at height y0.
    Returns the heights of the drawn circles, from top to bottom (needed to draw the edges).

    The circles are 1 unit apart. If the layer is wider than the number of circles (see nodes_shown), one slot
    in the middle of the column stays empty and gets three dots, which stand for the omitted nodes; the true
    width n is then the number written under the column. `top` and `bottom` are optional texts above and below."""
    k = nodes_shown(n, max_nodes, growth)
    capped = k < n
    slots = k + 1 if capped else k                         # one extra slot for the dots
    y = y0 + (slots - 1) / 2 - np.arange(slots)            # heights of the slots, from top to bottom
    if capped:
        mid = slots // 2
        ax.scatter([x] * 3, y[mid] + np.array([-0.25, 0.0, 0.25]), s=6, color="k", zorder=3)
        y = np.delete(y, mid)                              # no circle in the dotted slot
    for yi in y:
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, yi), r, facecolor=color, edgecolor="k", lw=0.8, zorder=3))
    under = (f"{n}" if show_width else "") + (f"\n{bottom}" if bottom else "")
    if under.strip():
        ax.text(x, y0 - (slots - 1) / 2 - 0.55, under.strip("\n"), ha="center", va="top", fontsize=fontsize, linespacing=1.1)
    if top:
        ax.text(x, y0 + (slots - 1) / 2 + 0.55, top, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fontsize, linespacing=1.1)
    return y


def connect(ax, x0, y0, x1, y1, one_to_one=False, color="0.45", alpha=0.35, lw=0.6, ls="-"):
    """Edges between two drawn layers at horizontal positions x0 and x1, whose circles are at heights y0 and y1.
    A dense layer joins every node to every node, one line per weight; an elementwise operation joins
    node j only to node j (one_to_one=True). The lines are thin and semi-transparent, and are drawn
    below the circles (zorder), so they seem to end at the circle boundaries."""
    pairs = zip(y0, y1) if one_to_one else [(a, b) for a in y0 for b in y1]
    segments = [[(x0, a), (x1, b)] for a, b in pairs]
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segments, colors=color, alpha=alpha, linewidths=lw, linestyles=ls, zorder=1))


def bracket(ax, x0, x1, y, text, color="k", fontsize=12):
    """A horizontal bracket from x0 to x1 at height y with a text above it; it marks a block of layers."""
    ax.plot([x0, x0, x1, x1], [y - 0.3, y, y, y - 0.3], color=color, lw=1.5)
    ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y + 0.2, text, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fontsize, color=color)


def finish(ax, title="", fontsize=12):
    """Equal scales on both axes (circles stay round), no axes, and a figure size proportional to the drawing."""
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.autoscale_view()
    ax.axis("off")
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=fontsize)
    (x0, x1), (y0, y1) = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()
    ax.figure.set_size_inches(SCALE * (x1 - x0) + 1.0, SCALE * (y1 - y0) + 1.2)
