10, 12   2.27050963      +1.32e-03     (13.8 s)
exact T_c = 2.26918531


The crossings approach \(T_c\) quickly, the deviation shrinking from \(1.86\times10^{-2}\) for the pair \((4,6)\) to \(1.32\times10^{-3}\) for \((10,12)\). With matrices of size at most \(2^{12}\times2^{12}\) we obtain \(T_c\) to about three digits, free of Monte Carlo noise. For \(L = 50\) the matrix would have \(2^{50}\approx10^{15}\) rows, which no computer can diagonalise. Onsager’s achievement was to find \(\lambda_0\) analytically for every \(L\) (Section 6).


3.3 One and two dimensions
The strips let us see directly why 2D differs from 1D. The 1D chain has \(\xi = -1/\ln\tanh K\), finite at every \(T>0\), and its specific heat \(K^2/\cosh^2K\) is one smooth bump. In 2D the strip correlation lengths grow without bound below \(T_c\), and above \(T_c\) they converge to the exact 2D correlation length along a lattice axis, \(\xi = 1/[2(K^*-K)]\), with \(K^*\) the dual coupling defined by \(e^{-2K^*}=\tanh K\) (the formula is derived and checked in Sections 5 and 6.1). This \(\xi\) diverges at \(T_c\), where \(K^*=K\).
A simple balance of energy against entropy explains the difference. Start from an open 1D chain of \(N\) spins, all up. Breaking one bond, that is inserting one domain wall, costs energy \(2J\), and the wall can sit at any of \(N-1\) positions, which is an entropy \(\ln(N-1)\). The free-energy change \(\Delta F = 2J - T\ln(N-1)\) is negative once \(N-1>e^{2J/T}\), so at any \(T>0\) a long enough chain breaks into domains, of typical length \(\sim e^{2K}\), in line with \(\xi\approx\frac12e^{2K}\) from Section 2.1.
In 2D a domain of flipped spins is bounded by a closed wall, and a wall of length \(\ell\) (number of broken bonds) costs \(2J\ell\) — an energy proportional to its length, not a constant. The number of closed walls of length \(\ell\) through a given bond is at most the number of lattice paths of \(\ell\) steps that never immediately step back, \(4\cdot3^{\ell-1}\). The entropy is therefore at most about \(\ell\ln3\), and \(\Delta F\gtrsim\ell\,(2J-T\ln3)\), which is positive for \(T<2J/\ln3\approx1.82\). Large flipped domains are suppressed and the order survives at low \(T\). This is the idea of Peierls’ argument [Peierls 1936; rigorous form: Griffiths 1964]; it gives a lower bound on the ordering temperature, consistent with \(T_c\approx2.269>1.82\).
The next cell evaluates these numbers — the temperature above which one wall lowers \(F\) for chains of \(10\), \(10^3\) and \(10^6\) spins drops towards zero as the chain grows, while the 2D bound stays at \(1.8205\) — and plots \(\xi\) and \(c\) for 1D and 2D side by side.


Code
# 1D chain versus 2D strips: correlation length and specific heat
for Nch in (10, 10**3, 10**6):
    print(f"1D chain, N = {Nch:>7d}: one domain wall lowers F (Delta F = 2 - T ln(N-1) < 0) for T > {2/np.log(Nch-1):.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax[0].plot(Tq, xi_1d, color=DSOrange, lw=2, label="1D chain (exact)")
for i, L in enumerate(Ls):

ax[0].set_yscale("log"); ax[0].set_ylim(0.3, 300); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"correlation length $\xi$")
ax[0].set_title("1D: finite for all T > 0;  2D: diverges at $T_c$")
ax[1].plot(Tq, 1 / Tq**2 / np.cosh(1 / Tq)**2, color=DSOrange, lw=2, label="1D chain (exact)")
for i, L in enumerate(Ls):
    ax[1].plot(Tgrid[2:-2], strip[L]["c"][2:-2], color=blues(i / (len(Ls) - 1)), lw=1.5, label=f"2D strip L = {L}")
ax[1].set_ylabel("specific heat per spin $c$"); ax[1].set_title("1D: one fixed bump;  2D: a peak growing with L")
for a in ax:
    a.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":", lw=1.2); a.set_xlabel("$T$"); a.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7)

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
4. High- and low-temperature expansions of \(Z\)
Before Onsager, the 2D model was studied through expansions of \(Z\) that are accurate far from \(T_c\), in powers of a small parameter at high \(T\) and at low \(T\). For us their value is structural: the two series turn out to count the same geometric objects, and this coincidence (Section 5) pins down \(T_c\) exactly.

4.1 High-temperature expansion and closed graphs
At high \(T\) the coupling \(K\) is small. Since \(ss'=\pm1\) and \(e^{\pm K}=\cosh K\pm\sinh K\), \[
e^{Kss'} = \cosh K + ss'\sinh K = \cosh K\,(1 + t\,ss'),\qquad t = \tanh K .
\] Inserting this for every one of the \(2N\) bonds gives \[
Z = (\cosh K)^{2N}\sum_{\mathbf s}\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle}\big(1 + t\,s_is_j\big).
\] To expand the product we pick from each bond factor either \(1\) or \(t\,s_is_j\). A choice is a subset \(G\) of bonds, those where \(t\,s_is_j\) was picked, and it contributes \(t^{|G|}\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle\in G}s_is_j = t^{|G|}\prod_i s_i^{d_i(G)}\), where \(d_i(G)\) is the number of bonds of \(G\) touching site \(i\). Summing over the spins now removes most subsets: \(\sum_{s=\pm1}s^d\) equals \(2\) for even \(d\) and \(0\) for odd \(d\), so a subset survives only if every site has an even number of its bonds, that is, if \(G\) is a closed graph (a union of closed loops). Hence \[
Z = 2^N(\cosh K)^{2N}\sum_{\text{closed } G}t^{|G|} = 2^N(\cosh K)^{2N}\big(1 + N t^4 + 2N t^6 + \dots\big).
\] The smallest closed graph is the boundary of one plaquette (4 bonds; there are \(N\) plaquettes), and the next is the boundary of a \(1\times2\) rectangle (6 bonds; \(N\) horizontal and \(N\) vertical ones).


4.2 Low-temperature expansion and domain walls
At low \(T\) almost all spins are parallel. Starting from all spins up, \(E_0 = -2N\), a configuration with \(b\) broken bonds has \(E=-2N+2b\) (Section 1.1) and hence the weight \(e^{2NK}x^{b}\) with \(x = e^{-2K}\), small at low \(T\). Draw a short segment across each broken bond. These segments live on the dual lattice, whose sites are the centres of the plaquettes. Going around a plaquette the spin returns to its starting value, so it changes sign an even number of times, and every dual site touches an even number of segments. The broken bonds therefore form closed graphs on the dual lattice — the domain walls. Each wall pattern comes from exactly two spin configurations, \(\mathbf s\) and \(-\mathbf s\), so \[
Z = 2e^{2NK}\sum_{\text{closed walls } W}x^{|W|} = 2e^{2NK}\big(1 + N x^4 + 2N x^6 + \dots\big):
\] one flipped spin breaks 4 bonds (\(N\) ways), and a flipped neighbouring pair breaks 6 bonds (\(2N\) ways).
The sketch below places the two expansions side by side. On the left are the two smallest closed graphs, the boundary of one plaquette (4 bonds, weight \(t^4\)) and of a \(1\times2\) rectangle (6 bonds, weight \(t^6\)); the spins have been summed out, so only the bonds matter. On the right are the two smallest excitations of the all-up state, one flipped spin and two flipped neighbours. Each broken bond is crossed by a segment of the dual lattice (dotted), and these segments form a closed domain wall of length 4 (weight \(x^4\)) or 6 (weight \(x^6\)). The shapes are the same on both sides.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,
# and shown here at a higher screen resolution.
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

NAVY, ORANGE, BLUE, GRAY, PURPLE, GREEN = "#002B5C", "#D35A05", "#005CA7", "#5A6270", "#AA3377", "#228833"
SKETCH_STYLE = {"font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11, "xtick.labelsize": 10,
                "ytick.labelsize": 10, "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 130, "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
                "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):
    # PNG copy for the lecture slides: white background, 300 dpi, included at its physical width
    os.makedirs("../beamer/figures", exist_ok=True)
    for d in ("../beamer/figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.26, sign=False, alpha=1.0, fs=10, lw=1.3):
    # one Ising spin at (x, y): navy disc for s = +1, white disc with orange rim for s = -1 (optionally with "+" / "-")
    face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if s > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x, y), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=lw, alpha=alpha, zorder=4))
    if sign:
        ax.text(x, y, "+" if s > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", alpha=alpha,
                fontsize=fs, fontweight="bold", zorder=5)

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):
    # bond between points p and q: solid blue if satisfied, dashed purple with a cross if broken
    c = color or (PURPLE if broken else BLUE)
    ax.plot([p[0], q[0]], [p[1], q[1]], color=c, lw=lw, ls=(0, (2.5, 1.5)) if broken else "-",
            alpha=alpha, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
    if broken and cross:
        ax.plot((p[0] + q[0]) / 2, (p[1] + q[1]) / 2, marker="x", ms=3.5 * lw, mew=lw * 0.9, color=c, alpha=alpha, zorder=3)

def sketch_closed_graphs_and_walls():
    n = 4                                                           # a 4 x 4 window of the lattice in each panel
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(5.5, 2.25))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.17, top=0.86, wspace=0.1)

    def lattice(ax, dual=False):
        # sites as grey dots, bonds as thin grey lines; optionally the dual lattice (plaquette centres) dotted
        for k in range(n):
            ax.plot([0, n - 1], [k, k], color=GRAY, lw=0.7, alpha=0.4); ax.plot([k, k], [0, n - 1], color=GRAY, lw=0.7, alpha=0.4)
        if dual:
            for k in range(n + 1):
                ax.plot([-0.5, n - 0.5], [k - 0.5, k - 0.5], color=PURPLE, lw=0.6, ls=":", alpha=0.6)
                ax.plot([k - 0.5, k - 0.5], [-0.5, n - 0.5], color=PURPLE, lw=0.6, ls=":", alpha=0.6)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.8, n - 0.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.8, n - 0.2); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

    def path(ax, pts, color, lw=3):
        pts = np.array(pts + [pts[0]], float)
        ax.plot(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], color=color, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round", solid_joinstyle="round", zorder=3)

    # high temperature: closed graphs of bonds on the lattice itself, weight t^{|G|}
    for ax, loop, title in [(axes[0], [(1, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (1, 2)], "plaquette: $t^4$"),
                            (axes[1], [(0, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (0, 2)], r"$1\times2$ loop: $t^6$")]:
        lattice(ax)
        for (x, y) in [(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n)]:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=3.5, zorder=2)
        path(ax, loop, BLUE)
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11, color=NAVY)

    # low temperature: flipped spins in the all-up state; broken bonds are crossed by dual-lattice segments
    for ax, flipped, title in [(axes[2], [(1, 1)], "one spin: $x^4$"),
                               (axes[3], [(1, 1), (2, 1)], "two spins: $x^6$")]:
        lattice(ax, dual=True)
        S = {(i, j): -1 if (i, j) in flipped else 1 for i in range(n) for j in range(n)}
        for (x, y), s in S.items():
            draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.22, lw=0.9)
        xs = [p[0] for p in flipped]
        wall = [(min(xs) - 0.5, 0.5), (max(xs) + 0.5, 0.5), (max(xs) + 0.5, 1.5), (min(xs) - 0.5, 1.5)]
        path(ax, wall, PURPLE, lw=2.6)
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11, color=NAVY)

    fig.text(0.26, 0.03, r"high $T$: closed graphs, $t=\tanh K$", ha="center", fontsize=10, color=BLUE)
    fig.text(0.75, 0.03, r"low $T$: dual-lattice walls, $x=e^{-2K}$", ha="center", fontsize=10, color=PURPLE)
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_closed_graphs_and_walls()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_ising_loops_walls.png")
plt.show()





The dual of the square lattice is again a square lattice. For \(N\to\infty\) the closed graphs of 4.1 and the domain walls of 4.2 are therefore the same set, and the two series have the same coefficients, with \(t=\tanh K\) at high \(T\) playing the role of \(x=e^{-2K}\) at low \(T\).
We can count both kinds of objects on the \(4\times4\) torus using the histogram of Section 1. The low-temperature coefficients are \(n_b/2\), so we expect \(N = 16\) at \(b=4\) and \(2N = 32\) at \(b = 6\). The high-temperature coefficients, the numbers of closed graphs with \(k\) bonds, also follow exactly from the same histogram: a satisfied bond contributes \(\cosh K\,(1+t)\) and a broken one \(\cosh K\,(1-t)\), so \(\sum_G t^{|G|} = 2^{-N}\sum_b n_b(1+t)^{2N-b}(1-t)^b\), a polynomial we expand with integer arithmetic. The first cell below confirms the identity \(e^{Kss'} = \cosh K(1+ss'\tanh K)\) symbolically, and the next two do the counting.


Code
# SymPy: e^{K s s'} = cosh K (1 + s s' tanh K) for both values of s s'
K = sp.symbols("K", positive=True)
for ssp in (1, -1):
    print(f"s s' = {ssp:+d}:  e^(K s s') - cosh K (1 + s s' tanh K) =", sp.simplify((sp.exp(K * ssp) - sp.cosh(K) * (1 + ssp * sp.tanh(K))).rewrite(sp.exp)))


s s' = +1:  e^(K s s') - cosh K (1 + s s' tanh K) = 0
s s' = -1:  e^(K s s') - cosh K (1 + s s' tanh K) = 0

print(f"            n_8/2 = {dos[4][8]//2}  (here also walls that wind around the small torus contribute)")

N = 16

        for j in range(b + 1):

On the small torus the two lists differ, and the reason is instructive. A straight loop of 4 bonds that winds around the \(4\times4\) torus is a closed graph, since every site touches 0 or 2 of its bonds, but it cannot be a domain wall: walking once around the torus perpendicular to it, the spin would change sign once and could not return to its starting value. Such winding graphs have length at least \(L\), and their contribution per spin vanishes for \(N\to\infty\), where the two series coincide.
The sketch below illustrates this argument. On the left, a straight row of four bonds closes on itself through the periodic boundary: each site touches 0 or 2 of its bonds, so it is a closed graph of the high-temperature series. On the right, two straight domain walls wind around the torus. Crossing a wall flips the spin, and a spin carried once around the torus must return to its own value, so it crosses an even number of walls: a single winding wall is impossible.

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):

    c = color or (PURPLE if broken else BLUE)

            alpha=alpha, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
    if broken and cross:
        ax.plot((p[0] + q[0]) / 2, (p[1] + q[1]) / 2, marker="x", ms=3.5 * lw, mew=lw * 0.9, color=c, alpha=alpha, zorder=3)

def sketch_winding_loop():
    L = 4
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.5, 2.9))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.01, top=0.9, wspace=0.08)
    for ax in (ax1, ax2):
        for k in range(L):
            ax.plot([0, L], [k, k], color=GRAY, lw=0.7, alpha=0.4); ax.plot([k, k], [0, L - 1], color=GRAY, lw=0.7, alpha=0.4)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, L + 0.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.7, L - 0.4); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

    # (a) a closed graph that winds around the torus: the 4 horizontal bonds of row 1, the last one wrapping to the copy of column 0
    for x in range(L + 1):
        for y in range(L):
            ax1.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=4, alpha=0.35 if x == L else 1, zorder=2)
    ax1.plot([0, L], [1, 1], color=BLUE, lw=3.5, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=3)
    ax1.text(L, 1.25, "= site 1", fontsize=10, color=GRAY, va="bottom", ha="center")

    # (b) a single winding domain wall is impossible: walking around the torus across it flips the spin once,

A second test compares the leading terms with the exact free energy of the infinite lattice. Per spin, \(\frac1N\ln(1 + Nt^4 + 2Nt^6+\dots) = t^4 + 2t^6 + O(t^8)\): pairs of separate plaquettes give a term \(\approx\frac{N^2}{2}t^8\) inside the logarithm, which is cancelled by \(-\frac12(Nt^4)^2\) from \(\ln(1+y)=y-\frac{y^2}{2}+\dots\), leaving only terms proportional to \(N\). The ratios \[
\begin{aligned}
R_{\rm high}(K) &= \frac{\ln Z/N - \ln2 - 2\ln\cosh K}{t^4 + 2t^6}\xrightarrow{K\to0}1,\\
R_{\rm low}(K) &= \frac{\ln Z/N - 2K}{x^4 + 2x^6}\xrightarrow{K\to\infty}1 ,
\end{aligned}
\] with \(\ln Z/N\) taken from Onsager’s formula (Section 6), should therefore approach one in the respective limits.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
section: 5. Kramers–Wannier duality and the self-dual point
text:
5. Kramers–Wannier duality and the self-dual point
The coincidence of the two series relates the free energy at a high temperature to the free energy at a low temperature. Kramers and Wannier [1941] used it to find \(T_c\) exactly, three years before Onsager’s full solution. It is the most economical route to \(T_c\), and it explains why the modulus \(\kappa\) of Onsager’s formula takes the same value at two different temperatures.
Let \(g(y) = \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\ln\sum_G y^{|G|}\), the sum running over closed graphs. Both expansions of Section 4 contain this same function, evaluated at two different arguments: \[
\varphi(K) \equiv \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\ln Z(K)}{N} = \ln 2 + 2\ln\cosh K + g(\tanh K) = 2K + g\big(e^{-2K}\big).
\] To compare them we need a coupling at which the low-temperature argument equals the high-temperature one. Define the dual coupling \(K^*\) by \(e^{-2K^*} = \tanh K\). The low-temperature form at \(K^*\) reads \(\varphi(K^*) = 2K^* + g(e^{-2K^*}) = 2K^* + g(\tanh K)\), and subtracting the high-temperature form at \(K\) eliminates the unknown \(g\): \[
\boxed{\ \varphi(K) - \ln2 - 2\ln\cosh K = \varphi(K^*) - 2K^*\ }.
\] The free energy at \(K\) is thus fixed by the free energy at \(K^*\) plus elementary analytic functions.
The map \(K\mapsto K^*\) has simple properties. With \(t=\tanh K = e^{-2K^*}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\sinh 2K^* &= \frac{e^{2K^*}-e^{-2K^*}}{2} = \frac{1/t - t}{2} = \frac{1-t^2}{2t},\\
\sinh 2K &= \frac{2\tanh K}{1-\tanh^2K} = \frac{2t}{1-t^2}\\
\Rightarrow\quad \sinh2K\,\sinh2K^* &= 1 .
\end{aligned}
\] This relation is symmetric in \(K\) and \(K^*\), so the map is an involution, \(K^{**}=K\), and equivalently \(\tanh K^* = e^{-2K}\). It is also decreasing: a small \(K\) (hot) maps to a large \(K^*\) (cold), and vice versa.
Now comes the argument for \(T_c\). The functions \(\ln 2\), \(2\ln\cosh K\) and \(2K^*\) are analytic for \(K>0\), so if \(\varphi\) is non-analytic at some \(K_c\), the boxed identity makes it non-analytic at \(K_c^*\) as well. If the model has a single transition, the two points must coincide, \(K_c = K_c^*\): \[
\sinh^2 2K_c = 1\ \Rightarrow\ \sinh 2K_c = 1\ \Rightarrow\ e^{2K_c}-e^{-2K_c} = 2 .
\] With \(y=e^{2K_c}\) this is \(y^2-2y-1=0\), whose positive root is \(y = 1+\sqrt2\). Hence \[
K_c = \tfrac12\ln(1+\sqrt2)\approx0.4407,\qquad T_c = \frac{2}{\ln(1+\sqrt2)}\approx2.2692 .
\] The assumption of a single transition is the only gap in the argument, and Onsager’s solution closes it.
Duality also explains a property of Onsager’s formula. With \(s=\sinh2K\) we have \(\cosh^22K = 1+s^2\) and \(\kappa = 2s/(1+s^2)\). Replacing \(s\) by \(s^*=1/s\) gives \(\kappa^* = \frac{2/s}{1+1/s^2} = \frac{2s}{s^2+1} = \kappa\), so the temperatures \(T\) and \(T^*\) give the same integrand in Onsager’s formula.
We confirm all of this in three cells: first symbolically, then numerically. The checks are that (i) \(\sinh2K\sinh2K^*=1\), (ii) \(\kappa(K) = \kappa(K^*)\), (iii) the boxed identity holds for Onsager’s \(f\), (iv) the fixed point of \(K\mapsto K^*\), found by root finding, is \(K_c\), and (v) at that point \(\tanh K_c = e^{-2K_c} = \sqrt2-1\).
SymPy first verifies the properties of the dual map, the self-duality of \(\kappa\) and the solution of \(\sinh 2K = 1\); the numerical table and the root finding follow.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
6. Onsager’s formula and its consequences
Section 3 showed that the free energy of the plane is \(\lim_{L\to\infty}-\frac{T}{L}\ln\lambda_0(L)\), but numerically we could reach only \(L\approx12\). Onsager found \(\lambda_0(L)\) in closed form for every \(L\) and took the limit. The result is \[
\begin{aligned}
-\beta f &= \ln(2\cosh2K) + \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi d\phi\,\ln\Big[\tfrac12\Big(1+\sqrt{1-\kappa^2\sin^2\phi}\Big)\Big],\\
\kappa &= \frac{2\sinh2K}{\cosh^22K} .
\end{aligned}
\] Subsection 6.1 outlines the modern derivation, in which the transfer matrix becomes a problem of free fermions [Kaufman 1949; Schultz, Mattis & Lieb 1964]. We state the key equation of each stage and verify each of them numerically; the full algebra is in Schultz, Mattis & Lieb (1964) and, in open access, in Gispen (2018). Subsections 6.2 and 6.3 then interpret the result and derive the energy, the specific heat and the magnetisation.

6.1 From spins to free fermions
The derivation begins by rewriting the transfer matrix with Pauli matrices. Let \(\sigma^x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(\sigma^z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\), and let \(\sigma^a_i\) act on the spin of row \(i\) (and as the identity on the other rows). For a single row, the horizontal-bond weight \(e^{Kss'}\) is the \(2\times2\) matrix \[
\begin{pmatrix}e^K&e^{-K}\\e^{-K}&e^K\end{pmatrix} = e^K\mathbb 1 + e^{-K}\sigma^x = \sqrt{2\sinh2K}\;e^{K^*\sigma^x},
\] with \(K^*\) the dual coupling of Section 5 (the identity is proved in Exercise 3). The vertical bonds inside a column are diagonal in the spin basis. Therefore \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf V &= (2\sinh 2K)^{L/2}\;\mathsf V_2^{1/2}\,\mathsf V_1\,\mathsf V_2^{1/2},\\
\mathsf V_1 &= \exp\Big(K^*\sum_{i=1}^L\sigma^x_i\Big),\qquad \mathsf V_2 = \exp\Big(K\sum_{i=1}^L\sigma^z_i\sigma^z_{i+1}\Big).
\end{aligned}
\] \(\mathsf V_2\) weighs the bonds within a column, and \(\mathsf V_1\) flips spins from one column to the next. The exponents are those of a quantum spin chain — an Ising coupling \(\sigma^z_i\sigma^z_{i+1}\) plus a transverse field \(\sigma^x_i\) — so the classical 2D model is equivalent to a quantum chain in 1D. The difficulty is that \(\sigma^x_i\) and \(\sigma^z_i\) do not commute, so \(\mathsf V_1\) and \(\mathsf V_2\) cannot be combined or diagonalised together.
The way out is the Jordan–Wigner transformation, which turns spins into fermions. First rename the axes, \(\sigma^x\to-\sigma^z\), \(\sigma^z\to\sigma^x\), a unitary change of basis that leaves the eigenvalues unchanged, so that \(\mathsf V_1=\exp(-K^*\sum_j\sigma^z_j)\) and \(\mathsf V_2=\exp(K\sum_j\sigma^x_j\sigma^x_{j+1})\). With \(\sigma^+=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\sigma^-=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) define \[
\psi_j = \Big(\prod_{k<j}(-\sigma^z_k)\Big)\,\sigma^-_j .
\] The “string” \(\prod_{k<j}(-\sigma^z_k)\) makes operators on different sites anticommute: \(\{\psi_i,\psi_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}\) and \(\{\psi_i,\psi_j\}=0\), where \(\{A,B\}=AB+BA\). These are the relations of fermion annihilation and creation operators, and \(n_j=\psi_j^\dagger\psi_j\), with eigenvalues 0 and 1, counts the fermion at site \(j\). The spin operators become \[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^z_j &= 2n_j-1,\\
\sigma^x_j\sigma^x_{j+1} &= (\psi_j^\dagger-\psi_j)(\psi_{j+1}^\dagger+\psi_{j+1})\quad(j<L),\\
\sigma^x_L\sigma^x_1 &= -(-1)^F(\psi_L^\dagger-\psi_L)(\psi_1^\dagger+\psi_1),
\end{aligned}
\] with \(F=\sum_jn_j\) the number of fermions and \((-1)^F=\prod_j(-\sigma^z_j)\). Both exponents are now quadratic in the fermion operators, which means that the fermions do not interact. The operator \((-1)^F\) is the global spin flip of Section 3 in the new basis, so the even sector has even \(F\); there the boundary term carries a minus sign, as if \(\psi_{L+1}=-\psi_1\) (antiperiodic boundary conditions), while the odd sector is periodic.
Non-interacting particles on a translation-invariant chain are diagonalised by plane waves. We set \(\psi_q\propto\sum_je^{-iqj}\psi_j\), with momenta \[
\begin{aligned}
q\in Q_{\rm even} &= \Big\{\pm\tfrac{\pi}{L},\pm\tfrac{3\pi}{L},\dots,\pm\tfrac{(L-1)\pi}{L}\Big\}\ \text{(antiperiodic)},\\
q\in Q_{\rm odd} &= \Big\{0,\pm\tfrac{2\pi}{L},\dots,\pm\tfrac{(L-2)\pi}{L},\pi\Big\}\ \text{(periodic)} .
\end{aligned}
\] The terms \(\psi\psi\) and \(\psi^\dagger\psi^\dagger\) in \(\sigma^x\sigma^x\) couple momentum \(q\) only to \(-q\), so \(\mathsf V\) factorises into commuting pieces \(\mathsf V_q\), one per pair \((q,-q)\) [Schultz, Mattis & Lieb 1964; Gispen 2018, Theorem 4.5.1]. On the two states “pair empty” and “pair occupied”, \(|0\rangle\) and \(\psi_q^\dagger\psi_{-q}^\dagger|0\rangle\), \[
\mathsf V_q = \begin{pmatrix}e^{2K^*}&0\\0&e^{-2K^*}\end{pmatrix}\exp\left[2K\begin{pmatrix}0&\sin q\\ \sin q&2\cos q\end{pmatrix}\right],
\qquad \text{eigenvalues } e^{2K\cos q\pm\gamma_q},
\] \[
\cosh\gamma_q = \cosh2K^*\cosh2K - \sinh2K^*\sinh2K\cos q .
\] The two singly occupied states \(\psi^\dagger_{\pm q}|0\rangle\) have the intermediate eigenvalue \(e^{2K\cos q}\). A problem of size \(2^L\times2^L\) has become \(L/2\) problems of size \(2\times2\).
The largest eigenvalue is now obtained by taking the larger eigenvalue in each block. Over \(Q_{\rm even}\) the values \(\cos q\) cancel in pairs (\(q\) and \(\pi-q\)), so \[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_0 &= (2\sinh2K)^{L/2}\exp\Big(\frac12\sum_{q\in Q_{\rm even}}\gamma_q\Big),\\
\lambda_1 &= (2\sinh2K)^{L/2}\exp\Big(\frac12\sum_{q\in Q_{\rm odd}}\gamma_q\Big),\quad \gamma_0\equiv2(K-K^*)\ \text{(with its sign)}.
\end{aligned}
\] These are the eigenvalues found by Kaufman (1949).
Finally we let the strip become infinitely wide. The momenta are spaced by \(2\pi/L\), so \(\frac1L\sum_q\to\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}dq\) and \[
\begin{aligned}
-\beta f &= \lim_{L\to\infty}\frac1L\ln\lambda_0\\
&= \frac12\ln(2\sinh2K) + \frac1{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\gamma(q)\,dq .
\end{aligned}
\] With the identity \(\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi\ln(2\cosh\gamma-2\cos\theta)\,d\theta=\gamma\) and with \(\cosh2K^*=\cosh2K/\sinh2K\), \(\sinh2K^*=1/\sinh2K\), this becomes the symmetric double integral \[
\begin{aligned}
-\beta f &= \ln2\\
&\quad + \frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta_1\,d\theta_2\,\ln\big[\cosh^22K - \sinh2K\,(\cos\theta_1+\cos\theta_2)\big],
\end{aligned}
\] and performing one of the two integrals gives the single-integral form with \(\kappa\) quoted at the top of this section [Onsager 1944].
The cell below follows the derivation stage by stage on small matrices. It checks the Pauli-matrix factorisation of \(\mathsf V\) for \(L=4\), the anticommutation relations and the fermion form of the spin operators, the eigenvalues of the \(2\times2\) blocks, Kaufman’s \(\lambda_0\) and \(\lambda_1\) against the numerical diagonalisation of Section 3 for \(L\) from 4 to 10, and finally the three integral forms of \(f\) and the integral identity used above.

# Step 4: Kaufman's lambda_0, lambda_1 against the numerical diagonalisation of Section 3
def kaufman(L, K):
    pre = 0.5 * L * np.log(2 * np.sinh(2 * K))
    q_even = np.pi * (2 * np.arange(L) + 1) / L
    q_odd = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(L) / L
    g_odd = gamma_q(q_odd, K); g_odd[0] = 2 * (K - K_dual(K))
    return pre + 0.5 * gamma_q(q_even, K).sum(), pre + 0.5 * g_odd.sum()       # ln lambda_0, ln lambda_1

Every printed residual is at the level of rounding errors. The free-fermion eigenvalues reproduce the diagonalisation of the \(2^L\times2^L\) matrix to machine precision for every \(L\) and \(K\), both in the even sector (\(\lambda_0\)) and in the odd sector (\(\lambda_1\)), and the three integral forms agree. The chain of transformations — Pauli form, fermions, Fourier modes, \(2\times2\) blocks — is therefore exact, not an approximation.


6.2 The origin of the singularity
Using \(\sinh2K\sinh2K^*=1\), the dispersion relation simplifies exactly: \[
\cosh\gamma_q = \cosh2K^*\cosh2K - \sinh2K^*\sinh2K + \sinh2K^*\sinh2K\,(1-\cos q) = \cosh\big(2(K-K^*)\big) + 1-\cos q .
\] The function \(\gamma_q\ge0\) is smallest at \(q=0\), where \(\gamma_0 = 2|K-K^*|\). This minimum, the gap, vanishes only at \(K=K^*\), the self-dual point of Section 5. For small \(q\) and \(K\) near \(K_c\), \(\cosh\gamma\approx1+\gamma^2/2\) gives \[
\gamma_q\approx\sqrt{m^2+q^2},\qquad m = 2(K-K^*)\propto T_c-T ,
\] the energy–momentum relation of a relativistic particle of mass \(m\); at \(T_c\) the fermions become massless.
The gap controls the correlation length. \(\ln(\lambda_0/\lambda_1)\) is the difference of the two sums for \(\lambda_0\) and \(\lambda_1\). Above \(T_c\) it tends to the gap, so that \(\xi = 1/[2(K^*-K)]\) along a lattice axis, which diverges as \(1/(T-T_c)\) (exponent \(\nu=1\), Section 8). Below \(T_c\), \(\gamma_0=2(K-K^*)>0\) and \(\lambda_1/\lambda_0\to1\) as \(L\to\infty\): the even and odd sectors become degenerate, which is the signature of two ordered states (all up, all down).
The gap also produces the singularity of the free energy. \(-\beta f\) contains \(\frac1{4\pi}\int\gamma(q)\,dq\), and near \(q=0\) \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\Lambda\sqrt{m^2+q^2}\,dq &= \frac{\Lambda}{2}\sqrt{\Lambda^2+m^2}\\
&\quad + \frac{m^2}{2}\ln\frac{\Lambda+\sqrt{\Lambda^2+m^2}}{|m|}
\end{aligned}
\] for any cutoff \(\Lambda>0\). The term \(-\frac{m^2}{2}\ln|m|\) is not analytic at \(m=0\): \(f\) and its first derivative are continuous, but the second derivative contains \(\ln|m|\). Since \(m\propto T-T_c\) and \(c=-T\,\partial^2f/\partial T^2\), the specific heat diverges as \(\ln|T-T_c|\) (compare Peskin’s notes, eqs. 63–67).
In Onsager’s variables the same non-analyticity appears differently. In the single-integral form, \(\kappa = 2s/(1+s^2)\) with \(s = \sinh 2K\). Since \(2s\le1+s^2\), \(\kappa\le1\), with equality only at \(s = 1\), that is at \(T_c\). There the square root \(\sqrt{1-\kappa^2\sin^2\phi}\) vanishes at \(\phi = \pi/2\) and the integrand develops a kink.
The cell below confirms the simplification of \(\cosh\gamma_q\) with SymPy and then tests the statements about the correlation length with Kaufman’s eigenvalues for \(L = 16\), \(64\) and \(256\) — cheap, because the formula needs only \(L\) numbers. Above \(T_c\) the value of \(\ln(\lambda_0/\lambda_1)\) should settle on \(2(K^*-K)\); below \(T_c\) it should fall to zero, and indeed it reaches the level of rounding errors, \(\sim10^{-13}\), at \(T=1.8\). The last lines check the antiderivative of \(\sqrt{m^2+q^2}\).

6.3 Energy, specific heat and magnetisation
The energy per spin, \(u = \partial(\beta f)/\partial\beta\), can be computed in two independent ways, and comparing them is a stringent test. The first is to differentiate the integral formula numerically, by central finite differences in \(\beta\). The second uses the closed formula [Onsager 1944] with the complete elliptic integral of the first kind \(K_1(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}d\phi/\sqrt{1-\kappa^2\sin^2\phi}\): \[
u = -\coth2K\Big[1 + \frac2\pi\big(2\tanh^22K - 1\big)K_1(\kappa)\Big].
\] \(K_1(\kappa)\) diverges logarithmically as \(\kappa\to1\), and this is the origin of the vertical tangent of \(u\) at \(T_c\). scipy.special.ellipkm1(p) returns \(K_1\) as a function of \(p = 1-\kappa^2\). Near \(T_c\), \(\kappa^2\) is so close to 1 that \(1-\kappa^2\) must be computed without cancellation, as \(1-\kappa^2 = \big(\frac{1-s^2}{1+s^2}\big)^2\) with \(s = \sinh 2K\).
The free energy at \(h=0\) does not give the spontaneous magnetisation, which needs a derivative with respect to \(h\). Onsager announced the formula in 1949 without publishing a derivation, and Yang [1952] published the first derivation [history: Baxter 2011]: \[
M = \big[1-\sinh^{-4}2K\big]^{1/8}\quad (T<T_c),\qquad M=0\quad(T>T_c).
\] Near \(T_c\), \(\sinh2K\approx1+2\sqrt2\,(K-K_c)\) (using \(\cosh2K_c=\sqrt2\)), so \(1-\sinh^{-4}2K\approx8\sqrt2\,(K-K_c)\propto T_c-T\) and \(M\propto(T_c-T)^{1/8}\): the exponent is \(\beta=1/8\).
The next cell compares the two routes to \(u\). They agree to between \(10^{-9}\) and \(10^{-7}\), the accuracy of the finite difference.


Code
def u_elliptic(T):
    K = 1.0 / np.asarray(T, dtype=float)
    s = np.sinh(2 * K)
    p = ((1 - s**2) / (1 + s**2))**2                 # 1 - kappa^2, without cancellation
    return -1 / np.tanh(2 * K) * (1 + 2 / np.pi * (2 * np.tanh(2 * K)**2 - 1) * ellipkm1(p))

def M_yang(T):
    T = np.asarray(T, dtype=float)
    out = np.zeros_like(T)
    below = T < TC
    out[below] = (1 - np.sinh(2 / T[below])**-4) ** 0.125
    return out

The free energy \(f\) looks perfectly smooth; \(u\) is continuous but has a vertical tangent at \(T_c\); \(c = du/dT\) diverges on both sides; and \(M\) drops to zero continuously but very steeply, with exponent \(1/8\). The singularity of \(f\) sits in its second derivative, and \(u\) has no jump (no latent heat): the transition is continuous, or of second order. The last figure shows the integrand of Onsager’s formula. At \(T\) and at its dual \(T^*\) it is identical (Section 5), and at \(T_c\) it touches zero at \(\phi=\pi/2\) with a kink.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
section: 7. The energy at the critical point
text:
7. The energy at the critical point
The value of \(u\) at \(T_c\) is a good test of the whole construction: we can obtain it once from Onsager’s solution and once from duality alone, without the solution. The comparison also shows how much information a symmetry carries.

7.1 The critical energy from Onsager’s solution
At \(T_c\) we have \(\sinh 2K_c = 1\), hence \(\cosh^2 2K_c = 1+\sinh^22K_c = 2\) and \(\tanh^22K_c = \tfrac12\), so the prefactor \(2\tanh^22K_c - 1\) vanishes. In the elliptic formula this prefactor multiplies the divergent \(K_1(\kappa\to1)\), and their product vanishes (a linear zero times a logarithmic divergence), so \(u(T_c) = -\coth2K_c = -\cosh 2K_c/\sinh 2K_c = -\sqrt2\). SymPy confirms the two exact values, and the next cell approaches \(T_c\) numerically from both sides; the two sequences close in on \(-\sqrt2\) from opposite directions, and the central difference of the integral at \(T_c\) gives \(-1.41421356\).


Code
# SymPy: the prefactor vanishes and coth 2K_c = sqrt 2
Kc_sym = sp.log(1 + sp.sqrt(2)) / 2
print("2 tanh^2 2K_c - 1 =", sp.simplify((2 * sp.tanh(2 * Kc_sym)**2 - 1).rewrite(sp.exp)))
print("-coth 2K_c        =", sp.radsimp(sp.simplify((-1 / sp.tanh(2 * Kc_sym)).rewrite(sp.exp))))

7.2 The critical energy from duality alone
The same number can be obtained without Onsager’s formula. Since \(\varphi = \ln Z/N\) and \(\partial\ln Z/\partial\beta = -\langle H\rangle\), with \(J=1\) we have \(K=\beta\) and \[
\varphi'(K) = -u(K) \equiv \varepsilon(K),
\] where \(\varepsilon = 2\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\rm nn}\) is twice the nearest-neighbour correlation (two bonds per spin). We differentiate the duality identity \(\ \varphi(K) - \ln2 - 2\ln\cosh K = \varphi(K^*) - 2K^*\ \) with respect to \(K\), using the chain rule on the right: \[
\varepsilon(K) - 2\tanh K = \big(\varepsilon(K^*) - 2\big)\frac{dK^*}{dK}.
\] The derivative of the dual map follows from \(e^{-2K^*} = \tanh K\): \(\ -2e^{-2K^*}dK^* = \frac{dK}{\cosh^2K}\), so \(\frac{dK^*}{dK} = -\frac{1}{2\tanh K\cosh^2K} = -\frac{1}{2\sinh K\cosh K} = -\frac{1}{\sinh 2K}\), which equals \(-1\) at \(K_c\).
At the self-dual point \(K = K^* = K_c\) both sides involve the same \(\varepsilon\), provided \(u\) is continuous there — no latent heat, as Section 6 showed. Then \[
\varepsilon - 2\tanh K_c = -(\varepsilon - 2)\ \Rightarrow\ \varepsilon(K_c) = 1 + \tanh K_c .
\] Finally \(\tanh K_c = e^{-2K_c}\) by self-duality, and this equals \(1/(1+\sqrt2) = \sqrt2 - 1\), so \(\varepsilon(K_c) = \sqrt2\) and \(u(T_c) = -\sqrt2\). Two exact results, \(T_c\) and \(u(T_c)\), thus follow from a symmetry argument alone. In the next two cells SymPy solves the equation at the self-dual point, and the numerical check confirms \(dK^*/dK = -1\) at \(K_c\), the value \(\sqrt2-1\), and the differentiated identity also away from \(K_c\), where both sides agree to all printed digits.


Code
# SymPy: solve Step 4 for epsilon at the self-dual point
eps_s = sp.symbols("epsilon")
Kc_sym = sp.log(1 + sp.sqrt(2)) / 2

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
8. Critical exponents
The critical temperature depends on the lattice; Section 10 will show a different value for the triangular lattice. What does not depend on such details is the way quantities diverge or vanish near \(T_c\), described by the critical exponents. They are the numbers that characterise a phase transition, and they are what the exact solution contributes beyond \(T_c\). With the reduced temperature \(t = (T-T_c)/T_c\) they are defined by \[
\begin{aligned}
c&\sim|t|^{-\alpha},\qquad M\sim(-t)^{\beta}\ (t<0),\qquad \chi\sim|t|^{-\gamma},\qquad \xi\sim|t|^{-\nu},\\
\langle s_0s_r\rangle&\sim r^{-(d-2+\eta)}\ \text{at } T_c ,
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\chi=\partial m/\partial h\) is the magnetic susceptibility and \(d\) the dimension (\(d=2\) here, so \(\langle s_0s_r\rangle\sim r^{-\eta}\) at \(T_c\)). The symbol \(\beta\) here denotes an exponent, not \(1/T\); the context makes the meaning clear. The 2D Ising model realises the case \(\alpha=0\) with a logarithm, \(c\sim-\ln|t|\).
For the magnetisation we fit \(\ln M\) against \(\ln(-t)\) close to \(T_c\) and also look at the local slope \(d\ln M/d\ln(-t)\), which must tend to \(\beta\). For the specific heat we fit \(c = -A\ln|t| + B_\pm\) on both sides of \(T_c\) and test the amplitude predicted by Onsager’s solution, \(A = \frac{2}{\pi}\big(\frac{2}{T_c}\big)^2 = \frac{2}{\pi}(2K_c)^2\) [Onsager 1944]. Here \(c\) is obtained from the elliptic \(u\) by a central difference with a step much smaller than \(|T-T_c|\).


Code
tt = np.logspace(-8, -2, 40)                                   # |t|
Mt = M_yang(TC * (1 - tt))
slope_fit = np.polyfit(np.log(tt[tt < 1e-4]), np.log(Mt[tt < 1e-4]), 1)[0]
local = np.gradient(np.log(Mt), np.log(tt))
print(f"beta from a fit of ln M vs ln(-t), |t| < 1e-4:  {slope_fit:.6f}    (1/8 = {1/8})")
print("local slope d lnM / d ln|t| at |t| = 1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8:",
      ", ".join(f"{np.interp(np.log(x), np.log(tt), local):.5f}" for x in (1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8)))

def c_exact(T, rel=1e-4):
    # c = du/dT by a central difference with step rel*|T - T_c|
    hstep = rel * np.abs(T - TC)
    return (u_elliptic(T + hstep) - u_elliptic(T - hstep)) / (2 * hstep)

A_exact = 2 / np.pi * (2 / TC)**2
for side, sgn in (("T < T_c", -1), ("T > T_c", +1)):
    tfit = np.logspace(-9, -4, 30)
    cfit = c_exact(TC * (1 + sgn * tfit))
    A, B = np.polyfit(-np.log(tfit), cfit, 1)
    print(f"{side}:  c = -A ln|t| + B  with  A = {A:.6f},  B = {B:+.4f}")
print(f"exact amplitude: A = (2/pi)(2/T_c)^2 = {A_exact:.6f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))

ax[1].semilogx(tl, c_exact(TC * (1 - tl)), color=UJBlue, lw=2, label="$T<T_c$")
ax[1].semilogx(tl, c_exact(TC * (1 + tl)), color=DSOrange, lw=2, label="$T>T_c$")
ax[1].set_xlabel(r"$|t|$"); ax[1].set_ylabel("$c$"); ax[1].legend(frameon=False)
ax[1].set_title("a straight line on a log axis = logarithmic divergence")  # the two sides nearly coincide: B_- and B_+ are close
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

local slope d lnM / d ln|t| at |t| = 1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8: 0.12310, 0.12498, 0.12500, 0.12500

T > T_c:  c = -A ln|t| + B  with  A = 0.494656,  B = -0.3078
exact amplitude: A = (2/pi)(2/T_c)^2 = 0.494539





The fit gives \(\beta = 0.124999\), and the local slope approaches \(1/8\) as \(|t|\to0\). The specific-heat amplitudes on the two sides, \(0.494517\) and \(0.494656\), agree with the exact \(A = 0.494539\), and on the logarithmic axis the two branches of \(c\) are straight lines, the signature of a logarithmic divergence.

8.1 Finite-size scaling of strips
The strips of Section 3 give two more exponents, independently of Onsager’s formula. Both rest on the idea of finite-size scaling: near \(T_c\) the only relevant lengths are \(\xi\) and the strip width \(L\), so dimensionless quantities depend only on their ratio.
At \(T_c\) the strip correlation length is proportional to the width, and conformal invariance of the critical point fixes the constant: \(\xi_L = L/(\pi\eta)\) on a periodic strip [Cardy 1984]. The quantity \(\eta_L = L/(\pi\,\xi_L(T_c))\) should therefore tend to \(\eta\), whose exact value is \(\eta = 1/4\). Near \(T_c\), \(\xi_L/L\) is a function of \(L/\xi\propto L\,|t|^{\nu}\), that is of \(L^{1/\nu}t\) only, so its slope at \(T_c\) grows as \(\frac{d(\xi_L/L)}{dT}\big|_{T_c}\propto L^{1/\nu}\); the exact value is \(\nu = 1\) (Section 6.2: \(\xi\propto1/(T-T_c)\)). The free energy at \(T_c\) carries a third universal number. It converges as \(f_L - f = -\frac{\pi\,c_{\rm CFT}\,T_c}{6L^2}\) [Blöte, Cardy & Nightingale 1986; Affleck 1986], where \(c_{\rm CFT}\) is the central charge of the conformal field theory (CFT) describing the critical point. For the Ising model \(c_{\rm CFT} = \frac12\), so \(L^2(f_L - f)\to-\pi T_c/12\). The cell below computes all three quantities for \(L = 4,\dots,12\).


Code
print(" L    eta_L = L/(pi xi_L(T_c))   L^2 (f_L - f)(T_c)    slope d(xi_L/L)/dT at T_c")
slopes, Lv = [], [4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for L in Lv:
    l0, l1 = lambda01(L, KC)
    xi = 1 / np.log(l0 / l1)
    dT = 1e-4
    s = (xi_over_L(L, TC + dT) - xi_over_L(L, TC - dT)) / (2 * dT)
    slopes.append(abs(s))
    print(f"{L:2d}       {L/(np.pi*xi):.6f}               {L**2 * (-TC*np.log(l0)/L - f_onsager(TC)):+.6f}            {s:+.4f}")
print(f"(computed in {time.perf_counter()-t0:.1f} s)        -pi T_c/12 = {-np.pi*TC/12:.6f}")
inv_nu = np.diff(np.log(slopes)) / np.diff(np.log(Lv))
print("1/nu from consecutive pairs of L:", ", ".join(f"{v:.4f}" for v in inv_nu))

All three columns converge monotonically in \(L\) towards the exact values: \(\eta_L\) falls from \(0.257845\) to \(0.250727\), \(L^2(f_L-f)\) approaches \(-\pi T_c/12 = -0.594071\), and the estimates of \(1/\nu\) from consecutive pairs of widths decrease from \(1.0912\) to \(1.0144\). The exponents are not independent of one another. Two scaling relations [Kardar 2007], the Fisher relation \(\gamma = \nu(2-\eta)\) and the Rushbrooke relation \(\alpha + 2\beta + \gamma = 2\), give the remaining exponent \(\gamma\) and a consistency check.


Code
nu, eta, alpha, beta_ = 1, 0.25, 0, 0.125
gamma = nu * (2 - eta)
print(f"gamma = nu (2 - eta) = {gamma}   (= 7/4);   Rushbrooke check alpha + 2 beta + gamma = {alpha + 2*beta_ + gamma}")


gamma = nu (2 - eta) = 1.75   (= 7/4);   Rushbrooke check alpha + 2 beta + gamma = 2.0


The relations give \(\gamma = 7/4\), and the Rushbrooke sum equals 2 as it should.
These exponents complete the phase diagram of the model, drawn below. A phase diagram is a map of the control parameters, here the temperature \(T\) and the magnetic field \(h\) of Section 1, divided into regions with qualitatively different behaviour, the phases, and the lines between them, the phase transitions.
The type of a transition is read off from the free energy per spin \(f(T,h)\) and its derivatives, such as the magnetisation \(m=-\partial f/\partial h\) and the energy. At a first-order transition a first derivative of \(f\) jumps: the order parameter changes discontinuously and the two phases coexist at the transition. At a continuous (or second-order) transition the first derivatives are continuous, the order parameter goes to zero continuously, and the correlation length \(\xi\), the distance over which spins influence each other, diverges as a power of the distance to the critical point, \(\xi\sim|T-T_c|^{-\nu}\); second derivatives such as the specific heat and the susceptibility then diverge or have a cusp.
In panel (a) the segment \(h=0\), \(T<T_c\) is a line of first-order transitions: when \(h\) changes sign below \(T_c\), the magnetisation \(m=-\partial f/\partial h\) jumps from \(-M\) to \(+M\). The line ends at the critical point \(T_c=2/\ln(1+\sqrt2)=2.269\), \(h=0\), and above \(T_c\) the magnetisation changes smoothly with \(h\). Panel (b) is the temperature axis at \(h=0\) with Yang’s exact magnetisation \(\pm M(T)\) (Section 6.3). At \(T_c\) the transition is continuous, with the exponents computed in this section: \(\beta=1/8\), \(\nu=1\), \(\gamma=7/4\) and \(\alpha=0\) with a logarithmic specific heat. Every model with the same symmetry (a two-state order parameter) and dimension \(d=2\) and short-range interactions shares them; this set of models is the two-dimensional Ising universality class, and Section 10 tests it on the triangular lattice.


Code

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
section: 9. Mean-field theory and the exact solution
text:
9. Mean-field theory and the exact solution
Mean-field theory is the approximation one uses when no exact solution exists. With the exact solution at hand we can measure precisely what it gets wrong, and why.
Spin \(i\) interacts with its \(z\) neighbours (\(z=4\) on the square lattice) through \(-Js_i\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)}s_j\). Mean-field theory replaces each neighbour by its average \(m=\langle s_j\rangle\), so that spin \(i\) feels an effective field \(zJm\); a single spin in a field \(B\) has \(\langle s\rangle = \tanh(\beta B)\). Self-consistency, \(\langle s_i\rangle = m\), then gives with \(J=1\) \[
m = \tanh\Big(\frac{zm}{T}\Big) = \tanh\Big(\frac{4m}{T}\Big).
\] The value \(m = 0\) is always a solution. A non-zero one exists when the slope of the right-hand side at \(m = 0\) exceeds 1, i.e. \(4/T > 1\), so \(T_c^{\rm MF} = z = 4\). Near \(T_c^{\rm MF}\), \(\tanh x\approx x - x^3/3\) gives \(m \approx \frac4Tm - \frac13\big(\frac4T\big)^3m^3\), i.e. \(m^2\approx 3\big(\frac4T-1\big)\big/\big(\frac4T\big)^3\), so \(m\sim(1 - T/T_c^{\rm MF})^{1/2}\) and \(\beta_{\rm MF} = \frac12\). For the energy, replacing \(s_is_j\) by \(m^2\) in each of the \(zN/2\) bonds gives \(u_{\rm MF} = -\frac z2m^2 = -2m^2\). It is zero above \(T_c^{\rm MF}\) and has a finite slope below, which produces a jump in \(c\) instead of a divergence.
The replacement assumes \(\langle s_is_j\rangle = \langle s_i\rangle\langle s_j\rangle\), that is, no correlations. Near \(T_c\) the correlation length diverges and correlated fluctuations dominate, so the approximation must fail there. In 1D (\(z=2\)) it even predicts a transition at \(T=2\), where the exact chain has none (Section 2). Mean-field exponents become exact only in high dimensions, above the upper critical dimension \(d=4\) of the Ising model [Kardar 2007]. SymPy reproduces the expansion of the self-consistency equation, and the following cell solves it numerically, fits \(\beta_{\rm MF}\), evaluates the jump of the specific heat and compares the mean-field magnetisation with Yang’s.


Code
# SymPy: m tanh-expansion near T_c^MF, with a = z/T = 4/T
m, a = sp.symbols("m a", positive=True)
cubic = sp.series(sp.tanh(a * m), m, 0, 4).removeO()                     # a m - a^3 m^3 / 3
print("tanh(a m) =", cubic, "+ O(m^5)")
print("non-zero solution of m = a m - a^3 m^3/3:  m =", sp.solve(sp.Eq(cubic / m, 1), m))


tanh(a m) = -a**3*m**3/3 + a*m + O(m^5)
non-zero solution of m = a m - a^3 m^3/3:  m = [sqrt(3)*sqrt(a - 1)/a**(3/2)]




Code
def m_meanfield(T):
    # largest solution of m = tanh(4 m / T)
    if 4 / T <= 1:
        return 0.0
    return brentq(lambda m: m - np.tanh(4 * m / T), 1e-12, 1.0)

# T_c^MF: the largest T with a non-zero solution (found by bisection, threshold m > 1e-6)
lo, hi = 2.0, 6.0
for _ in range(80):
    mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
    lo, hi = (mid, hi) if m_meanfield(mid) > 1e-6 else (lo, mid)
print(f"T_c (mean field, numerical) = {lo:.6f}     exact 2D: T_c = {TC:.6f}     ratio = {lo/TC:.4f}")

tt = np.logspace(-8, -3, 20)
mf = np.array([m_meanfield(4 * (1 - x)) for x in tt])
print(f"beta_MF from a fit near T_c^MF: {np.polyfit(np.log(tt), np.log(mf), 1)[0]:.5f}")
cm = [(-2*m_meanfield(4*(1-x))**2 + 2*m_meanfield(4*(1-2*x))**2) / (4*x) for x in (1e-3, 1e-5)]
print("mean-field specific heat just below T_c^MF:", ", ".join(f"{v:.5f}" for v in cm), "  (and exactly 0 above)")

T = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 600)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
ax.plot(T, M_yang(T), color=UJBlue, lw=2, label="exact (Onsager, Yang)")
ax.plot(T, [m_meanfield(t) for t in T], color=DSOrange, lw=2, ls="--", label="mean field")
ax.axvline(TC, color=UJBlue, ls=":", lw=1); ax.axvline(4, color=DSOrange, ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("$T$"); ax.set_ylabel("$M$"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_title("mean field overestimates $T_c$ and gets the exponent wrong")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


T_c (mean field, numerical) = 4.000000     exact 2D: T_c = 2.269185     ratio = 1.7627
beta_MF from a fit near T_c^MF: 0.49998
mean-field specific heat just below T_c^MF: 1.49640, 1.49996   (and exactly 0 above)





The numbers make the failure quantitative: mean field puts \(T_c\) at \(4\), a factor \(1.7627\) above the exact value, its exponent comes out as \(0.49998\approx\frac12\), and its specific heat jumps to about \(1.5\) instead of diverging. Mean field neglects fluctuations, and in 2D they are strong: they lower \(T_c\) from \(4\) to \(2.269\), change \(\beta\) from \(\frac12\) to \(\frac18\), and turn the jump in \(c\) into a logarithmic divergence. The same self-consistency equation \(m=\tanh(\cdot)\) reappears in the energy-based models of the course, as the update rule of a recurrent \(\tanh\) network.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
10. Universality and the triangular lattice
Section 8 claimed that the exponents, unlike \(T_c\), do not depend on lattice details, and we now test this on a different lattice. Exponents depend only on the dimension, on the symmetry of the order parameter (here \(s\to-s\)) and on the range of the interactions [Kardar 2007]; models sharing these form a universality class.
Add one diagonal bond to every plaquette: each spin now has \(z = 6\) neighbours and the lattice becomes triangular. In the transfer matrix this is the extra term \(K\sum_is_is'_{i+1}\) (flag lattice="triangular"); \(\mathsf V\) is then no longer symmetric, so we use a general eigensolver. The exact critical temperature is \(T_c^{\triangle} = 4/\ln3\) [Houtappel 1950], and the exponents should be those of the square lattice. We test both with the crossing method of Section 3 and with \(\eta_L\) of Section 8.1.
One geometric detail must be taken into account. In the triangular lattice the columns are \(\sqrt3/2\) apart while the sites of one column are at distance 1, so the physical correlation length is \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\xi_L\) and \(\eta_L = L\big/\big(\pi\,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\xi_L\big)\).


Code
print(" L, L+2   crossing T*(L)     eta at the crossing")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for L in (4, 6, 8, 10):
    Tx = brentq(lambda T: xi_over_L(L, T, "triangular") - xi_over_L(L + 2, T, "triangular"), 3.0, 4.2, xtol=1e-12)
    xi = xi_over_L(L + 2, Tx, "triangular") * (L + 2)
    print(f"{L:2d}, {L+2:2d}   {Tx:.8f}       {(L + 2) / (np.pi * np.sqrt(3) / 2 * xi):.5f}")
print(f"4/ln 3 = {4/np.log(3):.8f}    ({time.perf_counter()-t0:.1f} s)")


 L, L+2   crossing T*(L)     eta at the crossing
 4,  6   3.64236593       0.25076
 6,  8   3.64117712       0.25016


 8, 10   3.64101598       0.25006


10, 12   3.64097803       0.25002
4/ln 3 = 3.64095691    (20.9 s)


The crossings converge to \(3.64097803\) for the widths \((10,12)\), against \(4/\ln3 = 3.64095691\), and \(\eta\) at the crossing approaches \(0.25\), ending at \(0.25002\). The critical temperature is different (more neighbours, more order), while the exponent \(\eta\) is the same: \(T_c\) is a lattice detail, the exponents are universal. A network trained on one lattice can transfer to another lattice only to the extent that it has learned something universal — the interpretability question raised in the lecture.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
Exercises

Exercise 1 — the 1D chain in a field
Using the transfer matrix, compute the magnetisation per spin of the infinite chain, \(m = \partial\ln\lambda_+/\partial\tilde h\), numerically (by a finite difference) and compare it with the closed form \(m = \dfrac{\sinh\tilde h}{\sqrt{\sinh^2\tilde h + e^{-4K}}}\). Plot \(m(h)\) at several \(T\) and decide whether there is a spontaneous magnetisation at \(h\to0^+\) for any \(T>0\).

Solution


Code
def lam_plus(K, ht):
    return np.exp(K) * np.cosh(ht) + np.sqrt(np.exp(2 * K) * np.sinh(ht)**2 + np.exp(-2 * K))

for K, ht in [(0.5, 0.1), (1.0, 0.05), (2.0, 0.01)]:
    d = 1e-6
    m_num = (np.log(lam_plus(K, ht + d)) - np.log(lam_plus(K, ht - d))) / (2 * d)
    m_cf = np.sinh(ht) / np.sqrt(np.sinh(ht)**2 + np.exp(-4 * K))
    print(f"K = {K}, beta h = {ht}:  m numerical = {m_num:.8f},  closed form = {m_cf:.8f}")

hgrid = np.linspace(-0.5, 0.5, 401)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
for T, col in [(0.5, UJNavy), (1.0, UJBlue), (2.0, "#9CC3E6")]:
    K = 1 / T; ht = hgrid / T
    ax.plot(hgrid, np.sinh(ht) / np.sqrt(np.sinh(ht)**2 + np.exp(-4 * K)), color=col, lw=2, label=f"T = {T}")
ax.set_xlabel("$h$"); ax.set_ylabel("$m$"); ax.legend(frameon=False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


K = 0.5, beta h = 0.1:  m numerical = 0.26271701,  closed form = 0.26271701
K = 1.0, beta h = 0.05:  m numerical = 0.34668443,  closed form = 0.34668443
K = 2.0, beta h = 0.01:  m numerical = 0.47921470,  closed form = 0.47921470





The curve \(m(h)\) is a smooth odd function with \(m(0) = 0\) for every \(T>0\). There is no spontaneous magnetisation, only an ever steeper curve as \(T\to0\): the slope at \(h = 0\) is \(\beta e^{2K}\), which grows exponentially in \(K\) but stays finite for every \(T>0\).



Exercise 2 — the specific-heat peak of strips
Using strip from Section 3, plot the maximum of \(c_L\) against \(\ln L\). A logarithmic divergence \(c\sim-A\ln|t|\) combined with \(|t|\sim1/L\) (because \(\nu = 1\)) predicts \(c_{\max}(L)\approx A\ln L + \text{const}\). Fit the slope and compare it with the amplitude \(A\) found in Section 8.

Solution


Code
cmax = []
t0 = time.perf_counter()
Lex = [4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
for L in Lex:
    if L in strip:
        cmax.append(strip[L]["c"][2:-2].max())
    else:                                     # L = 12 was not in the scan: maximise c_L near its peak
        def cL(T, L=L, d=2e-3):
            fm, f0, fp = (-(T + s) * np.log(lambda01(L, 1 / (T + s))[0]) / L for s in (-d, 0, d))
            return -T * (fp - 2 * f0 + fm) / d**2
        from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
        res = minimize_scalar(lambda T: -cL(T), bounds=(2.24, 2.30), method="bounded", options={"xatol": 1e-3})
        cmax.append(-res.fun)
print(f"(L = 12 peak search: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.1f} s)")
slope = np.polyfit(np.log(Lex[1:]), cmax[1:], 1)[0]
for L, cm in zip(Lex, cmax):
    print(f"L = {L:2d}: c_max = {cm:.4f}")
print(f"slope of c_max vs ln L (L = 6..12): {slope:.4f};   A from Section 8: {A_exact:.4f}")


(L = 12 peak search: 18.2 s)
L =  4: c_max = 0.8728
L =  6: c_max = 1.0739
L =  8: c_max = 1.2160
L = 10: c_max = 1.3262
L = 12: c_max = 1.4170
slope of c_max vs ln L (L = 6..12): 0.4947;   A from Section 8: 0.4945


The slope, \(0.4947\) for \(L = 6,\dots,12\), approaches \(A = 0.4945\); the smallest strips still carry visible corrections. The specific-heat peak of a finite lattice grows only logarithmically with its size, which is one reason why a Monte Carlo study (and the CNN of Lab 011) sees a broad, shifted feature rather than a sharp singularity.



Exercise 3 (open) — the quantum connection
Section 6.1 used the identity \(e^{K}\mathbb 1 + e^{-K}\sigma^x = \sqrt{2\sinh2K}\;e^{K^*\sigma^x}\) to write the strip transfer matrix as \(\mathsf V = (2\sinh2K)^{L/2}\,\mathsf V_2^{1/2}\mathsf V_1\mathsf V_2^{1/2}\): a classical Ising coupling along the column and a transverse field of strength \(K^*\). Prove the identity and verify it numerically for a few values of \(K\). This is the bridge to the transverse-field Ising chain used later in the course.

Solution


Code
sx = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]])
from scipy.linalg import expm
for K in (0.2, KC, 0.8):
    lhs = np.exp(K) * np.eye(2) + np.exp(-K) * sx
    rhs = np.sqrt(2 * np.sinh(2 * K)) * expm(K_dual(K) * sx)
    print(f"K = {K:.4f}:  max |lhs - rhs| = {np.abs(lhs - rhs).max():.1e}")


K = 0.2000:  max |lhs - rhs| = 1.1e-16
K = 0.4407:  max |lhs - rhs| = 2.2e-16
K = 0.8000:  max |lhs - rhs| = 1.1e-16




Code
# SymPy: the same identity symbolically (coefficients of 1 and sigma^x)
K = sp.symbols("K", positive=True)
K_star = -sp.log(sp.tanh(K)) / 2
pref = sp.sqrt(2 * sp.sinh(2 * K))
print("coefficient of 1      :", sp.simplify((pref * sp.cosh(K_star) - sp.exp(K)).rewrite(sp.exp)))
print("coefficient of sigma^x:", sp.simplify((pref * sp.sinh(K_star) - sp.exp(-K)).rewrite(sp.exp)))


coefficient of 1      : 0
coefficient of sigma^x: 0


For the proof, note that \(e^{K^*\sigma^x} = \cosh K^*\,\mathbb1 + \sinh K^*\sigma^x\) because \((\sigma^x)^2=\mathbb 1\). The ratio of the two coefficients must be \(e^{-K}/e^{K}=e^{-2K}\), and indeed \(\tanh K^* = e^{-2K}\) (Section 5). For the prefactor, \(\cosh^2K^* = 1/(1-\tanh^2K^*) = 1/(1-e^{-4K}) = e^{2K}/(2\sinh2K)\), so \(\sqrt{2\sinh2K}\cosh K^* = e^{K}\). At the self-dual point \(K = K^* = K_c\) the column coupling and the transverse field are equal, which is the critical point of the quantum chain.

title: Lab 016: PCA, t-SNE and clustering in JAX
text:
1. High-dimensional data
A \(28\times28\) MNIST image is a vector \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{784}\), one coordinate per pixel. We cannot look at 784 dimensions. But real images are not spread over all of \(\mathbb R^{784}\): 784 random pixel values give noise, never a digit. The digits fill a thin, low-dimensional part of the space.
Analysis of such data therefore usually starts with dimensionality reduction: a map \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{D}\mapsto\mathbf z\in\mathbb R^{d}\) with \(d\ll D\) (here \(d=2\) or \(3\), so that we can plot it) that keeps the structure of the data. We then look at the points \(\mathbf z_i\): do they form groups, which samples are close?
The MNIST files have a simple binary format (idx): a 4-byte magic number whose last byte is the number of dimensions, then the size of each dimension as a 4-byte big-endian integer, then the raw uint8 values. We decode it with gzip and numpy and scale the pixels to \([0,1]\).


Code
DATA_DIR = "data/MNIST_raw"
MIRRORS = ["https://ossci-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/mnist/",
           "https://storage.googleapis.com/cvdf-datasets/mnist/"]

def mnist_file(name):
    # path of one MNIST file; downloaded once if it is not on disk
    path = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, name)
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        os.makedirs(DATA_DIR, exist_ok=True)
        for m in MIRRORS:
            try:
                urllib.request.urlretrieve(m + name, path); break
            except Exception as err:
                print(f"{m} failed: {err}")
    return path

def read_idx(path):
    with gzip.open(path, "rb") as f:
        raw = f.read()
    ndim = raw[3]                                            # last byte of the magic number
    shape = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=">i4", count=ndim, offset=4)
    return np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8, offset=4 + 4 * ndim).reshape(shape)

Xtr = jnp.asarray(read_idx(mnist_file("train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz")).reshape(-1, 784), jnp.float32) / 255.0
ytr = np.asarray(read_idx(mnist_file("train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz")))
Xte = jnp.asarray(read_idx(mnist_file("t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz")).reshape(-1, 784), jnp.float32) / 255.0
yte = np.asarray(read_idx(mnist_file("t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz")))

# 5000 test images for all maps; the labels only colour the points afterwards
sel = np.asarray(jax.random.choice(section_key(1), len(Xte), (5000,), replace=False))
X5, y5 = Xte[sel], yte[sel]
print("training images:", Xtr.shape, "| test images:", Xte.shape, "| subset for the maps:", X5.shape)


training images: (60000, 784) | test images: (10000, 784) | subset for the maps: (5000, 784)


Ten digits of the subset, and a “random image” with 784 independent uniform pixel values. The random image is a perfectly valid point of \(\mathbb R^{784}\), yet nothing like it appears among the digits.


Code
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 11, figsize=(11, 1.4))
for j, a in enumerate(axs[:10]):
    i = int(np.flatnonzero(y5 == j)[0])
    a.imshow(np.asarray(X5[i]).reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r"); a.set_title(f"digit {j}", fontsize=8)
noise = jax.random.uniform(section_key(2), (784,))
axs[10].imshow(np.asarray(noise).reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r"); axs[10].set_title("random", fontsize=8)
for a in axs: a.axis("off")
plt.show()

title: Lab 016: PCA, t-SNE and clustering in JAX
text:
2. Principal component analysis
PCA is a linear projection. The data are \(n\) samples \(\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n\in\mathbb R^D\) with mean \(\bar{\mathbf x}=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf x_i\). We write \(x_{ij}\) for feature \(j\) (pixel \(j\)) of sample \(i\). The covariance matrix of the features is the \(D\times D\) matrix
\[C_{jl}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)(x_{il}-\bar x_l),\qquad C=\frac1n X_c^{\top}X_c ,\]
with \(X_c\) the \(n\times D\) matrix of centred samples. \(C_{jj}\) is the variance of pixel \(j\); \(C_{jl}\) says how pixels \(j\) and \(l\) vary together.

2.1 Variance maximisation
To find the directions that describe the data best, project every centred sample on a unit vector \(\mathbf u\): \(z_i=\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x})\). The variance of the projections is
\[\mathrm{Var}(z)=\frac1n\sum_i z_i^2=\frac1n\sum_i \mathbf u^{\top}(\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x})(\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x})^{\top}\mathbf u=\mathbf u^{\top}C\,\mathbf u .\]
We look for the direction of largest variance: maximise \(\mathbf u^{\top}C\mathbf u\) subject to \(\mathbf u^{\top}\mathbf u=1\). With a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\),
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf u}\Big[\mathbf u^{\top}C\mathbf u-\lambda(\mathbf u^{\top}\mathbf u-1)\Big]=2C\mathbf u-2\lambda\mathbf u=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C\mathbf u=\lambda\mathbf u .\]
The stationary directions are the eigenvectors of \(C\), and at an eigenvector the variance is \(\mathbf u^{\top}C\mathbf u=\lambda\). So the best direction is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue. Repeating the argument with the extra constraint that \(\mathbf u\) is orthogonal to the directions already found gives the next eigenvectors in order.
\(C\) is symmetric and positive semi-definite, so it has \(D\) orthonormal eigenvectors \(C\mathbf v_a=\lambda_a\mathbf v_a\) with \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_D\ge 0\). The leading \(m\) eigenvectors are the principal components, and the projection is
\[z_{ia}=\mathbf v_a\cdot(\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}),\qquad a=1,\dots,m,\qquad \text{fraction of variance kept}=\frac{\sum_{a\le m}\lambda_a}{\sum_{a\le D}\lambda_a}.\]
The same subspace also minimises the mean squared reconstruction error \(\frac1n\sum_i\lVert\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}-\sum_{a\le m}z_{ia}\mathbf v_a\rVert^2=\sum_{a>m}\lambda_a\): keeping the largest eigenvalues throws away the least.


2.2 Relation to the singular value decomposition
The covariance matrix need not be formed explicitly. Write the centred data matrix through its singular value decomposition (SVD), \(X_c=USV^{\top}\). Then \(C=\frac1n VS^2V^{\top}\): the right singular vectors are the principal components and \(\lambda_a=s_a^2/n\). Both routes are used below.
Two conventions must be fixed before results from different programs can be compared. scikit-learn divides by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\); this rescales all eigenvalues by the same factor and changes neither the eigenvectors nor the fractions of variance. The sign of each eigenvector is arbitrary; we fix it so that its largest entry (in absolute value) is positive.


2.3 PCA implementation in JAX
The function pca below is decorated with @jax.jit. The first call traces it and compiles it for the given array shape; the next call with the same shape reuses the compiled code. jnp.linalg.eigh diagonalises a symmetric matrix and returns the eigenvalues in increasing order, so we reverse them.


Code
@jax.jit
def covariance(X):
    xbar = X.mean(axis=0)
    Xc = X - xbar
    return xbar, Xc.T @ Xc / X.shape[0]

def fix_signs(V):
    # make the largest-|entry| of every column positive (the sign of an eigenvector is arbitrary)
    idx = jnp.argmax(jnp.abs(V), axis=0)
    return V * jnp.sign(V[idx, jnp.arange(V.shape[1])])

@jax.jit
def pca(X):
    # mean, eigenvalues (largest first) and eigenvectors (columns) of the covariance matrix
    xbar, C = covariance(X)
    lam, V = jnp.linalg.eigh(C)
    return xbar, lam[::-1], fix_signs(V[:, ::-1])


We apply it first to a case small enough to see: a two-dimensional cloud of 400 correlated Gaussian points (jax.random.multivariate_normal takes a key, a mean and a covariance). The first principal axis should point along the long direction of the cloud.
The same cell tests the variance-maximisation argument numerically: we compute \(\mathrm{Var}(z)=\mathbf u(\theta)^{\top}C\,\mathbf u(\theta)\) for 721 unit vectors \(\mathbf u(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). The function var_along is written for one angle; jax.vmap(var_along) evaluates it for the whole array of angles at once (it adds a batch dimension to every operation, instead of a Python loop). The largest variance over all angles must equal \(\lambda_1\), and it must occur at the angle of \(\mathbf v_1\); the printout and the second plot show both.


Code
pts = jax.random.multivariate_normal(section_key(3), jnp.zeros(2), jnp.array([[3.0, 1.6], [1.6, 1.2]]), (400,))
xbar_t, lam_t, V_t = pca(pts)
ratio_t = lam_t / lam_t.sum()
nums["pca_toy_var"] = [round(float(r), 3) for r in ratio_t]
print("eigenvalues:", np.round(np.asarray(lam_t), 3), "| fraction of the variance:", nums["pca_toy_var"])

_, C_t = covariance(pts)
def var_along(theta):
    u = jnp.array([jnp.cos(theta), jnp.sin(theta)])
    return u @ C_t @ u
thetas = jnp.linspace(0, jnp.pi, 721)
var_theta = jax.vmap(var_along)(thetas)
theta_pc1 = jnp.arctan2(V_t[1, 0], V_t[0, 0]) % jnp.pi
print(f"largest variance over the angles: {float(var_theta.max()):.4f} at theta = {float(thetas[jnp.argmax(var_theta)]):.3f}"
      f" | lambda_1 = {float(lam_t[0]):.4f}, direction of v_1: theta = {float(theta_pc1):.3f}")

# figure for the slides: the cloud and its principal axes
P_ = np.asarray(pts - xbar_t)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 3.6))
ax.scatter(P_[:, 0], P_[:, 1], s=8, color=blue, alpha=0.5)
for a_, c, name in zip(range(2), [orange, navy], ["PC 1", "PC 2"]):
    v = np.asarray(V_t[:, a_]); L_ = float(lam_t[a_])
    ax.annotate("", xy=2 * np.sqrt(L_) * v, xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=c, lw=2.5))
    ax.text(*(2.25 * np.sqrt(L_) * v), name, color=c, fontsize=12, ha="center")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$"); clean(ax)
save("gen_pca_toy.png"); plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 2.8))
ax.plot(np.asarray(thetas), np.asarray(var_theta), color=blue)
ax.axvline(float(theta_pc1), color=orange, ls="--", lw=1, label=r"direction of $\mathbf{v}_1$")
ax.axhline(float(lam_t[0]), color="k", ls=":", lw=1, label=r"$\lambda_1$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"angle $\theta$ of $\mathbf{u}$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\mathbf{u}^\top C\,\mathbf{u}$"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9); clean(ax)
plt.show()


eigenvalues: [3.56 0.25] | fraction of the variance: [0.934, 0.066]


largest variance over the angles: 3.5604 at theta = 0.537 | lambda_1 = 3.5604, direction of v_1: theta = 0.535










2.4 PCA on MNIST
The same computation on the 60 000 training images: \(C\) is \(784\times784\), and its leading eigenvectors are themselves \(28\times28\) images (red and blue: positive and negative weights). We then compute the same eigenvalues a second way, from the SVD of the centred \(60000\times784\) data matrix, and compare.


Code
xbar, lam, V = pca(Xtr)
_, C = covariance(Xtr)
frac = jnp.cumsum(lam) / lam.sum()                 # fraction of the variance kept by the first m components
nums["mnist_pca_var2"]  = float(frac[1])
nums["mnist_pca_var3"]  = float(frac[2])
nums["mnist_pca_var10"] = float(frac[9])
nums["mnist_pca_var50"] = float(frac[49])
nums["mnist_pca_frac_2_10_50"] = [round(float(frac[m - 1]), 3) for m in (2, 10, 50)]
nums["mnist_pca_k_for_90"] = int(jnp.searchsorted(frac, 0.90) + 1)
print("variance kept by 2, 3, 10, 50 components:", [round(float(frac[m - 1]), 3) for m in (2, 3, 10, 50)],
      "| components needed for 90%:", nums["mnist_pca_k_for_90"])

# the same eigenvalues from the SVD of the centred data
s = jnp.linalg.svd(Xtr - xbar, compute_uv=False)
lam_svd = s ** 2 / Xtr.shape[0]
print("largest relative difference of the first 50 eigenvalues (eigh vs SVD):",
      f"{float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(lam_svd[:50] - lam[:50]) / lam[:50])):.1e}")

lam_np, V_np, C_np = np.asarray(lam), np.asarray(V), np.asarray(C)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 3.0))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 8, width_ratios=[1.3, 0.25, 1.6, 0.3, 1.6, 0.25, 1, 1], wspace=0.15, hspace=0.3)
a = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 0]); a.imshow(np.asarray(xbar).reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r")
a.set_title(r"mean image $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$", fontsize=10); a.axis("off")
a = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 2]); vm = np.abs(C_np).max(); a.imshow(C_np, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vm, vmax=vm)
a.set_title(r"covariance $C$, $784\times784$", fontsize=10); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
a = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 4]); a.semilogy(np.arange(1, 101), lam_np[:100] / lam_np.sum(), ".-", color=blue)
a.set_title(r"eigenvalues $\lambda_k/\sum_j\lambda_j$", fontsize=10); a.set_xlabel("$k$"); clean(a)
for j in range(4):
    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[j // 2, 6 + j % 2]); w = V_np[:, j]; m = np.abs(w).max()
    a.imshow(w.reshape(28, 28), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-m, vmax=m); a.set_title(rf"$\mathbf{{v}}_{j+1}$", fontsize=10); a.axis("off")
save("gen_pca_mnist_steps.png"); plt.show()

The eigenvalues fall quickly: two components keep about a sixth of the variance, and the number of components needed for 90% is printed above. The two routes, eigendecomposition of \(C\) and SVD of \(X_c\), give the same eigenvalues to float32 precision.


2.5 PCA with scikit-learn
In scikit-learn every method is an estimator object. Its parameters are set when it is created, PCA(n_components=50); the method fit(X) learns from the data and stores the results as attributes with a trailing underscore: the mean image mean_, the principal components as the rows of components_, their variances explained_variance_ and the fractions explained_variance_ratio_. The method transform(X) then projects any data, the training set or new samples, on the learned components (it subtracts mean_ first), fit_transform(X) does both steps at once, and inverse_transform(Z) maps projections back to pixels, \(\bar{\mathbf x}+\sum_a z_a\mathbf v_a\). With svd_solver="full" the components come from a complete SVD of the centred data, the same computation as our second route; scikit-learn fixes the signs with the same convention as we do (largest entry of each component positive).
Since both programs solve the same eigenproblem, the results must agree to float32 precision, and the cell asserts it: the fractions of variance, the components (compared through the cosine of the angle between our \(\mathbf v_a\) and scikit-learn’s), and the projections of the 5000 test images. The variances themselves differ by the factor \(n/(n-1)\) of the two conventions.


Code
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

t = time.time()
sk_pca = PCA(n_components=50, svd_solver="full").fit(np.asarray(Xtr))
print(f"scikit-learn PCA of 60000 x 784: {time.time() - t:.1f} s")

ratio_jax = np.asarray(lam[:50] / lam.sum())
ratio_sk = sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_
cos_v = np.sum(np.asarray(V[:, :50]).T * sk_pca.components_, axis=1)   # cosine between v_a (ours) and component a (sklearn)
n = Xtr.shape[0]
print("fraction of variance, first 5 components:")
print("  JAX         ", np.round(ratio_jax[:5], 5))
print("  scikit-learn", np.round(ratio_sk[:5], 5))
print(f"largest relative difference over 50 components: {np.max(np.abs(ratio_sk - ratio_jax) / ratio_jax):.1e}")
print(f"explained_variance_ / lambda for the first component: {sk_pca.explained_variance_[0] / float(lam[0]):.6f}"
      f"  (n/(n-1) = {n / (n - 1):.6f})")
print(f"cosine between the components: min over the first 10 {cos_v[:10].min():.6f}, min over 50 {cos_v.min():.6f}")

Z_sk = sk_pca.transform(np.asarray(X5))[:, :10]
Z_jax = np.asarray((X5 - xbar) @ V[:, :10])
print(f"projections of the 5000 test images on 10 components: largest |difference| {np.abs(Z_sk - Z_jax).max():.1e}"
      f" (typical |z| {np.abs(Z_jax).mean():.2f})")

assert np.allclose(ratio_sk, ratio_jax, rtol=1e-3)
assert cos_v[:10].min() > 0.9999                       # same components, same signs
assert np.abs(Z_sk - Z_jax).max() < 1e-2 * np.abs(Z_jax).mean()

The fractions of variance agree to float32 precision, and so do the components and the projections; with the common sign convention even the signs coincide. Beyond the first few components the eigenvalues lie closer together, and a small rounding difference can rotate two neighbouring eigenvectors slightly into each other; the minimum cosine over all 50 components, printed above, shows how small this effect is here.


2.6 Reconstruction from a few components
An image is rebuilt from its first \(m\) projections as \(\hat{\mathbf x}=\bar{\mathbf x}+\sum_{a\le m}z_a\mathbf v_a\). With all 784 components the reconstruction is exact; with few components only the coarse shape survives. The column titles give \(m\). The printout compares, for each \(m\), the mean squared reconstruction error per pixel on the 5000 test images with \(\frac1{784}\sum_{a>m}\lambda_a\); the two agree exactly on the training data and closely on the test data.

To see whether the digits form groups in the PCA coordinates, we project the 5000 test images on the 50 leading components and plot the first two, called PC 1 and PC 2 in the figures. The left panel shows what PCA sees, points without labels; the right panel colours the same points by the true digit. Look for digits that occupy their own region and for digits that overlap.
