title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
5. Latent space
Every test image is now described by \(16\) latent numbers. We treat them as a new data set: a linear projection with PCA (computed in JAX with a singular value decomposition, SVD, of the centred latent vectors) and a non-linear map with t-SNE. The colours are the true digits, used only for plotting.
Lab 016 implemented t-SNE and k-means in JAX and compared them with scikit-learn; here we use the scikit-learn estimators directly. TSNE(2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit_transform(Z) returns the two-dimensional map, and KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Z).labels_ the cluster of every point, the best of 10 k-means++ starts. t-SNE places the points in the plane so that the probabilities of being neighbours, computed from the distances in the 16-dimensional space and in the plane, agree as well as possible (it minimises the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the two sets of probabilities). k-means splits the points into \(k\) groups \(S_c\) with centres \(\boldsymbol\mu_c\) so that the sum of squared distances \(\sum_c\sum_{i\in S_c}\lVert\mathbf z_i-\boldsymbol\mu_c\rVert^2\) is as small as possible.
The agreement of a clustering with the true digits is measured by the adjusted Rand index (ARI), adjusted_rand_score(labels, clusters). The Rand index RI is the fraction of pairs of samples on which two partitions agree (both partitions put the pair in the same group, or both in different groups). Even random groups agree on many pairs, so the ARI corrects for chance, \(\mathrm{ARI}=(\mathrm{RI}-\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}])/(1-\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}])\), with \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{RI}]\) the mean of RI over random partitions with the same group sizes: ARI \(=1\) for a perfect match and about \(0\) for a random assignment (Lab 016, Section 4.6).
The question is whether the digits form clusters in the latent space itself. We run k-means (\(k=10\)) directly on the \(16\) latent numbers and on their t-SNE map, and compare with k-means on the pixels (on \(50\) PCA components).


Code
def pca_2d(Z):
    """Projection on the first two principal components, via the SVD of the centred data (in JAX)."""
    Zc = jnp.asarray(Z) - jnp.mean(jnp.asarray(Z), 0)
    _, s, Vt = jnp.linalg.svd(Zc, full_matrices=False)
    return np.asarray(Zc @ Vt[:2].T), float((s[:2] ** 2).sum() / (s ** 2).sum())

def tsne(Z):
    return TSNE(2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit_transform(np.asarray(Z))

def kmeans_ari(Z, labels):
    return float(adjusted_rand_score(labels, KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(np.asarray(Z)).labels_))

def plot_two_maps(P_left, P_right, titles, labels, names=None):
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.9))
    for a, P2, t in zip(axs, [P_left, P_right], titles):
        for c in range(10):
            m = labels == c
            a.scatter(P2[m, 0], P2[m, 1], s=3, color=cmap10(c), label=(names[c] if names else str(c)))
        a.set_title(t, fontsize=11); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    axs[1].legend(markerscale=4, fontsize=8, ncol=2, loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.3, 1))
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig

L16 = encode(ae16, X5_d)                                     # (5000, 16)
L16_pca, _ = pca_2d(L16)
L16_tsne = tsne(L16)
fig = plot_two_maps(L16_pca, L16_tsne, ["PCA of the 16D latent vectors", "t-SNE of the 16D latent vectors"], y5)
save(fig, "gen_ae_latent16_maps.png"); plt.show()

Z50 = np.asarray((X5_d - xbar) @ V[:, :50])                  # the pixels, on 50 principal components
nums["pixels_pca50_kmeans_ari"] = kmeans_ari(Z50, y5)
nums["ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct"] = kmeans_ari(L16, y5)
nums["ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne"] = kmeans_ari(L16_tsne, y5)
print("k-means (k = 10), adjusted Rand index with the true digits:")
print(f"  pixels, 50 PCA components : {nums['pixels_pca50_kmeans_ari']:.3f}")
print(f"  16 latent numbers, directly: {nums['ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct']:.3f}")
print(f"  t-SNE map of the 16 latent numbers: {nums['ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne']:.3f}")





k-means (k = 10), adjusted Rand index with the true digits:
  pixels, 50 PCA components : 0.384
  16 latent numbers, directly: 0.284
  t-SNE map of the 16 latent numbers: 0.696


In the PCA projection the digits overlap: they differ along many of the \(16\) directions, and any two of them show only part of it. The t-SNE map keeps the neighbours of each point and shows groups. k-means directly in the latent space does not recover the digits better than on the pixels: the digits are kept in the latent space, but not as the round, equally sized groups that k-means looks for.

Exercise
Repeat the analysis with the latent space of the \(d=2\) autoencoder (L2), where no projection is needed. Is k-means better or worse there?

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
6. Convolutional autoencoders

A small convolutional autoencoder, \(d=2\)
A dense layer sees an image as a flat list of \(784\) numbers: it does not know which pixels are neighbours. A convolutional encoder uses the 2D structure, like the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) of Lecture 4. Here two convolutions with \(3\times3\) kernels and stride \(2\) (\(28\to14\to7\) pixels, \(16\) and \(32\) channels), then dense layers \(32\cdot7\cdot7\to128\to d\). The decoder mirrors it: dense layers back to \(32\cdot7\cdot7\), then two transposed convolutions with stride \(2\) (\(7\to14\to28\)), the last one with a single channel and a sigmoid.
nnx.Conv expects images with the channels last, of shape (batch, height, width, channels) (NHWC: number of images, height, width, channels), unlike PyTorch’s NCHW, which puts the channels before the height; our MNIST images become (n, 28, 28, 1) with a reshape, which costs nothing. nnx.ConvTranspose(..., strides=2, padding="SAME") doubles the height and width exactly.
On a CPU a convolutional layer costs far more arithmetic per image than a dense layer of similar size, and its gradient even more. To keep the notebook fast we use few channels and train the convolutional models on a random subset of the training images, for fewer epochs (N_CONV, EPOCHS_CONV below). To make up for the fewer images we use smaller minibatches of \(64\): the same arithmetic per epoch, but four times as many gradient steps. The dense autoencoders above used all \(60\,000\) images.


Code
class ConvAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=2, ch=(16, 32), *, rngs):
        c1, c2 = ch
        self.ch = ch
        self.c1 = nnx.Conv(1, c1, (3, 3), strides=2, padding=1, rngs=rngs)           # 28 -> 14
        self.c2 = nnx.Conv(c1, c2, (3, 3), strides=2, padding=1, rngs=rngs)          # 14 -> 7
        self.e1 = nnx.Linear(c2 * 7 * 7, 128, rngs=rngs)
        self.e2 = nnx.Linear(128, d, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.Linear(d, 128, rngs=rngs)
        self.d2 = nnx.Linear(128, c2 * 7 * 7, rngs=rngs)
        self.t1 = nnx.ConvTranspose(c2, c1, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)   # 7 -> 14
        self.t2 = nnx.ConvTranspose(c1, 1, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)    # 14 -> 28

    def encode(self, x, train=False):
        h = nnx.relu(self.c2(nnx.relu(self.c1(x))))
        return self.e2(nnx.relu(self.e1(h.reshape(h.shape[0], -1))))

    def decode(self, z, train=False):
        h = nnx.relu(self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(z)))).reshape(-1, 7, 7, self.ch[1])
        return nnx.sigmoid(self.t2(nnx.relu(self.t1(h))))

    def __call__(self, x, train=False):
        return self.decode(self.encode(x, train), train)

Xtr_img, X5_img = Xtr_d.reshape(-1, 28, 28, 1), X5_d.reshape(-1, 28, 28, 1)
N_CONV, EPOCHS_CONV = 20000, 8                              # training subset and epochs for the convolutional models
sub = np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(len(Xtr))[:N_CONV]
Xsub_img = Xtr_img[sub]
print("training images:", Xsub_img.shape[0], "| epochs:", EPOCHS_CONV)
cae2, hist_c2 = train_autoencoder(ConvAE(2, rngs=nnx.Rngs(3)), Xsub_img, epochs=EPOCHS_CONV, seed=3, batch_size=64)
print("parameters:", n_params(cae2))
Lc = encode(cae2, X5_img)
nums["cae2_test_mse"] = float(errors(cae2, X5_img).mean())
nums["ae2_latent_kmeans_ari"] = kmeans_ari(L2, y5)
nums["cae2_latent_kmeans_ari"] = kmeans_ari(Lc, y5)

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 3.9))
for a, P2, t in zip(axs, [L2, Lc], [f"dense autoencoder (k-means ARI {nums['ae2_latent_kmeans_ari']:.2f})",
                                    f"convolutional autoencoder (k-means ARI {nums['cae2_latent_kmeans_ari']:.2f})"]):
    for c in range(10):
        m = y5 == c
        a.scatter(P2[m, 0], P2[m, 1], s=3, color=cmap10(c), label=str(c))
    a.set_title(t, fontsize=10); a.set_xlabel("latent $z_1$"); a.set_ylabel("latent $z_2$")
axs[1].legend(markerscale=4, fontsize=8, ncol=2, loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.3, 1))
plt.tight_layout(); save(fig, "gen_ae_dense_vs_conv.png"); plt.show()
print({k: round(nums[k], 4) for k in ["ae2_test_mse", "cae2_test_mse", "ae2_latent_kmeans_ari", "cae2_latent_kmeans_ari"]})


training images: 20000 | epochs: 8


  epoch   1: training loss 0.07243   ( 20.1 s)


  epoch   5: training loss 0.04875   (101.7 s)


parameters: 413315





{'ae2_test_mse': 0.0389, 'cae2_test_mse': 0.0445, 'ae2_latent_kmeans_ari': 0.2409, 'cae2_latent_kmeans_ari': 0.2684}


With the same two latent numbers the convolutional encoder gives the higher ARI (printed above), although it saw only a third of the training images and has the larger test MSE: it compares neighbouring pixels, as a CNN does, and builds its two numbers from local strokes rather than from individual pixel positions. The colours are not used in training, so a better ARI is a by-product, not a goal, of the reconstruction loss.


A deeper convolutional autoencoder, \(d=16\)
A deeper model: three convolutions (\(8\), \(16\), \(32\) channels, the last two with stride \(2\)), each followed by batch normalisation and ReLU, then dense layers \(32\cdot7\cdot7\to128\to16\). To save CPU time it is trained on a smaller subset (N_DEEP images, EPOCHS_DEEP epochs). The decoder mirrors it with transposed convolutions and ends with a \(3\times3\) convolution to one channel and a sigmoid.
Batch normalisation rescales every channel to zero mean and unit variance over the current minibatch, then applies a learned scale and shift. During training it uses the minibatch statistics and updates running averages of them; at evaluation it uses the running averages, so that the output for one image does not depend on the other images in the batch. In flax the running averages are nnx.BatchStat variables, not parameters: they are not differentiated, they are part of rest in our training function and are carried through lax.scan next to the parameters. The argument train selects the mode (use_running_average=not train).


Code
class DeepConvAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=16, ch=(8, 16, 32), hidden=128, *, rngs):
        c1, c2, c3 = ch
        self.c3 = c3
        conv = lambda i, o, s: nnx.Conv(i, o, (3, 3), strides=s, padding=1, rngs=rngs)
        tconv = lambda i, o: nnx.ConvTranspose(i, o, (3, 3), strides=2, padding="SAME", rngs=rngs)
        self.enc_convs = nnx.List([conv(1, c1, 1), conv(c1, c2, 2), conv(c2, c3, 2)])     # 28 -> 28 -> 14 -> 7
        self.enc_bns = nnx.List([nnx.BatchNorm(c, rngs=rngs) for c in (c1, c2, c3)])
        self.e1, self.e2 = nnx.Linear(c3 * 7 * 7, hidden, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(hidden, d, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1, self.d2 = nnx.Linear(d, hidden, rngs=rngs), nnx.Linear(hidden, c3 * 7 * 7, rngs=rngs)
        self.dec_tconvs = nnx.List([tconv(c3, c2), tconv(c2, c1)])                       # 7 -> 14 -> 28
        self.dec_bns = nnx.List([nnx.BatchNorm(c, rngs=rngs) for c in (c2, c1)])
        self.out = conv(c1, 1, 1)

    def encode(self, x, train=False):
        for c, bn in zip(self.enc_convs, self.enc_bns):
            x = nnx.relu(bn(c(x), use_running_average=not train))
        return self.e2(nnx.relu(self.e1(x.reshape(x.shape[0], -1))))

    def decode(self, z, train=False):
        h = nnx.relu(self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(z)))).reshape(-1, 7, 7, self.c3)
        for t, bn in zip(self.dec_tconvs, self.dec_bns):
            h = nnx.relu(bn(t(h), use_running_average=not train))
        return nnx.sigmoid(self.out(h))

    def __call__(self, x, train=False):
        return self.decode(self.encode(x, train), train)

N_DEEP, EPOCHS_DEEP = 12000, 6
dcae, hist_d = train_autoencoder(DeepConvAE(16, rngs=nnx.Rngs(4)), Xtr_img[sub[:N_DEEP]], epochs=EPOCHS_DEEP, seed=4, batch_size=64)
print("parameters:", n_params(dcae))
LD = encode(dcae, X5_img)
nums["dcae16_test_mse"] = float(errors(dcae, X5_img).mean())
LD_pca, nums["dcae16_pca2_var"] = pca_2d(LD)
LD_tsne = tsne(LD)
nums["dcae16_kmeans_ari_direct"] = kmeans_ari(LD, y5)
nums["dcae16_kmeans_ari_tsne"] = kmeans_ari(LD_tsne, y5)
fig = plot_two_maps(LD_pca, LD_tsne, ["PCA of the 16D latent vectors (deep conv.)", "t-SNE of the 16D latent vectors (deep conv.)"], y5)
plt.show()
print({k: round(nums[k], 4) for k in ["ae16_test_mse", "dcae16_test_mse", "dcae16_pca2_var",
                                      "ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct", "dcae16_kmeans_ari_direct",
                                      "ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne", "dcae16_kmeans_ari_tsne"]})


  epoch   1: training loss 0.07130   ( 44.9 s)


  epoch   5: training loss 0.01287   (196.3 s)


parameters: 419249





{'ae16_test_mse': 0.0121, 'dcae16_test_mse': 0.0121, 'dcae16_pca2_var': 0.3886, 'ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_direct': 0.2838, 'dcae16_kmeans_ari_direct': 0.4558, 'ae16_latent_kmeans_ari_tsne': 0.6963, 'dcae16_kmeans_ari_tsne': 0.8153}


Compare the two \(d=16\) models: the dense one (all training images, \(15\) epochs) and the convolutional one (a subset, fewer epochs). The test MSE measures how well each rebuilds the pixels, the ARI how well its latent space groups the digits; the two need not go together, since the loss rewards rebuilding pixels, not separating digits.

Exercises

Train DeepConvAE with more channels, e.g. ch=(32, 64, 128), on all \(60\,000\) images (best on a GPU). How do the test MSE and the ARI change?
Remove the batch normalisation layers from DeepConvAE (replace bn(...) by the identity) and train again with the same seed. How do the training curve and the test MSE change?

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
7. Anomaly detection
An autoencoder trained only on normal data rebuilds similar samples well and unusual ones badly. The reconstruction error \[
s(\mathbf x)=e(\mathbf x)=\frac1D\big\lVert\mathbf x-G_{\boldsymbol\theta_D}\big(E_{\boldsymbol\theta_E}(\mathbf x)\big)\big\rVert^2
\] is therefore an anomaly score: the larger, the more surprising the sample for the model. No example of an anomaly is needed for training. To turn the score into a decision we choose a threshold \(\tau\) and flag every sample with \(s(\mathbf x)>\tau\). A natural choice uses only normal data: \(\tau\) = the \(95\)th percentile of the scores of normal samples, so that \(5\%\) of the normal samples are flagged (the false-alarm rate).
To test this idea we train the dense autoencoder (\(d=16\), the same architecture and training as above) on all training digits except the 7s. For the network every 7 is then an unknown kind of image. We compute the score of all \(10\,000\) test digits and ask whether the 7s stand out.


Code
HELD_OUT = 7
aeA, _ = train_autoencoder(DenseAE(d=16, rngs=nnx.Rngs(5)), jnp.asarray(Xtr[ytr != HELD_OUT]), epochs=15, seed=5)
errA = errors(aeA, Xte_d)                                    # anomaly score of every test digit
is7 = yte == HELD_OUT
thr = float(np.percentile(errA[~is7], 95))                   # flags 5% of the normal test digits

print(f"fraction of 7s in the test set {is7.mean():.3f} | 7s among the 16 / 100 largest errors: "
      f"{nums['anom_top16_sevens']} / {nums['anom_top100_sevens']}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.3))
bins = np.linspace(0, np.percentile(errA, 99.5), 60)
ax.hist(errA[~is7], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, color=UJBlue, label="normal digits (0-6, 8, 9)")
ax.hist(errA[is7], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, color=DSOrange, label="7s (never seen)")
ax.axvline(thr, color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label="threshold: 5% of normal digits")
ax.set_xlabel("reconstruction error"); ax.set_ylabel("density"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
save(fig, "gen_anomaly_hist.png"); plt.show()

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(8, 2.4))
for j, a in enumerate(axs.ravel()):
    t = top[j]
    a.imshow(Xte[t].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r"); noframe(a)
    a.set_title(f"true {yte[t]}", fontsize=8, color=DSOrange if is7[t] else "k")
fig.suptitle("the 16 test digits with the largest reconstruction error", fontsize=10)
save(fig, "gen_anomaly_top.png"); plt.show()

threshold (95th percentile of normal digits) 0.0268: flags 0.130 of the 7s

The two histograms overlap strongly. A 7 shares strokes with 1s and 9s, which the network has seen, so many 7s are rebuilt well. Among the digits with the largest error some are 7s, others are badly written digits of the trained classes: for the autoencoder these are anomalies too.

ROC curve and AUC
Every threshold \(\tau\) gives one decision rule. For each we count

the true-positive rate \(\mathrm{TPR}(\tau)=\frac{\#\{\text{anomalies with } s>\tau\}}{\#\{\text{anomalies}\}}\): the fraction of anomalies (here the 7s) found;
the false-positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}(\tau)=\frac{\#\{\text{normal samples with } s>\tau\}}{\#\{\text{normal samples}\}}\): the fraction of normal samples flagged, the false alarms.

Lowering \(\tau\) from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\) traces the ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) \(\big(\mathrm{FPR}(\tau),\mathrm{TPR}(\tau)\big)\) from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\). A useless score lies on the diagonal (as many false alarms as hits); a perfect one goes straight up to \(\mathrm{TPR}=1\) at \(\mathrm{FPR}=0\).
The AUC is the area under the ROC curve. It does not depend on any threshold, and it has a simple probabilistic meaning: if \(s_+\) is the score of a randomly chosen anomaly and \(s_-\) that of a randomly chosen normal sample, \[
\mathrm{AUC}=P(s_+>s_-)+\tfrac12P(s_+=s_-) =\frac{1}{n_+n_-}\sum_{a\in+}\sum_{b\in-}\Big[\mathbb 1(s_a>s_b)+\tfrac12\mathbb 1(s_a=s_b)\Big].
\] \(\mathrm{AUC}=\tfrac12\) for chance, \(1\) for a perfect separation. (This is the Mann–Whitney \(U\) statistic divided by \(n_+n_-\).)


ROC implementation in JAX
Our JAX implementation of the ROC curve sorts the samples by decreasing score: walking down the sorted list is lowering the threshold, and the cumulative counts of anomalies and normal samples give TPR and FPR. Samples with equal scores share one threshold and give one point. The area follows from the trapezoidal rule, and we compare it with the pairwise formula, a single vectorised comparison of all \(n_+\times n_-\) pairs; the two must agree, since the trapezoidal area of the ROC curve is exactly the Mann–Whitney statistic.


Code
def roc_curve(scores, labels):
    """ROC curve of `scores` for binary `labels` (1 = anomaly). Returns FPR, TPR (from (0,0) to (1,1)) and the thresholds."""
    s, y = jnp.asarray(scores), jnp.asarray(labels, dtype=jnp.float32)
    order = jnp.argsort(-s)                                  # decreasing score = decreasing threshold
    s, y = s[order], y[order]
    tp, fp = jnp.cumsum(y), jnp.cumsum(1.0 - y)              # counts above the threshold placed after each sample
    last_of_tie = jnp.append(s[1:] != s[:-1], True)          # equal scores: one threshold, one point
    tpr = jnp.concatenate([jnp.zeros(1), tp[last_of_tie] / y.sum()])
    fpr = jnp.concatenate([jnp.zeros(1), fp[last_of_tie] / (1.0 - y).sum()])
    return np.asarray(fpr), np.asarray(tpr), np.asarray(s[last_of_tie])

def auc_trapezoid(fpr, tpr):
    return float(jnp.trapezoid(jnp.asarray(tpr), jnp.asarray(fpr)))

@jax.jit
def auc_pairwise(s_pos, s_neg):
    """P(s+ > s-) + P(s+ = s-)/2 over all pairs (Mann-Whitney)."""
    diff = s_pos[:, None] - s_neg[None, :]
    return jnp.mean((diff > 0) + 0.5 * (diff == 0))

fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(errA, is7)
nums["anom_auc"] = auc_trapezoid(fpr, tpr)
auc_pairs = float(auc_pairwise(jnp.asarray(errA[is7]), jnp.asarray(errA[~is7])))
print(f"AUC (trapezoid on the ROC curve) = {nums['anom_auc']:.4f}  |  AUC (all {is7.sum()} x {(~is7).sum()} pairs) = {auc_pairs:.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.4, 4.0))
ax.fill_between(fpr, tpr, color=DSOrange, alpha=0.15)
ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color=DSOrange, lw=2, label=f"7s, never seen: AUC = {nums['anom_auc']:.2f}")
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", lw=1, label="chance: AUC = 0.5")
ax.plot(0.05, nums["anom_frac7_flagged"], "o", color="k", ms=6)
ax.annotate("threshold: 5% false alarms", (0.05, nums["anom_frac7_flagged"]), xytext=(0.22, 0.12), fontsize=9,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=0.8))
ax.set_xlabel("false-positive rate (normal digits flagged)"); ax.set_ylabel("true-positive rate (7s flagged)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower right")
save(fig, "gen_anomaly_roc.png"); plt.show()


AUC (trapezoid on the ROC curve) = 0.6958  |  AUC (all 1028 x 8972 pairs) = 0.6958





The black dot is the decision rule of the histogram: at \(5\%\) false alarms it finds the fraction of 7s printed above. An AUC of about \(0.7\) means that a randomly chosen 7 has a larger reconstruction error than a randomly chosen normal digit in about seven cases out of ten: a real signal, but a weak one.


ROC curve and AUC with scikit-learn
The same analysis is available in sklearn.metrics. roc_curve(y_true, y_score) takes the true binary labels (1 for the positive class, here the anomalies) and the scores, and returns three arrays: the FPR, the TPR and the thresholds, in decreasing order of the threshold, starting from the point \((0,0)\) with the threshold \(+\infty\). By default (drop_intermediate=True) it removes points that lie on a straight segment of the curve and do not change its shape; with drop_intermediate=False it keeps one point per distinct score, which is exactly our construction. roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score) returns the area.
Both are deterministic functions of the scores, so they must agree with ours exactly (up to float32 rounding of our cumulative sums), and the cell asserts it: the full curves point by point and the AUC.


Code
fpr_sk, tpr_sk, thr_sk = metrics.roc_curve(is7, errA, drop_intermediate=False)
auc_sk = float(metrics.roc_auc_score(is7, errA))
print(f"points on the curve: JAX {len(fpr)} | scikit-learn {len(fpr_sk)}"
      f" (with drop_intermediate=True: {len(metrics.roc_curve(is7, errA)[0])})")
print(f"largest difference of the curves: FPR {np.abs(fpr_sk - fpr).max():.1e}, TPR {np.abs(tpr_sk - tpr).max():.1e}")
print(f"AUC: JAX {nums['anom_auc']:.6f} | scikit-learn {auc_sk:.6f}")
assert len(fpr_sk) == len(fpr) and np.allclose(fpr_sk, fpr, atol=1e-5) and np.allclose(tpr_sk, tpr, atol=1e-5)
assert abs(auc_sk - nums["anom_auc"]) < 1e-5


points on the curve: JAX 9998 | scikit-learn 9998 (with drop_intermediate=True: 1799)
largest difference of the curves: FPR 3.8e-08, TPR 3.0e-08
AUC: JAX 0.695764 | scikit-learn 0.695764



Exercises

Hold out another digit instead of the 7 (change HELD_OUT). Which digits are easy anomalies and which are hard? Can you relate this to the shapes of the digits?
Use the deep convolutional autoencoder for the anomaly score. Does a model that rebuilds digits better also detect the 7s better?

8. CIFAR-10: photographs
CIFAR-10 (Lecture 4) contains \(32\times32\) colour photographs in \(10\) classes, \(50\,000\) for training and \(10\,000\) for testing, so \(D=32\cdot32\cdot3=3072\). Each image is stored as one row of \(3072\) bytes: first the \(1024\) red values, then the green, then the blue, each in row-major order. The files are Python pickles; we read them with pickle and numpy.


Code
CIFAR_DIR = "data/cifar-10-batches-py"
if not os.path.isdir(CIFAR_DIR):
    os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
    urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar-10-python.tar.gz", "data/cifar-10-python.tar.gz")
    with tarfile.open("data/cifar-10-python.tar.gz") as tf:
        tf.extractall("data")

def cifar_batch(name):
    with open(os.path.join(CIFAR_DIR, name), "rb") as fh:
        d = pickle.load(fh, encoding="bytes")
    return d[b"data"].astype(np.float32) / 255.0, np.array(d[b"labels"])

Ctr = np.concatenate([p[0] for p in parts]); cytr = np.concatenate([p[1] for p in parts])

The reconstructions keep the colours and the coarse layout of the scene but lose the details, and the classes do not separate in the latent space: two photographs of the same class can differ in almost every pixel (pose, background, lighting), and a pixel-wise loss puts them far apart.

Exercise
Compare with MNIST: why are the CIFAR-10 classes so much harder to separate from the pixels? Train the CNN of Lecture 4 and run t-SNE on its last hidden layer instead.



Anomaly detection: a clear case
The 7s were a subtle anomaly. Now a very different input: the dense autoencoder trained on all MNIST digits (\(d=16\), ae16 from Section 4) receives CIFAR-10 photographs, converted to grayscale with the luminance weights \(0.299R+0.587G+0.114B\) and resized from \(32\times32\) to \(28\times28\) with jax.image.resize (bilinear interpolation). The normal samples are the \(10\,000\) MNIST test digits, the anomalies the first \(5000\) CIFAR-10 test photographs; the threshold again flags \(5\%\) of the normal samples. The cell also compares our AUC with metrics.roc_auc_score.


Code
gray = 0.299 * Cte[:5000, :1024] + 0.587 * Cte[:5000, 1024:2048] + 0.114 * Cte[:5000, 2048:]
ood = jax.image.resize(jnp.asarray(gray).reshape(-1, 32, 32), (5000, 28, 28), method="bilinear").reshape(-1, 784)
ood = jnp.clip(ood, 0.0, 1.0)

err_in = errors(ae16, Xte_d)                                 # normal: MNIST test digits
err_ood = errors(ae16, ood)                                  # anomalies: photographs
thr_in = float(np.percentile(err_in, 95))
nums["ood_threshold"] = thr_in
nums["ood_frac_flagged"] = float((err_ood > thr_in).mean())
fpr_o, tpr_o, _ = roc_curve(np.r_[err_in, err_ood], np.r_[np.zeros(len(err_in)), np.ones(len(err_ood))])
nums["ood_auc"] = auc_trapezoid(fpr_o, tpr_o)
nums["ood_auc_pairwise"] = float(auc_pairwise(jnp.asarray(err_ood), jnp.asarray(err_in)))

nums["ood_median_err_photos"] = float(np.median(err_ood))

print(f"AUC (trapezoid) {nums['ood_auc']:.4f} | AUC (pairs) {nums['ood_auc_pairwise']:.4f}")
print(f"median error: digits {nums['ood_median_err_digits']:.4f} | photographs {nums['ood_median_err_photos']:.4f}")
auc_ood_sk = float(metrics.roc_auc_score(np.r_[np.zeros(len(err_in)), np.ones(len(err_ood))], np.r_[err_in, err_ood]))
print(f"AUC: JAX {nums['ood_auc']:.6f} | scikit-learn {auc_ood_sk:.6f}")
assert abs(auc_ood_sk - nums["ood_auc"]) < 1e-5

rec_ood = reconstruct(ae16, ood[:4])
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.5, 3.2))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 6, width_ratios=[1.6, 0.25, 0.55, 0.55, 0.55, 0.55], wspace=0.08, hspace=0.08)

ax.hist(err_ood, bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, color=DSOrange, label="CIFAR-10, grayscale 28x28")
ax.axvline(thr_in, color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label="threshold: 5% of the digits")
ax.set_xlabel("reconstruction error"); ax.set_ylabel("density"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)

        a = fig.add_subplot(gs[r, 2 + j]); a.imshow(src.reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1)

        if j == 0: a.set_ylabel(["input", "reconstruction"][r], fontsize=9)

Code

The autoencoder trained on all digits rebuilds a digit well: small reconstruction error. A photograph is unlike anything it was trained on: the decoder can only produce digit-like images, the error is large, and the photograph is flagged. We show a typical case of each: the digit and the photograph whose errors are the medians of their groups. The two error maps share one colour scale.

title: Lab 017: Autoencoders and anomaly detection
text:
9. Summary
An autoencoder is an encoder and a decoder trained together to rebuild their input through a bottleneck of \(d\) numbers. The loss is the pixel-wise MSE, so no labels are needed, and the bottleneck acts as a learned, lossy compression. A linear autoencoder spans the PCA subspace, while non-linear layers compress better than any projection.
The latent space keeps the structure of the data, in the sense that similar images get nearby \(\mathbf z\), but its geometry is not designed for clustering; convolutional encoders, which see neighbouring pixels, separate the digits better. The reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained on normal data is an anomaly score. The ROC curve shows all thresholds at once, and the AUC is the probability that an anomaly scores higher than a normal sample. Anomalies far from the training data, such as photographs for an MNIST autoencoder, are easy to detect; anomalies that resemble the training data, such as a held-out digit, are hard.
The numbers quoted on the slides are saved below.

title: Lab 018: Classical spin models in JAX, the 2D Ising and the J1–J2 model
text:
1. The model
Spins \(s_i=\pm1\) sit on an \(L\times L\) square lattice with periodic boundaries. Every spin has four nearest neighbours (left, right, up, down) and four next-nearest neighbours (along the diagonals). The energy is \[
H(\boldsymbol s) = -J_1\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} s_i s_j \;+\; J_2\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle} s_i s_j ,
\qquad J_1>0,\quad J_2\ge 0,
\] with \(\langle i,j\rangle\) the \(2N\) nearest-neighbour bonds and \(\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle\) the \(2N\) diagonal bonds (\(N=L^2\)).

\(J_1>0\) is ferromagnetic: nearest neighbours want to be parallel.
\(J_2>0\) (with the \(+\) sign in \(H\)) is antiferromagnetic: diagonal neighbours want to be antiparallel.

We set \(J_1=1\) and use the single control parameter \[
g = J_2/J_1 .
\] Together with the temperature \(T\) (with \(k_B=1\)) this gives a two-dimensional phase diagram in the \((g,T)\) plane.
Two limits are already understood. At \(g=0\) the model is the 2D Ising model, solved exactly by Onsager, with \(T_c=2/\ln(1+\sqrt2)\approx 2.269\). For \(g\to\infty\) (\(J_1\to0\)) only diagonal bonds remain. The diagonal bonds connect sites of the same chessboard colour, so the lattice splits into two independent square lattices (rotated by \(45^\circ\)), each an antiferromagnetic Ising model with coupling \(J_2\). Flipping every second spin of such a lattice maps the antiferromagnet onto a ferromagnet with the same partition function, so each sub-lattice orders at \(T = J_2\,T_c^{\rm Ising}\), i.e. \(T_c/J_1 \to g\,T_c^{\rm Ising}\) for large \(g\).
Between these limits the two couplings compete, and that is where the interesting physics is.

1.1 Ground states
At \(T=0\) the system sits in the configuration of lowest energy. Consider three candidate patterns and count the bonds per spin (2 nearest-neighbour bonds and 2 diagonal bonds per spin):









pattern
nearest-neighbour bonds
diagonal bonds

The Néel state is never favourable for \(J_1>0\). The ferromagnet and the stripe state have equal energy when \(-2J_1+2J_2=-2J_2\), i.e. at \[
g = \tfrac12 .
\] For \(g<1/2\) the ground state is ferromagnetic (2 states: all up, all down). For \(g>1/2\) it is the stripe (also called collinear or super-antiferromagnetic) state: 4 states (vertical or horizontal stripes, and the global flip).
At exactly \(g=1/2\) a single ferromagnetic row can be inserted into a stripe pattern at no energy cost, and many mixed patterns become degenerate: the system is frustrated, it cannot satisfy both couplings, and the number of ground states grows exponentially with the system size.
The table only compared three guesses. On a small lattice we can check all \(2^{N}\) configurations, which is a good first exercise in JAX.


1.2 Exhaustive enumeration on a \(4\times4\) lattice
A \(4\times4\) lattice has \(2^{16}=65\,536\) configurations, few enough to compute the energy of every one of them; this is also a first look at vmap and jit. We write the energy of one configuration, then let jax.vmap turn it into a function of a whole batch, and jax.jit compile it.
Two building blocks are used throughout the notebook. The function jnp.roll(s, 1, axis) shifts the lattice by one site with periodic wrap-around, so s * jnp.roll(s, 1, 0) lists the products over all vertical bonds at once. And the energy splits into two integers, \(H = -J_1\,B_1(\boldsymbol s) + J_2\,B_2(\boldsymbol s)\), with \(B_1=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\) and \(B_2=\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}s_is_j\); we compute \(B_1\), \(B_2\) once and then get \(H\) for every \(g\) for free.


Code
def bond_sums(s):
    # B1 = sum over nearest-neighbour bonds of s_i s_j,  B2 = same over diagonal bonds  (each bond counted once)
    b1 = jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, 1, 0)) + jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, 1, 1))
    b2 = jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, (1, 1), (0, 1))) + jnp.sum(s * jnp.roll(s, (1, -1), (0, 1)))
    return b1, b2

def all_configs(L):
    n = L * L
    idx = jnp.arange(2**n, dtype=jnp.int32)
    bits = (idx[:, None] >> jnp.arange(n)) & 1
    return (2 * bits - 1).reshape(-1, L, L).astype(jnp.float32)

S4 = all_configs(4)
B1, B2 = jax.jit(jax.vmap(bond_sums))(S4)          # one call, 65 536 configurations

1.3 Order parameters
Each ordered phase is characterised by a quantity that is non-zero in that phase and zero elsewhere, an order parameter. For ordering patterns that repeat with a wave vector \(\boldsymbol k\) the natural choice is the Fourier component of the spins, \[
m_{\boldsymbol k}(\boldsymbol s) = \frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol r} s_{\boldsymbol r}\, e^{i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r},
\] and its square summed over many \(\boldsymbol k\) is the static structure factor \(S(\boldsymbol k)=N\langle|m_{\boldsymbol k}|^2\rangle\), measured in neutron scattering.

The stripe order parameter combines the two wave vectors because vertical and horizontal stripes have the same energy.
The table contains the key point for this lecture: the magnetisation \(m\) is zero in the stripe phase: half of the spins are up and half are down. A scan of \(\langle|m|\rangle\) over the \((g,T)\) plane therefore sees the stripe phase as “disordered”. To see it, one has to know that stripes exist and measure \(m_{\rm str}\). For the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model we know this from the ground-state analysis. For a new material or a new model we often do not know which quantity to plot.


Code
def order_parameters(s):
    # s: (..., L, L) with values +-1.  Returns |m|, m_stripe, m_neel, and energy terms B1, B2 per spin.
    L = s.shape[-1]
    ph = jnp.where(jnp.arange(L) % 2 == 0, 1.0, -1.0)                 # e^{i pi x} = (-1)^x
    m = s.mean((-2, -1))
    m_pi0 = (s * ph[:, None]).mean((-2, -1))                           # k = (pi, 0)
    m_0pi = (s * ph[None, :]).mean((-2, -1))                           # k = (0, pi)
    m_pipi = (s * ph[:, None] * ph[None, :]).mean((-2, -1))           # k = (pi, pi)
    return {"m": jnp.abs(m), "m_str": jnp.sqrt(m_pi0**2 + m_0pi**2), "m_neel": jnp.abs(m_pipi)}

for name, p in patterns.items():
    o = order_parameters(jnp.asarray(p))

1.4 Mean-field theory at finite temperature
The simplest approximation at \(T>0\) is mean-field theory: replace the neighbours of spin \(i\) by their thermal averages \(\langle s_j\rangle\). The spin then feels the field \[
h_i = J_1\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)}\langle s_j\rangle - J_2\sum_{j\in{\rm nnn}(i)}\langle s_j\rangle, \qquad \langle s_i\rangle = \tanh(\beta h_i).
\] For the ferromagnetic ansatz \(\langle s_j\rangle = m\) this gives \(h = (4J_1-4J_2)m\), so \(m=\tanh(\beta(4J_1-4J_2)m)\), which has a non-zero solution below \(T^{\rm MF}_{\rm FM} = 4J_1-4J_2 = 4(1-g)\). For the stripe ansatz (columns alternate, \(\langle s_j\rangle=\pm m\)) the nearest-neighbour contributions cancel (two parallel, two antiparallel), and all four diagonal neighbours are antiparallel, so \(h = 4J_2 m\) and \(T^{\rm MF}_{\rm str}=4J_2 = 4g\).
Mean-field theory predicts the two lines meet at \(g=1/2\) at \(T=2\). This is wrong: fluctuations between the many degenerate ground states destroy the order, and the true transition temperature goes to zero at \(g=1/2\). Mean field also overestimates \(T_c\) at \(g=0\) (\(4\) instead of \(2.269\)), because it neglects fluctuations, which are strong in two dimensions.
Large-scale numerics give the following picture, although the questions are subtle and partly still debated. For \(g<1/2\) there is a continuous transition from the paramagnet to the ferromagnet, in the 2D Ising universality class, with \(T_c(g)\) decreasing to \(0\) at \(g=1/2\). For \(g>1/2\) there is a transition to the stripe phase. For \(g\) slightly above \(1/2\) it is weakly first order; above a multicritical point it is continuous, with exponents that vary along the line (Ashkin–Teller criticality) and approach the Ising ones as \(g\to\infty\). Kalz, Honecker, Fuchs and Pruschke (Eur. Phys. J. B 65, 533 (2008)) found weakly first-order transitions for moderate \(J_2>J_1/2\); Jin, Sen and Sandvik (Phys. Rev. Lett. 108, 045702 (2012)) and Jin, Sen, Guo and Sandvik (Phys. Rev. B 87, 144406 (2013)) placed the multicritical point at \(g^*\approx0.67\) and showed that continuous transitions above \(g^*\) can look first order on finite lattices; tensor-network calculations by Li and Yang (Phys. Rev. E 104, 024118 (2021)) suggest that the first-order window is narrower.
The lesson: even for a model this simple, the phase diagram required decades of work, careful finite-size analysis, and knowledge of the right order parameters. In Lab 020 we ask how much of it an algorithm can find without being told what to look for.


1.5 Thermal averages and their estimators
Before we sample, we fix what every number in this notebook means. In thermal equilibrium at temperature \(T\) (inverse temperature \(\beta=1/T\), \(k_B=1\)) a configuration \(\boldsymbol s\) occurs with the Boltzmann probability \[
p(\boldsymbol s)=\frac{e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)}}{Z},\qquad Z=\sum_{\boldsymbol s}e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)},
\] and an observable \(O(\boldsymbol s)\) of a single configuration has the thermal average \(\langle O\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\boldsymbol s}O(\boldsymbol s)\,e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol s)}\). The partition function also generates the thermodynamics: the energy per spin is the first derivative of \(\ln Z\) with respect to \(\beta\), and the specific heat per spin is the second derivative, which equals the variance of the energy, \[
\langle e\rangle=\frac{\langle H\rangle}{N}=-\frac1N\,\frac{\partial\ln Z}{\partial\beta},\qquad
c=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\,\frac{\partial^2\ln Z}{\partial\beta^2}=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\big(\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2\big)=N\beta^2\big(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\big).
\] On the \(4\times4\) lattice the sums over all \(2^{16}\) configurations can be done, and the function exact_4x4 below computes \(\langle e\rangle\), \(\langle|m|\rangle\) and \(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle\) literally as these weighted sums. On larger lattices Monte Carlo draws \(n\) configurations \(\boldsymbol s^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol s^{(n)}\) with probability \(p(\boldsymbol s)\) at each \((g,T)\), and every average is estimated by the sample mean \(\overline{O}=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nO(\boldsymbol s^{(k)})\). The table lists each observable in both forms; the estimators are those of the functions energy_per_spin, order_parameters and observables below. Here \(e_k=H(\boldsymbol s^{(k)})/N\) (computed as \(-\frac1{2N}\sum_i s_ih_i\), since every bond appears twice in \(\sum_is_ih_i\)), \(m_k=\frac1N\sum_is^{(k)}_i\), and \(\overline{x}\) is the mean over the \(n\) samples. On a finite lattice without a field \(\langle m\rangle=0\) by the symmetry \(\boldsymbol s\to-\boldsymbol s\), which is why \(|m|\) is used.

All variances in the maps of Section 5 are population variances (division by \(n\), jnp.var); the subsampling study of Section 5.1 uses the unbiased variance (division by \(n-1\), var(ddof=1)), which matters for its small subsets of 10 samples.
Section 2.2 also uses a dynamical quantity, the autocorrelation of \(|m|\) along a chain. With \(x_t=|m|\) after step \(t\) of one chain, \(\delta x_t=x_t-\overline{x}\) (mean over the chain) and \(v=\overline{\delta x^2}\), its definition and estimator are \[
A(t)=\frac{\langle x_sx_{s+t}\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2}{\langle x^2\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2},\qquad
\widehat A(t)=\frac{1}{n_{\rm ch}}\sum_{\rm chains}\frac{1}{v}\,\frac{1}{n-t}\sum_{s=1}^{n-t}\delta x_s\,\delta x_{s+t},
\] averaged over the \(n_{\rm ch}\) chains, and the integrated autocorrelation time is estimated as \(\tau=\tfrac12+\sum_{t=1}^{t^*-1}\widehat A(t)\), with \(t^*\) the first lag at which \(\widehat A(t)<0.05\).

title: Lab 018: Classical spin models in JAX, the 2D Ising and the J1–J2 model
text:
2. Metropolis Monte Carlo in JAX
The algorithm, derived in Lab 010, proposes to flip spin \(i\) and accepts with probability \(\min(1, e^{-\beta\Delta E})\). With the local field \[
h_i = J_1\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)} s_j - J_2\sum_{j\in{\rm nnn}(i)} s_j ,\qquad \Delta E_i = 2\,s_i\,h_i .
\]
Spins can be flipped simultaneously only if they do not interact. For the Ising model the chessboard colouring works, but here diagonal neighbours have the same chessboard colour. We use four sub-lattices labelled by \((x \bmod 2,\, y \bmod 2)\): nearest neighbours differ in one parity, diagonal neighbours in both, so no two spins of one sub-lattice are coupled. In code a sub-lattice is the strided slice s[a::2, b::2], and we only draw random numbers for the spins we update. One sweep = four sub-lattice updates = one attempted flip per spin.
The JAX structure follows from this. A pure function sweep(s, key, g, beta) updates one lattice; randomness is explicit, a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) key goes in and a new key comes out. lax.scan repeats a step many times inside one compiled program, with no Python loop overhead. jax.vmap maps the whole simulation over chains, every chain with its own \(g\) and its own random key, so all values of \(g\) run at once. jax.jit compiles the result into a single program (XLA, Accelerated Linear Algebra, the compiler behind JAX, fuses the array operations; on a graphics processing unit, GPU, the same code runs unchanged).
Each chain is annealed: it starts at the highest temperature and is cooled step by step; at each temperature it first equilibrates for n_equil sweeps and then stores n_samples configurations separated by n_between sweeps (to reduce correlations between stored samples). Cooling slowly, rather than starting each temperature from a random state, helps the chain find the ordered state at low \(T\).


Code
def local_field(s, g):
    # s: (..., L, L); the rolls act on the two lattice axes, so the same function works for one lattice or a batch
    nn = jnp.roll(s, 1, -2) + jnp.roll(s, -1, -2) + jnp.roll(s, 1, -1) + jnp.roll(s, -1, -1)
    nnn = (jnp.roll(s, (1, 1), (-2, -1)) + jnp.roll(s, (1, -1), (-2, -1))
           + jnp.roll(s, (-1, 1), (-2, -1)) + jnp.roll(s, (-1, -1), (-2, -1)))
    return nn - g * nnn                                     # J1 = 1, J2 = g

def energy_per_spin(s, g):
    return -0.5 * jnp.mean(s * local_field(s, g), axis=(-2, -1))   # each bond appears twice in sum_i s_i h_i

def sweep(s, key, g, beta):
    for a, b in ((0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)):          # the four sub-lattices (a Python loop, unrolled by jit)
        key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
        si = s[a::2, b::2]
        dE = 2.0 * si * local_field(s, g)[a::2, b::2]
        accept = jax.random.uniform(sub, si.shape) < jnp.exp(-beta * dE)
        s = s.at[a::2, b::2].set(jnp.where(accept, -si, si))
    return s, key

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_samples", "n_between"))
def anneal_chains(s0, keys, gs, Ts, n_equil, n_samples, n_between):
    # s0: (chains, L, L), keys: (chains, 2), gs: (chains,), Ts: (nT,) in the order visited.
    # Returns int8 samples of shape (chains, nT, n_samples, L, L).
    def one_chain(s, key, g):
        def at_T(carry, T):
            step = lambda c, _: (sweep(c[0], c[1], g, 1.0 / T), None)
            carry, _ = lax.scan(step, carry, None, length=n_equil)
            def store(c, _):
                c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
                return c, c[0].astype(jnp.int8)
            return lax.scan(store, carry, None, length=n_samples)
        _, samples = lax.scan(at_T, (s, key), Ts)
        return samples
    return jax.vmap(one_chain)(s0, keys, gs)

def run(L, gs, Ts, n_chains, n_equil, n_samples, n_between, seed):
    # gs: (nG,) couplings; every g gets n_chains independent chains. Returns (nG, nT, n_chains * n_samples, L, L) int8.
    G = jnp.repeat(jnp.asarray(gs, jnp.float32), n_chains)
    k_init, k_run = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    s0 = jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(k_init, 0.5, (G.size, L, L)), 1.0, -1.0)
    out = anneal_chains(s0, jax.random.split(k_run, G.size), G, jnp.asarray(Ts, jnp.float32),
                        n_equil, n_samples, n_between)
    out = np.asarray(out).reshape(len(gs), n_chains, len(Ts), n_samples, L, L)
    return out.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5).reshape(len(gs), len(Ts), n_chains * n_samples, L, L)



2.1 Exact benchmarks
Before producing data we test the sampler against two exact results. On the \(4\times4\) lattice we know the exact thermal averages for any \(g\) from the \(2^{16}\) states enumerated above. At \(g=0\) and large \(L\) the magnetisation must follow Yang’s exact result \(M(T)=\left(1-\sinh^{-4}(2/T)\right)^{1/8}\) below \(T_c\), and the energy must follow Onsager’s \(u(T)\).


Code
def exact_4x4(g, T):
    e = (-np.asarray(B1) + g * np.asarray(B2)) / 16
    o = order_parameters(S4)
    w = np.exp(-16 * (e - e.min()) / T); w /= w.sum()
    return (w * e).sum(), (w * np.asarray(o["m"])).sum(), (w * np.asarray(o["m_str"])).sum()

checks = [(0.0, 1.5), (0.3, 1.0), (0.5, 0.8), (0.8, 1.5), (1.0, 3.0)]
t0 = time.time()
for g, T in checks:
    smp = run(4, [g], [T], n_chains=256, n_equil=500, n_samples=50, n_between=5, seed=1)[0, 0].astype(np.float32)
    o = order_parameters(jnp.asarray(smp)); e = np.asarray(energy_per_spin(jnp.asarray(smp), g))
    e_ex, m_ex, ms_ex = exact_4x4(g, T)
    print(f"g={g:.1f} T={T:.1f}:  <e> {e.mean():+.4f} (exact {e_ex:+.4f})   <|m|> {float(o['m'].mean()):.4f} "
          f"(exact {m_ex:.4f})   <m_str> {float(o['m_str'].mean()):.4f} (exact {ms_ex:.4f})")
print(f"{time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

def M_exact(T):
    T = np.asarray(T, float); out = np.zeros_like(T); low = T < TC_ISING
    out[low] = (1 - np.sinh(2 / T[low]) ** -4) ** 0.125
    return out

def u_exact(T):
    K = 1.0 / np.asarray(T, float)
    kap = 2 * np.sinh(2 * K) / np.cosh(2 * K) ** 2
    return -1 / np.tanh(2 * K) * (1 + 2 / np.pi * (2 * np.tanh(2 * K) ** 2 - 1) * ellipk(kap**2))

Away from \(T_c\) the Monte Carlo points lie on the exact curves. Near \(T_c\) the finite lattice rounds the transition: \(\langle|m|\rangle\) stays non-zero above \(T_c\) because a finite system always has a finite magnetisation fluctuation. This finite-size rounding is the subject of Lab 019.

Exercise
Set n_equil=50 in the cell above and look at the points just below \(T_c\). Why does the agreement get worse there first?



2.2 Critical slowing down and the Swendsen–Wang algorithm
Near \(T_c\) the lattice is made of correlated domains of all sizes up to \(L\). Metropolis flips one spin at a time, and a single flip inside a large domain is almost always rejected (it costs energy at every bond). To turn a whole domain around the chain must move its boundary step by step, which takes very many sweeps: consecutive samples are nearly copies of each other. This is critical slowing down; the autocorrelation time grows as a power of \(L\) (measured below).
The remedy is to flip whole domains at once, but to choose them randomly in a way that keeps the Boltzmann distribution exact. The tool is a one-line identity for the weight of a single bond, with \(p = 1-e^{-2\beta J}\): \[
e^{\beta J s_is_j} \;=\; e^{\beta J}\Big[\,(1-p) \;+\; p\,\delta_{s_i s_j}\Big].
\] (For \(s_i=s_j\) the bracket is \(1\); for \(s_i\neq s_j\) it is \(1-p=e^{-2\beta J}\).) Read the two terms as a bond variable \(b_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\): “no bond” with weight \(1-p\), or “bond” with weight \(p\), allowed only between parallel spins. Multiplying over all bonds gives a joint distribution of spins and bonds whose sum over bonds is exactly \(e^{-\beta H}\) (Fortuin and Kasteleyn’s random-cluster representation). Sampling the two variables alternately is the algorithm:

bonds given spins: between every pair of parallel neighbours, place a bond with probability \(p\), independently;
spins given bonds: the only constraint is that bonded spins are equal, so every connected cluster of bonds carries one common sign, chosen independently with probability \(1/2\) for each cluster.

Each step samples exactly from a conditional distribution of the joint distribution, so the pair of steps leaves \(e^{-\beta H}\) invariant. Near \(T_c\) the clusters have all sizes, and one update can turn around a domain as large as the lattice. The method works for ferromagnetic couplings (a bond requires parallel spins to lower the energy); for the frustrated \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model we keep Metropolis.
Finding connected clusters is usually a sequential graph search. In array form, as JAX needs it, every site starts with a label (its own index) and we repeat two operations until nothing changes: each site takes the smallest label among itself and its bonded neighbours, and then the label of its label (pointer jumping). Each iteration is a few jnp.roll and jnp.minimum operations on the whole lattice, inside a lax.while_loop.
References: R. H. Swendsen, J.-S. Wang, Phys. Rev. Lett. 58, 86 (1987), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86; C. M. Fortuin, P. W. Kasteleyn, Physica 57, 536 (1972); the single-cluster variant: U. Wolff, Phys. Rev. Lett. 62, 361 (1989), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.62.361; textbook: Newman and Barkema (references at the end).


Code
def cluster_labels(bond_r, bond_d):
    # bond_r[x, y]: (x, y) bonded to (x, y+1);  bond_d[x, y]: (x, y) bonded to (x+1, y);  periodic lattice
    L = bond_r.shape[0]
    big = L * L
    bond_l, bond_u = jnp.roll(bond_r, 1, 1), jnp.roll(bond_d, 1, 0)       # bonds to the left / upper neighbour
    def body(carry):
        lab, _ = carry
        m = lab
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_r, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 1), big))
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_l, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 1), big))
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_d, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 0), big))
        m = jnp.minimum(m, jnp.where(bond_u, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 0), big))
        m = m.ravel()[m]                                                  # pointer jumping
        return m, jnp.any(m != lab)
    lab, _ = lax.while_loop(lambda c: c[1], body, (jnp.arange(L * L).reshape(L, L), True))
    return lab

def sw_step(s, key, beta):
    k1, k2, k3 = jax.random.split(key, 3)
    p = 1.0 - jnp.exp(-2.0 * beta)
    bond_r = (s == jnp.roll(s, -1, 1)) & (jax.random.uniform(k1, s.shape) < p)
    bond_d = (s == jnp.roll(s, -1, 0)) & (jax.random.uniform(k2, s.shape) < p)
    lab = cluster_labels(bond_r, bond_d)
    flip = jax.random.bernoulli(k3, 0.5, (s.size,))                       # one coin per cluster label
    return jnp.where(flip[lab], -s, s)

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_samples", "n_between"))
def sw_chains(s0, keys, Ts, n_equil, n_samples, n_between):
    def one_chain(s, key):
        def at_T(carry, T):
            def step(c, _):
                s, key = c
                key, k = jax.random.split(key)
                return (sw_step(s, k, 1.0 / T), key), None
            carry, _ = lax.scan(step, carry, None, length=n_equil)
            def store(c, _):
                c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
                return c, c[0].astype(jnp.int8)
            return lax.scan(store, carry, None, length=n_samples)
        return lax.scan(at_T, (s, key), Ts)[1]
    return jax.vmap(one_chain)(s0, keys)

def run_sw(L, Ts, n_chains, n_equil, n_samples, n_between, seed):
    k_init, k_run = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    s0 = jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(k_init, 0.5, (n_chains, L, L)), 1.0, -1.0)
    out = np.asarray(sw_chains(s0, jax.random.split(k_run, n_chains), jnp.asarray(Ts, jnp.float32), n_equil, n_samples, n_between))
    return out.transpose(1, 0, 2, 3, 4).reshape(len(Ts), n_chains * n_samples, L, L)     # (nT, samples, L, L)

# check against exact enumeration of the 4x4 lattice at g = 0; error bars from the spread between independent chains
for T in (1.5, 2.27, 3.0):

    e_c = np.asarray(energy_per_spin(jnp.asarray(smp), 0.0)).mean(1); m_c = np.abs(smp.mean((-1, -2))).mean(1)
    e_ex, m_ex, _ = exact_4x4(0.0, T)

To measure the gain, we compare the autocorrelation of \(|m|\) along one chain at \(T_c\) for \(L=50\), for Metropolis with one sweep per step and for Swendsen–Wang with one cluster update per step, \[
A(t) = \frac{\langle |m|_{s}\,|m|_{s+t}\rangle - \langle|m|\rangle^2}{\langle |m|^2\rangle - \langle|m|\rangle^2}.
\] The faster \(A(t)\) decays, the more independent the stored samples are.


Code
def autocorr(x, t_max):
    x = x - x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    v = (x * x).mean(-1)
    return np.array([np.mean((x[:, : x.shape[1] - t] * x[:, t:]).mean(-1) / v) for t in range(t_max)])

t_met = time.time() - t0; t0 = time.time()
sw = run_sw(L_ac, [T_ac], n_chains=n_ch, n_equil=100, n_samples=n_steps, n_between=1, seed=22)[0]
t_sw = time.time() - t0
m_met = np.abs(met.reshape(n_ch, n_steps, -1).mean(-1)); m_sw = np.abs(sw.reshape(n_ch, n_steps, -1).mean(-1))
A_met, A_sw = autocorr(m_met, 150), autocorr(m_sw, 150)
tau = lambda A: 0.5 + A[1:np.argmax(A < 0.05) if (A < 0.05).any() else len(A)].sum()   # integrated autocorrelation time
print(f"L = {L_ac}, T = T_c:  integrated autocorrelation time  Metropolis {tau(A_met):.1f} sweeps,  Swendsen-Wang {tau(A_sw):.1f} updates")
print(f"wall time for {n_steps} steps of {n_ch} chains:  Metropolis {t_met:.1f} s,  Swendsen-Wang {t_sw:.1f} s")

3. Ising data set for several lattice sizes
For finite-size scaling (Lab 019) we need the same temperature grid for several \(L\), and nearly independent samples close to \(T_c\). We use the Swendsen–Wang sampler: 32 chains per size, each cooled through the temperature grid, 8 samples per temperature separated by 4 cluster updates. We store configurations as bits (np.packbits), eight spins per byte.


Code
def pack(configs):
    return np.packbits(configs > 0, axis=-1)

def unpack(packed, L):
    return np.unpackbits(packed, axis=-1, count=L).astype(np.int8) * 2 - 1

ISING_L = [20, 30, 50]

5. Choice of observable
Suppose we know nothing about stripes and we do what is natural for a magnet: we measure \(\langle|m|\rangle\) at every point of the grid. Then we measure \(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle\), which requires knowing the stripe pattern. Finally we measure the specific heat \[
c = \frac{N}{T^2}\left(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\right),
\] which does not need any order parameter: it peaks at a transition whatever the order is.


Code
@jax.jit
def observables(s, g):
    # s: (nT, n, L, L) float, g scalar -> per-temperature averages
    o = order_parameters(s)
    e = energy_per_spin(s, g)
    return o["m"].mean(1), o["m_str"].mean(1), e.mean(1), e.var(1)

N = J_L**2
# one coupling at a time keeps the memory small (the whole dataset as float32 would need ~0.7 GB)
res = [observables(jnp.asarray(cj[i], jnp.float32), J_G[i]) for i in range(len(J_G))]
M_map, Ms_map, E_map, varE = (np.stack([np.asarray(r[k]) for r in res]) for k in range(4))
C_map = N * varE / J_T[None, :] ** 2

def show_map(ax, Z, title, cmap="viridis", vmax=None):
    im = ax.pcolormesh(J_G, J_T, Z.T, shading="nearest", cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_xlabel("$g=J_2/J_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$T$"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
show_map(ax[0], M_map, r"magnetisation $\langle|m|\rangle$", vmax=1)
show_map(ax[1], Ms_map, r"stripe order $\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle$", vmax=1)
show_map(ax[2], C_map, r"specific heat $c$", cmap="magma", vmax=np.percentile(C_map, 99))
gg = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
for a in ax:
    a.plot(gg[gg <= 0.5], 4 * (1 - gg[gg <= 0.5]), "--", color="w", lw=1)
    a.plot(gg[gg >= 0.5], 4 * gg[gg >= 0.5], "--", color="w", lw=1)
    a.set_ylim(J_T.min(), J_T.max())
fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_j1j2_physicist_maps.png"); plt.show()





The dashed white lines are the mean-field predictions \(T^{\rm MF}=4(1-g)\) and \(4g\); they overshoot everywhere and miss the dip to \(T_c=0\) at \(g=1/2\).
The magnetisation map shows one ordered region, \(g<1/2\); the whole stripe phase looks like a paramagnet. The stripe map shows the other ordered region, but only because we told it what pattern to look for. The specific-heat map shows both boundaries without any order parameter. Its price is noise: \(c\) is a variance, and variances need many more samples than means.

5.1 Cost of a dense scan
A boundary from the specific heat needs a peak position, so it needs \(c\) on a fine grid with small error bars. How many samples per grid point does that take? We estimate \(c\) from subsets of \(n\) samples and look at the scatter of the estimates.


Code
ig = np.argmin(abs(J_G - 0.25))
e_line = np.asarray(energy_per_spin(jnp.asarray(cj[ig], jnp.float32), J_G[ig]))           # (nT, samples)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.1), sharey=True)
for a, n in zip(ax, [10, 30, cj.shape[2]]):
    for rep in range(5 if n < cj.shape[2] else 1):
        idx = rng.choice(cj.shape[2], n, replace=False)
        a.plot(J_T, N * e_line[:, idx].var(1, ddof=1) / J_T**2, "-", lw=1, alpha=0.8, color=UJBlue if n < cj.shape[2] else UJNavy)
    a.set_title(f"{n} samples per point" + ("" if n < cj.shape[2] else " (all)"), fontsize=10)
    a.set_xlabel("$T$")
ax[0].set_ylabel("$c$ at $g=0.25$")
fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_j1j2_cost.png"); plt.show()

n_points = len(J_G) * len(J_T)
NUMBERS.update(j1j2_grid_points=n_points, j1j2_total_configs=int(n_points * cj.shape[2]))
print(f"{n_points} grid points x {cj.shape[2]} samples = {n_points * cj.shape[2]} configurations")





6399 grid points x 100 samples = 639900 configurations


With 10 samples per point the peak position of \(c\) jumps around from one repetition to the next. A reliable peak needs of order a hundred decorrelated samples per point, and the decorrelation time itself grows near the transition (critical slowing down). In a laboratory, every grid point is a separate preparation of the sample at a given pressure, field or temperature.
This is the motivation for Labs 019 and 020, which ask two questions. Can an algorithm that has never been told about magnetisation or stripes find the ordered phases from raw snapshots? And can it do this from a coarse scan, and tell us where a dense scan is worth paying for?

title: Lab 018: Classical spin models in JAX, the 2D Ising and the J1–J2 model
text:
Summary
The \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) Ising model has a ferromagnetic phase (\(g<1/2\)) and a stripe phase (\(g>1/2\)); at \(g=1/2\) the competition makes the ground state massively degenerate and the transition temperature vanishes, a point that mean-field theory gets qualitatively wrong. The natural “magnet” observable, \(\langle|m|\rangle\), is blind to the stripe phase, so choosing the right observable requires prior knowledge, and fluctuation observables such as \(c\), which see every transition, are expensive because they need many samples per grid point.
On the computational side, the whole simulation is one pure sweep function, lax.scan for time loops, vmap over chains and couplings, and jit for the whole program. Near \(T_c\) local updates slow down; the Swendsen–Wang cluster algorithm (ferromagnetic couplings only) gives nearly independent samples, and its cluster search is a lax.while_loop of array operations.

Exercises

Add a \(J_3\) coupling (third neighbours, two sites apart along the axes) to local_field. Which sub-lattice decomposition is now needed?
Replace annealing by independent random starts at every temperature. What happens to the stripe phase at low \(T\) near \(g=0.55\)?
Compute the full structure factor \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) with jnp.fft.fft2 for snapshots at \(g=0.25\) and \(g=0.75\), \(T=0.5\). Where are the peaks?

title: Lab 019: The 2D Ising transition without labels
text:
1. Exact results and finite-size scaling
For the infinite lattice (\(J=k_B=1\)) the following is known exactly: * Onsager (1944): \(T_c = 2/\ln(1+\sqrt2) = 2.2692\ldots\), and the specific heat diverges logarithmically. * Yang (1952): \(M(T)=\left(1-\sinh^{-4}(2/T)\right)^{1/8}\) below \(T_c\), so \(M\sim (T_c-T)^{\beta}\) with \(\beta=1/8\). * The correlation length diverges as \(\xi\sim|T-T_c|^{-\nu}\) with \(\nu=1\), and the susceptibility as \(\chi\sim|T-T_c|^{-\gamma}\) with \(\gamma=7/4\).
On a finite lattice nothing diverges: when \(\xi\) reaches \(L\) the growth stops. Finite-size scaling turns this limitation into a tool. Near \(T_c\) every observable depends on \(T\) and \(L\) only through \(L/\xi\), i.e. through the scaling variable \(t\,L^{1/\nu}\) with \(t=(T-T_c)/T_c\): \[
\langle|m|\rangle = L^{-\beta/\nu}\,\tilde m\!\left(tL^{1/\nu}\right),\qquad
\chi = L^{\gamma/\nu}\,\tilde\chi\!\left(tL^{1/\nu}\right),\qquad
U_4 = \tilde U\!\left(tL^{1/\nu}\right).
\] Two consequences are used in practice. The Binder cumulant \(U_4 = 1-\dfrac{\langle m^4\rangle}{3\langle m^2\rangle^2}\) is dimensionless, so at \(t=0\) it takes the same value for every \(L\): the curves for different \(L\) cross at \(T_c\). Its limits are \(U_4\to 2/3\) in the ordered phase (\(m=\pm M\) sharp) and \(U_4\to0\) in the paramagnet (\(m\) Gaussian, \(\langle m^4\rangle = 3\langle m^2\rangle^2\)). The susceptibility peak sits at \(T_c(L)\) with \(T_c(L)-T_c\propto L^{-1/\nu}\), and extrapolating to \(L\to\infty\) gives \(T_c\).
All these quantities are thermal averages over the Boltzmann distribution, \(\langle O\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf s}O(\mathbf s)\,e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}\) with \(Z=\sum_{\mathbf s}e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}\) and \(\beta=1/T\). The data of Lab 018 contain, for every lattice size and temperature, \(n=256\) configurations \(\mathbf s^{(k)}\) sampled from this distribution, and every average is estimated by a sample mean over them. With \(m_k=\frac1N\sum_is^{(k)}_i\) the magnetisation of sample \(k\) and \(\overline{x}=\frac1n\sum_kx_k\), the code below (functions moments and blocked) computes:








observable
definition through \(Z\)
estimator from \(n\) samples (as in the code)




magnetisation
\(\langle\lvert m\rvert\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf s}\lvert m(\mathbf s)\rvert e^{-\beta H}\)
\(\overline{\lvert m\rvert}=\frac1n\sum_k\lvert m_k\rvert\)


susceptibility
\(\chi=N\beta\big(\langle m^2\rangle-\langle\lvert m\rvert\rangle^2\big)\)
\(N\beta\big(\overline{m^2}-\overline{\lvert m\rvert}^{\,2}\big)\)


Binder cumulant
\(U_4=1-\dfrac{\langle m^4\rangle}{3\langle m^2\rangle^2}\)
\(1-\dfrac{\overline{m^4}}{3\,\overline{m^2}^{\,2}}\)



On a finite lattice \(\langle m\rangle=0\) by the symmetry \(\mathbf s\to-\mathbf s\), so the susceptibility is built from \(|m|\); the variance in \(\chi\) is a population variance (division by \(n\)). The error bar of an observable comes from \(B=8\) blocks of consecutive columns of the data (groups of chains): the observable \(O_b\) is computed on each block, and the error is \(\sigma_B/\sqrt{B-1}\), with \(\sigma_B\) the population standard deviation of the \(O_b\).
Both observables were constructed: we had to know that \(m\) is the order parameter. In the figure, look for the crossing of the Binder curves and for the drift of the susceptibility peak towards \(T_c\) as \(L\) grows.


Code
def moments(x):
    # x: (nT, n) samples of a scalar order parameter -> U4, chi-like variance, mean |x|
    x2, x4 = (x**2).mean(1), (x**4).mean(1)
    return 1 - x4 / (3 * x2**2), x2 - np.abs(x).mean(1) ** 2, np.abs(x).mean(1)

def blocked(f, x, n_blocks=8):
    # mean and error of f(x) from n_blocks independent groups of samples (columns are grouped by chain in Lab 018)
    vals = np.stack([f(b) for b in np.array_split(x, n_blocks, axis=1)])
    return f(x), vals.std(0) / np.sqrt(n_blocks - 1)

M = {L: s.mean((-2, -1)).astype(np.float64) for L, (T, s) in DATA_SETS.items()}

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.5, 2.1))
    chi_peak = {}
    for L in L_LIST:
        T = DATA_SETS[L][0]; N = L * L
        (U, U_err) = blocked(lambda x: moments(x)[0], M[L])
        (chi, chi_err) = blocked(lambda x: N * moments(x)[1], M[L])
        chi = chi / T; chi_err = chi_err / T
        ax[0].plot(T, np.abs(M[L]).mean(1), ".-", color=size_colors[L], label=f"$L={L}$")
        ax[1].errorbar(T, U, U_err, fmt=".-", color=size_colors[L], label=f"$L={L}$", ms=3, capsize=1)
        ax[2].errorbar(T, chi, chi_err, fmt=".-", color=size_colors[L], ms=3, capsize=1)
        chi_peak[L] = T[np.argmax(chi)]
    for a, lab in zip(ax, [r"$\langle|m|\rangle$", r"$U_4$", r"$\chi$"]):
        a.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":"); a.set_xlabel("$T$"); a.set_ylabel(lab)
    ax[1].set_xlim(2.1, 2.5); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="lower left"); ax[2].set_xlim(1.9, 3.0)
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_fss_observables.png"); plt.show()
print("chi peak positions:", chi_peak)





chi peak positions: {20: np.float64(2.38), 30: np.float64(2.36), 50: np.float64(2.3)}



1.1 Binder crossings and susceptibility peaks
To turn the figure into numbers, we find for each pair of consecutive sizes where \(U_4(L)\) and \(U_4(L')\) cross (linear interpolation between grid points). For the susceptibility we fit \(T_c(L) = T_c + a\,L^{-1/\nu}\) with the exact \(\nu=1\); the peak position is refined by a parabola through the three highest points.


Code
def crossing(T, y1, y2, lo=2.1, hi=2.5):
    d = y1 - y2; sel = (T >= lo) & (T <= hi)
    T, d = T[sel], d[sel]
    idx = np.where(np.sign(d[:-1]) != np.sign(d[1:]))[0]
    if len(idx) == 0: return np.nan
    i = idx[np.argmin(abs(T[idx] - TC))] if len(idx) > 1 else idx[0]
    return T[i] - d[i] * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (d[i + 1] - d[i])

def peak(T, y):
    i = int(np.clip(np.argmax(y), 1, len(y) - 2))
    c = np.polyfit(T[i - 1:i + 2], y[i - 1:i + 2], 2)
    return -c[1] / (2 * c[0])

U4 = {L: moments(M[L])[0] for L in L_LIST}
cross = {(L1, L2): crossing(T_GRID, U4[L1], U4[L2]) for L1, L2 in zip(L_LIST[:-1], L_LIST[1:])}
for k, v in cross.items(): print(f"U4 crossing {k}: T = {v:.4f}")
chi_T = np.array([peak(T_GRID, L * L * moments(M[L])[1] / T_GRID) for L in L_LIST])
A = np.vstack([np.ones(len(L_LIST)), 1.0 / np.array(L_LIST)]).T
tc_chi, a_chi = np.linalg.lstsq(A, chi_T, rcond=None)[0]
print("chi peaks T_c(L):", np.round(chi_T, 4), f"-> extrapolated T_c = {tc_chi:.4f}  (exact {TC:.4f})")
NUMBERS.update(fss_U4_crossings={f"{a}-{b}": round(float(v), 4) for (a, b), v in cross.items()},
               fss_chi_peaks=[round(float(x), 4) for x in chi_T], fss_tc_chi=round(float(tc_chi), 4))


U4 crossing (20, 30): T = 2.2495
U4 crossing (30, 50): T = 2.2784
chi peaks T_c(L): [2.3714 2.3616 2.3031] -> extrapolated T_c = 2.2694  (exact 2.2692)

title: Lab 019: The 2D Ising transition without labels
text:
2. PCA on raw spins
PCA (Lab 016) diagonalises the covariance matrix of the data. Here a data point is one configuration, a vector of \(N=L^2\) spins; the data set contains all temperatures, and no temperature or label is given to PCA. ### 2.1 PCA implementation in JAX
We compute the decomposition with a singular value decomposition in JAX, for \(L=30\), and look at three things: how much variance the first component carries, what its weights \(\mathbf v_1\) look like on the lattice, and how its projection compares with the magnetisation.


Code
@jax.jit
def pca(X):
    mu = X.mean(0)
    _, S, Vt = jnp.linalg.svd(X - mu, full_matrices=False)
    return mu, S**2 / jnp.sum(S**2), Vt

L = 30
T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
X = jnp.asarray(s.reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32)
mu, var_ratio, Vt = pca(X)
z = np.asarray((X - mu) @ Vt[:2].T).reshape(len(T), -1, 2)
v1 = np.asarray(Vt[0]) * np.sign(np.asarray(Vt[0]).sum())
print("explained variance ratio of the first 5 components:", np.round(np.asarray(var_ratio[:5]), 4))
corr = np.corrcoef(np.abs(z[..., 0]).ravel(), np.abs(M[L]).ravel())[0, 1]
print(f"correlation between |PC1| and |m| over all configurations: {corr:.6f}")
print(f"entries of sqrt(N) v1: mean {np.mean(v1 * L):.4f}, std {np.std(v1 * L):.4f}")
NUMBERS.update(pca_L=L, pca_var1=round(float(var_ratio[0]), 4), pca_var2=round(float(var_ratio[1]), 4),
               pca_corr_pc1_m=round(float(corr), 6), pca_v1_std=round(float(np.std(v1 * L)), 4))

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(4.7, 2.1), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.2, 1]))
    sc = ax[0].scatter(z[..., 0].ravel(), z[..., 1].ravel(), c=np.repeat(T, z.shape[1]), cmap="coolwarm", s=2)
    plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax[0], label="$T$"); ax[0].set_xlabel("PC 1"); ax[0].set_ylabel("PC 2")
    ax[1].plot(T, np.abs(z[..., 0]).mean(1) / L, "o", ms=3, color=UJBlue, label=r"$\langle|\mathrm{PC\,1}|\rangle/\sqrt{N}$")
    ax[1].plot(T, np.abs(M[L]).mean(1), "-", color=DSOrange, label=r"$\langle|m|\rangle$")
    ax[1].axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":"); ax[1].set_xlabel("$T$"); ax[1].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_pca.png"); plt.show()

with mpl.rc_context(SLIDE):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.1, 1.9))
    im = ax.imshow((v1 * L).reshape(L, L), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=0.9, vmax=1.1); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(r"$\sqrt{N}\,\mathbf{v}_1$"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    fig.tight_layout(); savefig(fig, "gen_ising_v1.png"); plt.show()


explained variance ratio of the first 5 components: [0.373  0.0141 0.0133 0.013  0.0124]
correlation between |PC1| and |m| over all configurations: 0.999960
entries of sqrt(N) v1: mean 1.0000, std 0.0096








The first component carries far more variance than all others, its weights are uniform over the lattice, and its projection is perfectly correlated with \(|m|\). The reason is simple. Below \(T_c\) the spins are strongly correlated, \(\langle s_is_j\rangle\approx M^2\) for all pairs; the covariance matrix has a large uniform block, and its leading eigenvector is the uniform vector \(\mathbf v_1\approx(1,\dots,1)/\sqrt N\). The projection is then \(z_1=\mathbf v_1\cdot\mathbf s=\sqrt N\,m\).
PCA has therefore not discovered anything we could not have guessed: the Ising order parameter is linear in the spins, and a linear method finds linear structure. That is still useful, because the first principal component is an order-parameter candidate produced without prior knowledge, and its weights \(\mathbf v_1\) show which pattern orders. Lab 020 tests the same idea on a model with two different ordering patterns; Lab 021 on a model where the relevant variables are not linear in the spins.
Because \(z_1\propto m\), every finite-size analysis of Section 1 can be repeated with \(z_1\) instead of \(m\) and gives the same numbers:


Code
z1 = {}
for L in L_LIST:
    T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
    Xl = jnp.asarray(s.reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32)
    mu_l, _, Vt_l = pca(Xl)
    z1[L] = np.asarray((Xl - mu_l) @ Vt_l[0]).reshape(len(T), -1) / L      # = m up to a sign
U4_pca = {L: moments(z1[L])[0] for L in L_LIST}
cross_pca = {(L1, L2): crossing(T_GRID, U4_pca[L1], U4_pca[L2]) for L1, L2 in zip(L_LIST[:-1], L_LIST[1:])}
for k in cross: print(f"crossing {k}:  U4(m) {cross[k]:.4f}   U4(PC1) {cross_pca[k]:.4f}")


crossing (20, 30):  U4(m) 2.2495   U4(PC1) 2.2495
crossing (30, 50):  U4(m) 2.2784   U4(PC1) 2.2773


The crossings from the first principal component reproduce those from \(m\): for the first pair of sizes to all printed digits, for the second up to a difference in the third decimal.

2.2 PCA with scikit-learn
The same decomposition with scikit-learn: the estimator PCA(n_components=5, svd_solver="full") is fitted to the same \(L=30\) configurations with fit(X); it stores the mean configuration in mean_, the components as the rows of components_ and their fractions of the variance in explained_variance_ratio_, and transform(X) returns the projections. With svd_solver="full" it performs a complete singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centred data, the same computation as our pca, so the fractions of variance must agree to float32 precision. The sign of a component is arbitrary in both programs, so components are compared through the absolute cosine of the angle between them. The first component is well separated from the rest of the spectrum and must agree; components 2–5 have almost equal variances, and a nearly degenerate eigenvalue leaves its eigenvector poorly defined, so for them only the variances are compared. The cell asserts the agreement and prints the correlation of the two projections on the first component.


Code
L = 30
X30 = np.asarray(DATA_SETS[L][1].reshape(-1, L * L), np.float32)
sk_pca = PCA(n_components=5, svd_solver="full").fit(X30)
mu30, ratio30, Vt30 = pca(jnp.asarray(X30))
ratio30, Vt30 = np.asarray(ratio30), np.asarray(Vt30)
cos1 = abs(float(sk_pca.components_[0] @ Vt30[0]))
z1_sk = sk_pca.transform(X30)[:, 0]
corr_sk = abs(np.corrcoef(z1_sk, np.asarray((jnp.asarray(X30) - mu30) @ Vt30[0]))[0, 1])
print("fraction of variance, first 5 components:")
print("  JAX         ", np.round(ratio30[:5], 5))
print("  scikit-learn", np.round(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 5))
print(f"|cos| between the first components: {cos1:.8f} | correlation of the projections on PC 1: {corr_sk:.8f}")
assert np.allclose(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_, ratio30[:5], rtol=1e-3)
assert cos1 > 0.99999 and corr_sk > 0.99999
NUMBERS["pca_sklearn_var1"] = round(float(sk_pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]), 4)


fraction of variance, first 5 components:
  JAX          [0.37303 0.01408 0.01333 0.01298 0.01245]
  scikit-learn [0.37303 0.01408 0.01333 0.01298 0.01245]
|cos| between the first components: 0.99999988 | correlation of the projections on PC 1: 1.00000000

title: Lab 019: The 2D Ising transition without labels
text:
3. Autoencoder anomaly detection
PCA found the order parameter because it is linear in the spins. A different unsupervised approach does not look for an order parameter at all (Kottmann, Huembeli, Lewenstein, Acín, Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 170603 (2020)): train an autoencoder only on configurations from a region we understand, and use its reconstruction error as an anomaly score everywhere else. Inside the training region the error is small; where the data stop looking like the training data, it rises.
The architecture is the same for every \(L\): the \(N\) spins enter a dense layer of 128 units with the rectified linear activation \(\mathrm{ReLU}(u)=\max(0,u)\), then a latent layer of 8 numbers; the decoder mirrors this and ends with \(\tanh\), so \(\hat s_i\in[-1,1]\). The loss is \(\frac1N\lVert\mathbf s-\hat{\mathbf s}\rVert^2\), minimised with Adam (adaptive moment estimation: gradient descent in which the step of every parameter is set by running averages of its gradient and of its squared gradient).
The model is built with Flax NNX, the current interface (flax.nnx) of the neural-network library Flax for JAX. A model is a Python object (nnx.Module) whose layers hold their parameters; nnx.Optimizer holds the optax state, nnx.value_and_grad differentiates a loss with respect to the model’s parameters, and nnx.jit compiles the whole training step.


Code
class DenseAE(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in, latent=8, hidden=128, *, rngs):
        self.e1 = nnx.Linear(n_in, hidden, rngs=rngs); self.e2 = nnx.Linear(hidden, latent, rngs=rngs)
        self.d1 = nnx.Linear(latent, hidden, rngs=rngs); self.d2 = nnx.Linear(hidden, n_in, rngs=rngs)
    def encode(self, x):
        return self.e2(nnx.relu(self.e1(x)))
    def __call__(self, x):
        return jnp.tanh(self.d2(nnx.relu(self.d1(self.encode(x)))))

@nnx.jit
def train_step(model, opt, x):
    loss, grads = nnx.value_and_grad(lambda m: jnp.mean((m(x) - x) ** 2))(model)
    opt.update(model, grads)
    return loss

@nnx.jit
def recon_error(model, x):
    return jnp.mean((model(x) - x) ** 2, axis=-1)

def train_ae(X_train, epochs=200, batch=64, seed=0, lr=1e-3):
    model = DenseAE(X_train.shape[1], rngs=nnx.Rngs(seed))
    opt = nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adam(lr), wrt=nnx.Param)
    X_train = jnp.asarray(X_train, jnp.float32); n = X_train.shape[0]
    key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed); hist = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        key, k = jax.random.split(key)
        perm = jax.random.permutation(k, n)
        for i in range(0, n - batch + 1, batch):
            loss = train_step(model, opt, X_train[perm[i:i + batch]])
        hist.append(float(loss))
    return model, hist

def error_vs_T(model, L):
    T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
    e = recon_error(model, jnp.asarray(s.reshape(-1, L * L), jnp.float32))
    return np.asarray(e).reshape(len(T), -1)



3.1 Training on the ordered phase
The well-understood region is the deep ordered phase, \(T\le1.7\), where Yang’s formula gives \(M>0.97\) (the cell prints the value). We train one autoencoder per lattice size and three random seeds per size, and record the reconstruction error at every temperature.
To locate the rise of the error we need a definition that is robust to noise. The mean error rises like a smoothed step, and we fit \[
\bar\varepsilon(T) = a + b\,\tanh\!\left(\frac{T-T^\ast}{w}\right)
\] on \(1.9\le T\le 3.0\): the signal temperature \(T^\ast(L)\) is the centre of the step, and \(w(L)\) its width. A fit uses all temperatures at once and is much less sensitive to noise than the position of the steepest slope between two grid points.
The susceptibility peak has a known finite-size law, \(T_c(L)-T_c\propto L^{-1/\nu}\), so it can be extrapolated. The autoencoder signal is not a thermodynamic observable and has no derived law. We therefore watch how \(T^\ast(L)\) and \(w(L)\) change with \(L\), and compare the width with the finite-size rounding of the transition, \(\propto L^{-1/\nu}=L^{-1}\).


Code
T_TRAIN_MAX = 1.7
print(f"Yang: M(T = {T_TRAIN_MAX}) = {(1 - np.sinh(2 / T_TRAIN_MAX) ** -4) ** 0.125:.4f}")

from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

def step_fit(T, err, lo=1.9, hi=3.0):
    sel = (T >= lo) & (T <= hi)
    f = lambda t, a, b, t0, w: a + b * np.tanh((t - t0) / w)
    p0 = [0.5 * (err[sel].max() + err[sel].min()), 0.5 * (err[sel].max() - err[sel].min()), TC, 0.1]
    (a, b, t0, w), _ = curve_fit(f, T[sel], err[sel], p0=p0, maxfev=20000)
    return t0, abs(w)

SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
ae_curves, T_star, W_star = {}, {}, {}
t0 = time.time()
for L in L_LIST:
    T, s = DATA_SETS[L]
    X_tr = s[T <= T_TRAIN_MAX].reshape(-1, L * L)
    curves = []
    for seed in SEEDS:
        model, hist = train_ae(X_tr, seed=seed)
        curves.append(error_vs_T(model, L).mean(1))
    ae_curves[L] = np.array(curves)
    fits = np.array([step_fit(T, c) for c in curves])
    T_star[L], W_star[L] = fits[:, 0], fits[:, 1]
    print(f"L = {L:2d}: train on {X_tr.shape[0]} configs, final loss {hist[-1]:.4f};  T* = {T_star[L].mean():.3f} +- {T_star[L].std():.3f},"
          f"  width w = {W_star[L].mean():.3f} +- {W_star[L].std():.3f}   ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
