The expansion \(m\approx\sqrt{3(1-T/T_{\rm MF})}\) is accurate only close to \(T_{\rm MF}\); far below, \(m\to1\) and the expansion overshoots. The site-dependent iteration lands, without being told, in the ferromagnet for \(g=0.25\) and in a stripe state for \(g=0.75\), with the amplitude of the uniform solution at \(T/T_{\rm MF}=0.9\). The figure below shows \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) over the Brillouin zone and the mean-field phase diagram.


Code
k = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 201); KX, KY = np.meshgrid(k, k, indexing="ij")
Jk_num = lambda g: 2 * (np.cos(KX) + np.cos(KY)) - 4 * g * np.cos(KX) * np.cos(KY)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.2))
for a, gv in zip(ax[:3], (0.25, 0.5, 0.75)):
    Z = Jk_num(gv)
    im = a.pcolormesh(KX, KY, Z, cmap="viridis", shading="auto")
    a.contour(KX, KY, Z, levels=[Z.max() - 1e-3], colors="w", linewidths=1.5)
    a.set_title(f"$\\mathcal{{J}}(\\mathbf{{k}})$, g = {gv}; max = {Z.max():.2f}", fontsize=10)
    a.set_xlabel("$k_x$"); a.set_ylabel("$k_y$"); a.set_aspect("equal"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=a, fraction=0.046)
gl = np.linspace(0, 1.5, 301)
ax[3].plot(gl[gl <= 0.5], 4 * (1 - gl[gl <= 0.5]), color=UJBlue, lw=2, label="ferromagnet: $4(J_1-J_2)$")
ax[3].plot(gl[gl >= 0.5], 4 * gl[gl >= 0.5], color=DSOrange, lw=2, label="stripes: $4J_2$")
ax[3].plot([0, 1.5], [TC_ISING, 1.5 * TC_ISING], ":", color=UJGray, label="exact limits: $2.269$ and $2.269\\,g$")
ax[3].set_xlabel("$g$"); ax[3].set_ylabel("$T_{\\rm MF}$"); ax[3].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8); ax[3].set_title("mean-field phase diagram")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The figure shows the V-shaped mean-field transition line, and the theory fails in three respects. The first is an overestimate of \(T_c\): at \(g=0\) mean field predicts \(4J_1\) instead of \(2.269J_1\) (a factor \(1.76\)); for \(g\to\infty\), \(4J_2\) instead of \(2.269J_2\). Mean field neglects the correlations between a spin and its neighbours: in reality the neighbours fluctuate together with the spin, ordered patches form and disappear, and these fluctuations lower \(T_c\). In two dimensions they are strong.
The second failure is the point \(g=1/2\). Mean field predicts \(T_{\rm MF}=2J_1\) there, the lowest point of the V but still a finite temperature. The truth is \(T_c\to0\) (Sections 4, 8, 9). The white contour shows the reason: at \(g=1/2\) the maximum of \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) is reached on the two lines \(k_x=0\) and \(k_y=0\), \(2L-1\) wave vectors on an \(L\times L\) torus (the multiplicity \(23=2\cdot12-1\) printed above). A mode \((0,k_y)\) is a pattern uniform along \(x\) with an arbitrary profile along \(y\): the row-flip degeneracy of Section 3.5. Mean field picks one mode and orders it; in reality the system fluctuates between all of them, and no order survives at \(T>0\).
The third failure concerns the nature of the transition. Mean field always gives a continuous transition with \(\beta=1/2\). The true ferromagnetic transition has the 2D Ising exponents, and the stripe transition is weakly first order or Ashkin–Teller-like (Section 10).
Mean field thus identifies the two ordered phases and the special role of \(g=1/2\) — the degenerate maximum of \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) — but turns it into the wrong prediction: fluctuations are the essence of the problem.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
section: 7. Monte Carlo and the static structure factor
text:
7. Monte Carlo and the static structure factor
The exact methods so far either work at \(T=0\) (Section 3) or neglect fluctuations (Section 6). To see the phases at finite temperature on a large lattice we sample the Boltzmann distribution with Monte Carlo. The snapshots also give the static structure factor, the quantity measured by neutron or X-ray scattering, which identifies the ordering pattern without knowing it in advance.

7.1 Four-sublattice Metropolis sampler
We use the Metropolis algorithm of Lab 010: propose flipping spin \(i\) and accept it with probability \(\min(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E_i})\), where \[
\Delta E_i = 2s_ih_i,\qquad h_i = J_1\sum_{j\in\rm nn(i)}s_j - J_2\sum_{j\in\rm diag(i)}s_j .
\] This choice satisfies detailed balance, \(p(\mathbf s)P(\mathbf s\to\mathbf s')=p(\mathbf s')P(\mathbf s'\to\mathbf s)\), so the Boltzmann distribution is stationary.
Spins that are not coupled to each other can be updated simultaneously. The chessboard decomposition used for the Ising model fails here, because diagonal neighbours have the same chessboard colour. The four sublattices \((x\bmod2,\,y\bmod2)\) work instead: nearest neighbours differ in one parity, diagonal neighbours in both, so no two spins of one sublattice interact (for \(L\) even and \(L\ge4\)). One sweep updates the four sublattices in turn, which amounts to one attempted flip per spin.
This suggests storing a configuration directly as its four sublattices, a tuple S of four arrays S[2a+b] = s[a::2, b::2], each of shape \((C, L/2, L/2)\) for \(C\) chains. The neighbours of a spin of sublattice \((a,b)\) lie on the other three sublattices: its two horizontal neighbours on \((1-a,b)\), its two vertical neighbours on \((a,1-b)\), its four diagonal neighbours on \((1-a,1-b)\). With nsum(X, a, axis) \(=X+\) roll\((X,\pm1)\) (sign \(+\) for \(a=0\), \(-\) for \(a=1\)) the local field is h = nsum(S[1-a,b], a, x) + nsum(S[a,1-b], b, y) - g * nsum(nsum(S[1-a,1-b], a, x), b, y). No work is wasted on spins that are not being updated, and all chains are processed by the same array operations.
In JAX the sampler is a pure function sweep(S, key, g, beta); lax.scan repeats sweeps inside one compiled program, and jax.jit compiles the whole simulation. The chains form the leading axis of every array (equivalent to jax.vmap over chains, written out explicitly); each chain has its own \(g\) and its own temperature schedule: T_sched has shape \((n_{\rm steps}, C)\), and at step \(k\) chain \(c\) runs n_equil sweeps of equilibration at temperature T_sched[k, c] followed by n_meas measurements separated by n_between sweeps. A decreasing schedule anneals the chains; a schedule with one row runs every chain at its own fixed temperature. Each measurement is the vector \((m,m_x,m_y,e)\), and with keep=True the configurations are stored as well. The input S0 consists of four arrays of shape \((C,L/2,L/2)\), g has shape \((C,)\) and T_sched shape \((n_{\rm steps},C)\); the output measurements have shape \((n_{\rm steps}, n_{\rm meas}, C, 4)\) and, with keep=True, the configurations shape \((n_{\rm steps}, n_{\rm meas}, C, L, L)\), stored as int8. The cell ends by checking the sublattice layout against a plain NumPy implementation.


Code
def nsum(X, a, axis):
    # X plus its copy shifted by one site along axis; for a = 0 the partner sites are i and i-1, for a = 1 they are i and i+1
    return X + jnp.roll(X, 1 if a == 0 else -1, axis)

def sublattice_field(S, a, b, g):
    # local field h on sublattice (a, b): nearest neighbours minus g times diagonal neighbours; shape (C, L/2, L/2)
    return (nsum(S[2 * (1 - a) + b], a, 1) + nsum(S[2 * a + 1 - b], b, 2)
            - g * nsum(nsum(S[2 * (1 - a) + 1 - b], a, 1), b, 2))

def sweep(S, key, g, beta):
    # one Metropolis sweep of all chains; g, beta: (C, 1, 1)
    S = list(S)
    for a, b in ((0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)):
        key, sub = jax.random.split(key)
        si = S[2 * a + b]
        dE = 2.0 * si * sublattice_field(S, a, b, g)
        accept = jax.random.uniform(sub, si.shape) < jnp.exp(-beta * dE)
        S[2 * a + b] = jnp.where(accept, -si, si)
    return tuple(S), key

def measure(S, g):
    # (m, m_x, m_y, e) per chain, shape (C, 4); g: (C,); the sign of (-1)^x on sublattice (a, b) is (-1)^a
    s00, s01, s10, s11 = S
    g = jnp.reshape(g, (-1, 1, 1))
    mean = lambda X: X.mean((1, 2)) / 4
    m, mx, my = mean(s00 + s01 + s10 + s11), mean(s00 + s01 - s10 - s11), mean(s00 - s01 + s10 - s11)
    e = -0.5 * sum(mean(S[2 * a + b] * sublattice_field(S, a, b, g)) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1))   # each bond twice
    return jnp.stack([m, mx, my, e], 1)

def assemble(S):
    # four sublattices (C, L/2, L/2) -> full configurations (C, L, L), s[c, 2i+a, 2j+b] = S[2a+b][c, i, j]
    X = jnp.stack(S)                                         # (4, C, h, h)
    C, h = X.shape[1], X.shape[2]
    return X.reshape(2, 2, C, h, h).transpose(2, 3, 0, 4, 1).reshape(C, 2 * h, 2 * h)

def split(s):
    # full configurations (C, L, L) -> tuple of four sublattices
    return tuple(jnp.asarray(s[:, a::2, b::2], jnp.float32) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1))

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_meas", "n_between", "keep"))
def simulate(S0, key, g, T_sched, n_equil, n_meas, n_between, keep=False):
    g = g[:, None, None]
    def at_step(carry, T):
        beta = (1.0 / T)[:, None, None]
        step = lambda c, _: (sweep(c[0], c[1], g, beta), None)
        carry, _ = lax.scan(step, carry, None, length=n_equil)
        def record(c, _):
            c, _ = lax.scan(step, c, None, length=n_between)
            obs = measure(c[0], g[:, 0, 0])
            return c, ((obs, assemble(c[0]).astype(jnp.int8)) if keep else (obs,))
        return lax.scan(record, carry, None, length=n_meas)
    return lax.scan(at_step, (S0, key), T_sched)[1]

def run_mc(s0, g, T_sched, n_equil, n_meas, n_between, seed, keep=False):
    # s0: (C, L, L) initial configurations; g: (C,); T_sched: (n_steps, C). Returns numpy arrays (see shapes above).
    out = simulate(split(np.asarray(s0)), jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), jnp.asarray(g, jnp.float32),
                   jnp.asarray(T_sched, jnp.float32), n_equil, n_meas, n_between, keep)
    return tuple(np.asarray(o) for o in out) if keep else np.asarray(out[0])

def random_configs(C, L, seed):
    return np.random.default_rng(seed).choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(C, L, L))

# consistency of the sublattice layout: assemble(split(s)) = s, and measure() agrees with the numpy functions of Sections 2-3
s_test = random_configs(6, 8, 0)
assert np.array_equal(np.asarray(assemble(split(s_test))), s_test)
obs = np.asarray(measure(split(s_test), jnp.full(6, 0.37)))
o_np = order_params(s_test)
assert np.allclose(obs[:, 0], o_np["m"]) and np.allclose(obs[:, 1], o_np["mx"]) and np.allclose(obs[:, 2], o_np["my"])
assert np.allclose(obs[:, 3], energy(s_test, 0.37) / 64, atol=1e-5)
print("sublattice layout: assemble/split round trip and (m, m_x, m_y, e) agree with the numpy reference")


sublattice layout: assemble/split round trip and (m, m_x, m_y, e) agree with the numpy reference


Before using the sampler for physics we compare it with exact enumeration. On the \(4\times4\) torus the exact averages of \(e\), \(|m|\) and \(m_{\rm str}=\sqrt{m_x^2+m_y^2}\) follow from the \(2^{16}\) configurations of Section 3.3, \(\langle A\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf s}A(\mathbf s)e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}/Z\). The Monte Carlo averages use 512 chains per point (all five points in one batch of \(C=2560\) chains), and the error bar is the standard error over chains. The Monte Carlo value and the exact value should agree within a few error bars at every point.


Code
o44 = order_params(S44)
m_abs_44, mstr_44 = np.abs(o44["m"]), np.hypot(o44["mx"], o44["my"])
def exact_4x4(g, T):
    E = -B1_44 + g * B2_44
    w = np.exp(-(E - E.min()) / T); w /= w.sum()
    return (w * E / 16).sum(), (w * m_abs_44).sum(), (w * mstr_44).sum()

checks = [(0.0, 2.0), (0.3, 1.2), (0.5, 0.6), (0.75, 1.0), (1.5, 3.0)]

    print(f"g = {gv:4.2f}, T = {T}:  " + "   ".join(f"{n} MC {a:+.4f}({b:.4f}) exact {c:+.4f}" for n, a, b, c in zip(["e", "|m|", "m_str"], mc, err, ex)))

g = 0.75, T = 1.0:  e MC -1.4758(0.0005) exact -1.4755   |m| MC +0.0079(0.0002) exact +0.0078   m_str MC +0.9895(0.0003) exact +0.9893
g = 1.50, T = 3.0:  e MC -2.6468(0.0026) exact -2.6509   |m| MC +0.0382(0.0003) exact +0.0377   m_str MC +0.9368(0.0005) exact +0.9375
(6.8 s)




7.2 Static structure factor
The agreement is good at all five points, so we can trust the sampler on larger lattices. For a configuration \(\mathbf s\) define the Fourier amplitude \(\hat s(\boldsymbol k)=\sum_{\boldsymbol r}s_{\boldsymbol r}e^{-i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}\) on the \(L^2\) wave vectors \(\boldsymbol k=\frac{2\pi}{L}(n_x,n_y)\). The static structure factor is \[
\begin{aligned}
S(\boldsymbol k) &= \frac1N\big\langle|\hat s(\boldsymbol k)|^2\big\rangle = N\big\langle|m_{\boldsymbol k}|^2\big\rangle\\
&= \sum_{\boldsymbol r}e^{-i\boldsymbol k\cdot\boldsymbol r}\,\frac1N\sum_{\boldsymbol r'}\langle s_{\boldsymbol r'}s_{\boldsymbol r'+\boldsymbol r}\rangle ,
\end{aligned}
\] the Fourier transform of the spin–spin correlation function and the quantity a scattering experiment measures.
In a phase with long-range order at wave vector \(\boldsymbol Q\), \(\langle|m_{\boldsymbol Q}|^2\rangle\) stays finite as \(N\to\infty\), so \(S(\boldsymbol Q)\propto N\): a Bragg peak. In the paramagnet correlations decay over a finite length and \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) is a broad, \(N\)-independent function. Parseval’s theorem adds a sum rule: \(\sum_{\boldsymbol k}|\hat s(\boldsymbol k)|^2=N\sum_{\boldsymbol r}s_{\boldsymbol r}^2=N^2\), so the average of \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) over the Brillouin zone is exactly \(1\), and ordering only redistributes the weight.
We compute \(S(\boldsymbol k)\) with np.fft.fft2 from Monte Carlo snapshots (\(L=32\), 16 annealed chains \(\times\) 20 snapshots per point, all four points in one batch) in four situations: the ferromagnet, the paramagnet, the frustrated point \(g=1/2\) at low \(T\), and the stripe phase.


Code
L_sk = 32
cases = [(0.25, 1.0, "ferromagnet"), (0.25, 3.0, "paramagnet"), (0.5, 0.3, "g = 1/2, low T"), (0.75, 0.8, "stripes")]
n_ch, n_steps = 16, 12
# every chain is cooled linearly from T = 4 to its target temperature in n_steps steps; snapshots are kept at the last step
g_sk = np.repeat([c[0] for c in cases], n_ch)                                          # (64,)
lam_sk = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_steps)[:, None]                                       # interpolation parameter, (12, 1)
T_sk = (1 - lam_sk) * 4.0 + lam_sk * np.repeat([c[1] for c in cases], n_ch)[None, :]   # (12, 64): from T = 4 to the target
t0 = time.perf_counter()
meas, conf = run_mc(random_configs(len(g_sk), L_sk, 2), g_sk, T_sk, n_equil=200, n_meas=20, n_between=10, seed=21, keep=True)
Sk, snaps = {}, {}
for k, (gv, T, name) in enumerate(cases):
    c = conf[-1, :, k * n_ch:(k + 1) * n_ch].reshape(-1, L_sk, L_sk).astype(np.float64)   # (320, 32, 32) snapshots at the target T
    Sk[name] = (np.abs(np.fft.fft2(c)) ** 2).mean(0) / L_sk**2                          # S(k) on the 32 x 32 grid of wave vectors
    snaps[name] = c[-1]
    print(f"{name:15s} (g = {gv}, T = {T}):  mean of S(k) over k = {Sk[name].mean():.6f} (sum rule: 1);   "
          f"S(0,0) = {Sk[name][0, 0]:7.2f},  S(pi,0) = {Sk[name][L_sk//2, 0]:7.2f},  S(0,pi) = {Sk[name][0, L_sk//2]:7.2f},  "
          f"S(pi,pi) = {Sk[name][L_sk//2, L_sk//2]:6.2f}   (N = {L_sk**2})")
print(f"({time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")

kgrid = 2 * np.pi * np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fftfreq(L_sk))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(13, 6.2))
for j, (gv, T, name) in enumerate(cases):
    ax[0, j].imshow(snaps[name].T, cmap=SPIN_CMAP, vmin=-1, vmax=1, origin="lower"); ax[0, j].set_xticks([]); ax[0, j].set_yticks([])
    ax[0, j].set_title(f"{name}\ng = {gv}, T = {T}", fontsize=10)
    im = ax[1, j].pcolormesh(kgrid, kgrid, np.log10(np.fft.fftshift(Sk[name]).T), cmap="magma", shading="nearest")
    ax[1, j].set_xlabel("$k_x$"); ax[1, j].set_ylabel("$k_y$"); ax[1, j].set_aspect("equal")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1, j], fraction=0.046, label=r"$\log_{10}S(\mathbf{k})$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


ferromagnet     (g = 0.25, T = 1.0):  mean of S(k) over k = 1.000000 (sum rule: 1);   S(0,0) = 1004.65,  S(pi,0) =    0.02,  S(0,pi) =    0.02,  S(pi,pi) =   0.01   (N = 1024)
paramagnet      (g = 0.25, T = 3.0):  mean of S(k) over k = 1.000000 (sum rule: 1);   S(0,0) =    3.54,  S(pi,0) =    0.86,  S(0,pi) =    1.07,  S(pi,pi) =   0.33   (N = 1024)
g = 1/2, low T  (g = 0.5, T = 0.3):  mean of S(k) over k = 1.000000 (sum rule: 1);   S(0,0) =   25.81,  S(pi,0) =    1.32,  S(0,pi) =    1.95,  S(pi,pi) =   0.01   (N = 1024)
stripes         (g = 0.75, T = 0.8):  mean of S(k) over k = 1.000000 (sum rule: 1);   S(0,0) =    0.00,  S(pi,0) =  638.27,  S(0,pi) =  382.89,  S(pi,pi) =   0.00   (N = 1024)
(14.5 s)





The sum rule holds to all printed digits, and the four maps look as the theory predicts. The ferromagnet shows one Bragg peak at \(\boldsymbol k=(0,0)\) of height comparable to \(N\) (\(S(0,0)\approx1005\) for \(N=1024\)). The paramagnet has a broad maximum around \((0,0)\) of height of order one (\(3.5\)) — short-range ferromagnetic correlations, no order. In the stripe phase the peaks sit at \((\pi,0)\) and \((0,\pi)\); the map averages over chains, which may have chosen different orientations, so both peaks appear. At \(g=1/2\) and low \(T\) the weight concentrates on the lines \(k_x=0\) and \(k_y=0\). These are the modes of the degenerate ground-state manifold (rows or columns with independent signs, Section 3.5) and the lines on which \(\mathcal J(\boldsymbol k)\) is maximal (Section 6). The snapshot shows domains of rows or columns, not a single ordered pattern.
The structure factor thus identifies the ordering wave vector without prior knowledge: a point peak for long-range order, a line of weight for the frustrated point. Lab 020 asks an algorithm to make the same distinction from raw snapshots.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
8. Transfer matrices of infinite strips
Monte Carlo has statistical errors and needs equilibration. For a strip of finite width \(L\) and infinite length the free energy can be computed exactly from the largest eigenvalue of the row transfer matrix — the method of Lab 012, here with diagonal bonds. The results are exact for each \(L\), and the limit \(L\to\infty\) is approached through a sequence of widths.
With the row-pair energy \(W(\sigma,\sigma')\) of Section 3.4 the transfer matrix is \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf V_{\sigma\sigma'} &= e^{-\beta W(\sigma,\sigma')}\\
&= \exp\Big\{\beta\Big[J_1\sum_xs_xs'_x - J_2\sum_xs_x\big(s'_{x+1}+s'_{x-1}\big) + \frac{J_1}{2}\sum_x\big(s_xs_{x+1}+s'_xs'_{x+1}\big)\Big]\Big\},
\end{aligned}
\] a \(2^L\times2^L\) matrix. It is symmetric (\(\sum_xs_x(s'_{x+1}+s'_{x-1})=\sum_xs'_x(s_{x-1}+s_{x+1})\)) and has positive entries. For a strip of length \(M\to\infty\), \(Z=\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf V^M\simeq\lambda_0^M\), so \[
f_L(T) = -\frac{T}{L}\ln\lambda_0,\qquad \xi_L = \frac{1}{\ln(\lambda_0/|\lambda_1|)},
\] where \(\lambda_0\) is the largest eigenvalue (positive and non-degenerate by the Perron–Frobenius theorem) and \(\lambda_1\) the eigenvalue of largest modulus among the eigenvectors odd under the global spin flip — the ones that carry the spin–spin correlation along the strip, \(\langle s_0s_r\rangle\sim(|\lambda_1|/\lambda_0)^r\). The modulus matters here: horizontal stripes (rows alternately \(+\) and \(-\)) appear as a negative eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\approx-\lambda_0\).
The spin-flip symmetry halves the work. The flip \(\sigma\to-\sigma\) maps the index \(n\to2^L-1-n\) and commutes with \(\mathsf V\). With \(\mathsf V^{\pm}_{ab}=\mathsf V_{ab}\pm\mathsf V_{a,\bar b}\) for \(a,b<2^{L-1}\) (Lab 012), the even and odd sectors are two symmetric matrices of half the size.
As a first test, \(Z\) of the \(4\times4\) torus is \(\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf V^4\) and must equal the enumeration of Section 3.3 at any \((g,T)\).


Code
_row_cache = {}
def log_V(L, J1, J2, T):
    # ln V[sigma, sigma'] = -W(sigma, sigma') / T, shape (2^L, 2^L)
    if L not in _row_cache:
        _row_cache[L] = row_terms(L)
    intra, nn, dd = _row_cache[L]
    return (J1 * nn - J2 * dd + 0.5 * J1 * (intra[:, None] + intra[None, :])) / T

def top_eig(A, which):
    # largest algebraic ("LA") or largest-modulus ("LM") eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix
    n = A.shape[0]
    if n <= 512:
        w = eigh(A, eigvals_only=True)
        return w[-1] if which == "LA" else w[np.argmax(np.abs(w))]
    return eigsh(A, k=1, which=which, tol=0)[0][0]

def strip_eigs(L, J1, J2, T, odd=True):
    # ln(lambda_0) and ln|lambda_1| of the strip of width L (lambda_1 only if odd=True)
    lv = log_V(L, J1, J2, T)
    shift = lv.max()
    V = np.exp(lv - shift)                                 # rescaled to avoid overflow; ln lambda = ln(eig) + shift
    n = V.shape[0] // 2
    Vf = V[:n, ::-1][:, :n]                                # V[a, flip(b)] for a, b < 2^(L-1)
    l0 = np.log(top_eig(V[:n, :n] + Vf, "LA")) + shift
    l1 = np.log(abs(top_eig(V[:n, :n] - Vf, "LM"))) + shift if odd else np.nan
    return l0, l1

# check against enumeration: Z(4x4 torus) = Tr V^4
for gv, T in [(0.0, 2.0), (0.4, 1.0), (0.5, 0.5), (0.8, 1.5)]:
    V = np.exp(log_V(4, 1.0, gv, T))
    lnZ_tm = np.log(np.trace(np.linalg.matrix_power(V, 4)))
    E = -B1_44 + gv * B2_44
    lnZ_ex = -E.min() / T + np.log(np.exp(-(E - E.min()) / T).sum())
    print(f"g = {gv}, T = {T}:  ln Z (Tr V^4) = {lnZ_tm:.12f}   ln Z (enumeration) = {lnZ_ex:.12f}")

8.1 Free energy, specific heat and residual entropy
The two values of \(\ln Z\) agree to twelve digits. For widths \(L=4,6,8,10\) and several \(g\) we compute \(f_L(T)\) on a fine grid and the specific heat \(c_L=-T\,\partial^2f_L/\partial T^2\) by finite differences (the eigenvalues are accurate to machine precision, so second differences are reliable). The results are stored in strip_f[(g, L)] and strip_c[(g, L)], each of shape \((n_T,)\). In the figure, watch how the specific-heat maximum moves as \(g\) approaches \(1/2\).


Code
g_curves = [0.0, 0.3, 0.45, 0.5, 0.55, 0.7, 1.0]
L_curves = [4, 6, 8, 10]
T_fine = np.linspace(0.05, 4.0, 159); dT = T_fine[1] - T_fine[0]
strip_f, strip_c = {}, {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for gv in g_curves:
    for L in L_curves:
        l0 = np.array([strip_eigs(L, 1.0, gv, T, odd=False)[0] for T in T_fine])
        strip_f[(gv, L)] = -T_fine * l0 / L
        strip_c[(gv, L)] = -T_fine * np.gradient(np.gradient(strip_f[(gv, L)], dT), dT)
print(f"strip free energies: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(14, 6), sharex=True)
for a, gv in zip(ax.ravel(), g_curves):
    for i, L in enumerate(L_curves):
        a.plot(T_fine[2:-2], strip_c[(gv, L)][2:-2], color=blues(i / (len(L_curves) - 1)), lw=1.8, label=f"L = {L}")
    a.set_title(f"g = {gv}", fontsize=10); a.set_ylabel("$c_L$")
ax[1, 3].axis("off")
for a in ax[1]: a.set_xlabel("$T$")
ax[0, 0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle("specific heat per spin of infinite strips of width L (exact)", color=UJNavy)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for gv in g_curves:

    print(f"g = {gv:4.2f}, L = {L_curves[-1]}:  maximum of c_L = {c.max():.3f} at T = {T_fine[2:-2][c.argmax()]:.3f}")

The strip free energy also reveals a residual entropy at \(g=1/2\). For \(T\to0\) only the ground states contribute: \(\lambda_0^M\simeq n_0\,e^{-\beta E_0}\) with \(E_0=-J_1LM\) at \(g=1/2\). Section 3.5 gives \(n_0\simeq2^M\) for a long strip (each row uniform with a free sign), so \[
\lambda_0\,e^{-\beta J_1 L}\xrightarrow{T\to0}2,\qquad s_L(T\to0) = \frac{\ln2}{L}\ \text{per spin}.
\] For \(g\neq1/2\) the ground states are a fixed finite number and the same ratio (with the corresponding \(E_0\)) tends to \(1\), i.e. zero entropy. The entropy per spin follows from the free energy as \(s=(u-f)/T\) with \(u=\partial(\beta f)/\partial\beta = f - T\,\partial f/\partial T\), so \(s=-\partial f/\partial T\). The cell evaluates the ratio and the entropy at low temperature for \(g=0.3\), \(0.5\) and \(0.7\).


Code
for gv in (0.3, 0.5, 0.7):
    e0_row = min(-2 + 2 * gv, -2 * gv)                                  # ground-state energy per spin
    for L in (6, 8, 10):
        ratios = [np.exp(strip_eigs(L, 1.0, gv, T, odd=False)[0] + e0_row * L / T) for T in (0.1, 0.05, 0.03)]

The ratio is exactly \(2\) at \(g=1/2\) and \(1\) at \(g=0.3\) and \(0.7\): at \(g=1/2\) the strip keeps an entropy \(\ln2/L\) per spin down to \(T=0\), the transfer-matrix version of the degeneracy \(2^M\), while away from \(g=1/2\) the entropy vanishes. For \(g\) near \(1/2\) the maximum of \(c_L\) moves to lower temperature (\(T\approx0.6\)–\(0.8\) for \(L=10\) at \(g=0.45,0.5,0.55\)), but at \(g=1/2\) it does not disappear, although there is no transition there: the strip specific heat also counts local excitations (a single flipped spin costs \(4J_1\) at \(g=1/2\), Exercise 1), so a peak of \(c_L\) alone does not prove a phase transition.


8.2 Transition temperature from the strips
For each \(g\) the position \(T_{\max}(g)\) of the maximum of \(c_L\) is a finite-size indicator of the transition (Lab 012: for the Ising model it approaches \(T_c\) slowly). A sharper indicator is the correlation length. Above \(T_c\), \(\xi_L\) saturates as \(L\) grows, so \(\xi_L/L\) decreases with \(L\); below \(T_c\) the ordered states become degenerate, \(|\lambda_1|\to\lambda_0\), and \(\xi_L/L\) increases with \(L\). The temperature \(T^*(L,L+2)\) where \(\xi_L/L=\xi_{L+2}/(L+2)\) therefore estimates \(T_c\), and it converges fast for the Ising model (Lab 012). We solve for the crossing with brentq in a bracket found on a coarse grid, for widths up to \(L=12\) (\(2^{12}\times2^{12}\) matrices); where no crossing exists in the bracket the table prints none.


Code
def xi_over_L(L, J1, J2, T):
    l0, l1 = strip_eigs(L, J1, J2, T)
    return 1.0 / (l0 - l1) / L

def crossing(L, J1, J2, T_lo, T_hi, n_grid=12):
    # temperature where xi_L/L = xi_{L+2}/(L+2), searched in [T_lo, T_hi]; None if no sign change
    F = lambda T: xi_over_L(L, J1, J2, T) - xi_over_L(L + 2, J1, J2, T)
    Tg = np.linspace(T_lo, T_hi, n_grid)
    Fg = np.array([F(T) for T in Tg])
    Fg = np.where(np.isfinite(Fg), Fg, 0.0)
    idx = np.where(Fg[:-1] * Fg[1:] < 0)[0]
    if len(idx) == 0:
        return None
    i = idx[-1]                                                       # the highest-temperature sign change
    return brentq(F, Tg[i], Tg[i + 1], xtol=1e-6)

def T_guess(g):
    # bracket centre from the mean-field shape, used only to place the search window
    return TC_ISING * max(1 - 2 * g, 2 * g - 1, 0.15) if g < 1 else TC_ISING * g

g_cross = [0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.45, 0.55, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0]
Tstar = {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for gv in g_cross:
    lo, hi = 0.25 * T_guess(gv), 1.6 * T_guess(gv) + 0.3
    for L in (6, 8):
        Tstar[(gv, L)] = crossing(L, 1.0, gv, lo, hi)
print(f"crossings for (6,8) and (8,10): {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for gv in (0.0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 2.0):                                  # the most expensive pair only for a few g
    ref = Tstar[(gv, 8)]
    Tstar[(gv, 10)] = crossing(10, 1.0, gv, 0.9 * ref, 1.1 * ref, n_grid=4) if ref else None
print(f"crossings for (10,12): {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
# g -> infinity: J1 = 0, J2 = 1 (two decoupled sublattices)
Tstar_inf = {L: crossing(L, 0.0, 1.0, 1.5, 3.0) for L in (6, 8)}

fmt = lambda v: f"{v:8.4f}" if v is not None else "    none"
print("\n     g    T*(6,8)  T*(8,10)  T*(10,12)   T*/g (g >= 1)   mean field")
for gv in g_cross:
    best = Tstar.get((gv, 10)) or Tstar[(gv, 8)] or Tstar[(gv, 6)]
    ratio = f"{best / gv:8.4f}" if (gv >= 1 and best) else "        "
    print(f"  {gv:4.2f}  {fmt(Tstar[(gv, 6)])}  {fmt(Tstar[(gv, 8)])}  {fmt(Tstar.get((gv, 10)))}      {ratio}       {max(4 * (1 - gv), 4 * gv):.3f}")
print(f"J1 = 0 (g -> infinity), T*/J2:  (6,8) {fmt(Tstar_inf[6])}   (8,10) {fmt(Tstar_inf[8])}   exact 2/ln(1+sqrt2) = {TC_ISING:.4f}")

At \(g=0\) the crossings converge to Onsager’s \(T_c\): the \((10,12)\) value \(2.2705\) lies \(0.0013\) above the exact \(2.2692\). For large \(g\), \(T^*/g\) grows towards \(2.269\) with \(g\), and the decoupled limit \(J_1=0\) gives \(T^*/J_2\) close to \(2.269\) directly. In between, the crossings trace a line far below mean field that dips towards \(g=1/2\). At these widths the dip stops at \(T^*\approx0.7\) for \(g=0.45\) and \(0.55\): close to \(g=1/2\) the relevant length scales exceed \(L\le12\), and Kalz et al. [2008] find from much larger Monte Carlo lattices that the data are consistent with \(T_c\to0\) at \(g=1/2\), as the domain-wall argument of Section 4 requires. The specific-heat maximum lies close to the crossings away from \(g=1/2\) but stays at a finite temperature at \(g=1/2\) itself, where there is no transition.

title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
9. Binder cumulants
The strips of Section 8 are exact but narrow (\(L\le12\)). Monte Carlo reaches larger lattices at the price of statistical errors. A finite lattice has no sharp transition (Lab 012, Section 1), so we need a quantity whose size dependence changes sign at \(T_c\); the Binder cumulant is such a quantity [Binder 1981]. For a scalar order parameter, here the ferromagnetic \(m\), it is defined as \[
U_m = 1-\frac{\langle m^4\rangle}{3\langle m^2\rangle^2}.
\] In the disordered phase, \(L\gg\xi\), \(m\) is a sum of many weakly correlated contributions, hence Gaussian by the central limit theorem; then \(\langle m^4\rangle=3\langle m^2\rangle^2\) and \(U_m\to0\). In the ordered phase \(m\approx\pm m_0\), \(\langle m^4\rangle=\langle m^2\rangle^2\) and \(U_m\to2/3\). At \(T_c\) the distribution of \(m/\sqrt{\langle m^2\rangle}\) has an \(L\)-independent shape (scale invariance), so \(U_m\) takes the same value for all large \(L\): the curves \(U_m(T)\) for different \(L\) cross at \(T_c\).
The stripe order parameter has two components \((m_x,m_y)\), and the normalisation must be adapted. For a two-dimensional Gaussian vector \(\langle r^4\rangle=2\langle r^2\rangle^2\), and for a vector of fixed length \(\langle r^4\rangle=\langle r^2\rangle^2\), so \[
U_{\rm str} = 2-\frac{\langle m_{\rm str}^4\rangle}{\langle m_{\rm str}^2\rangle^2}
\] goes from \(0\) (disordered) to \(1\) (ordered). SymPy verifies the Gaussian moments.


Code
xg, yg, sg = sp.symbols("x y sigma", positive=True)
gauss1 = sp.exp(-xg**2 / (2 * sg**2)) / sp.sqrt(2 * sp.pi * sg**2)
mom = lambda k: sp.integrate(xg**k * gauss1, (xg, -sp.oo, sp.oo))
print("1D Gaussian:  <x^4> / <x^2>^2 =", sp.simplify(mom(4) / mom(2)**2), "  ->  U_m = 1 - 3/3 =", 1 - sp.simplify(mom(4) / mom(2)**2) / 3)
r, ph_ = sp.symbols("r phi", positive=True)
gauss2_r = r * sp.exp(-r**2 / (2 * sg**2)) / (2 * sp.pi * sg**2)          # density in polar coordinates, times the Jacobian r
mom2 = lambda k: sp.integrate(sp.integrate(r**k * gauss2_r, (r, 0, sp.oo)), (ph_, 0, 2 * sp.pi))
print("2D Gaussian:  <r^4> / <r^2>^2 =", sp.simplify(mom2(4) / mom2(2)**2), "  ->  U_str = 2 - 2 =", 2 - sp.simplify(mom2(4) / mom2(2)**2))


1D Gaussian:  <x^4> / <x^2>^2 = 3   ->  U_m = 1 - 3/3 = 0
2D Gaussian:  <r^4> / <r^2>^2 = 2   ->  U_str = 2 - 2 = 0


For the simulations we choose, for each \(g\), a temperature window around the transfer-matrix estimate \(T^*\) of Section 8.2 and simulate three sizes, \(L=16,24,32\), at 8 temperatures with 16 independent chains per \((g,T,L)\); all \(5\times8\times16=640\) chains of one size run in a single batch. Each chain starts in the ordered state and runs at fixed temperature: n_equil sweeps of equilibration, then n_meas measurements separated by n_between sweeps. Error bars come from a jackknife over chains (leave one block of 2 chains out). The ferromagnetic side uses \(U_m\) and the stripe side \(U_{\rm str}\); at \(g=2\) the comparison with \(2.269\,g\) tests the large-\(g\) limit of Section 5.

def binder(meas, stripe):
    # meas: (chains, nT, n_meas, 4) -> U(T) and its jackknife error over blocks of chains; shapes (nT,), (nT,)
    q = np.hypot(meas[..., 1], meas[..., 2]) if stripe else meas[..., 0]
    q2, q4 = (q**2).mean(2), (q**4).mean(2)                         # per chain and temperature: (chains, nT)
    U = (lambda a2, a4: 2 - a4 / a2**2) if stripe else (lambda a2, a4: 1 - a4 / (3 * a2**2))
    full = U(q2.mean(0), q4.mean(0))
    blocks = np.array_split(np.arange(q2.shape[0]), 8)
    jk = np.array([U(np.delete(q2, b, 0).mean(0), np.delete(q4, b, 0).mean(0)) for b in blocks])
    err = np.sqrt((len(blocks) - 1) * ((jk - jk.mean(0))**2).mean(0))
    return full, err

def crossing_T(T, Ua, Ub, T_ref):
    # temperature where the interpolated curves Ua(T), Ub(T) cross, the crossing closest to T_ref; None if none
    d = Ua - Ub
    idx = np.where(d[:-1] * d[1:] < 0)[0]
    if len(idx) == 0:
        return None
    Tx = [T[i] - d[i] * (T[i + 1] - T[i]) / (d[i + 1] - d[i]) for i in idx]
    return min(Tx, key=lambda t: abs(t - T_ref))

The Binder crossings for \(L=16,24,32\) agree with the transfer-matrix crossings to within a few per cent; the largest deviations (\(g=0\) and \(g=0.3\), crossings below the exact or transfer-matrix values) and the spread between the \((16,24)\) and \((24,32)\) crossings show the statistical and equilibration limits of local Metropolis updates with 16 chains per point (Lab 018 discusses critical slowing down). title: Lab 029: Physics of the frustrated J1–J2 Ising model
text:
10. First-order and continuous transitions
Our calculations locate the transition line but cannot decide its nature close to \(g=1/2\): that needs lattices far larger than ours, histogram analysis and dedicated methods. The model has a long history of conflicting answers, which makes it a good benchmark — and a warning that small-lattice data can mislead. In what follows, each statement is attributed to the paper that makes it. Some papers take the nearest-neighbour coupling antiferromagnetic, others write the ferromagnetic one as \(J_1<0\); by the checkerboard gauge of Section 2 all these results apply to our model with \(g=|J_2/J_1|\) (an antiferromagnetic \(J_1\) turns our ferromagnet into a Néel state).
On the ferromagnetic side, \(g<1/2\), the order parameter is a scalar with \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry. Kalz, Honecker, Fuchs and Pruschke [2008] find a transition in the two-dimensional Ising universality class (for example \(\nu=0.99(1)\) at \(g=0.3\), against the Ising value \(\nu=1\)), and a transition temperature consistent with \(T_c\to0\) at \(g=1/2\).
On the stripe side, \(g>1/2\), the literature records a long debate. Early Monte Carlo work [Landau & Binder 1985, among others] was interpreted as a continuous transition with non-universal (continuously varying) exponents (as summarised by Kalz et al. [2008]). Kalz et al. [2008] then observed a double-peaked energy histogram at \(g=0.6\), the signature of a first-order transition (coexistence of the ordered and disordered phases), and concluded that the transition is weakly first order for moderate \(g>1/2\). Kalz, Honecker and Moliner [2011] found doubly peaked histograms for \(1/2<g\lesssim1\) and, by perturbation theory around the two decoupled critical Ising models at \(J_1=0\) (our Section 5.2), derived the Ashkin–Teller model as the effective theory.
Jin, Sen and Sandvik [2012] reached a different picture. They showed that for \(g\ge g^*\) the transition is continuous with Ashkin–Teller exponents that vary continuously from those of the 4-state Potts model at \(g=g^*\) to those of the Ising model for \(g\to\infty\), with \(g^*=0.67(1)\); the transition is first order for \(1/2<g<g^*\), and pseudo-first-order for \(g^*<g<1\): on finite lattices a continuous transition near the Potts point shows first-order-like features such as double-peaked histograms. Jin, Sen, Guo and Sandvik [2013] extended this with cluster mean-field theory, Monte Carlo and transfer matrices: a line of very weak first-order transitions for \(1/2<g<g^*\), and continuous transitions above \(g^*\) that map onto the critical line of the Ashkin–Teller model from its 4-state Potts point to the decoupled-Ising limit. Finally, Li and Yang [2021] used tensor networks and found that if a first-order region exists, it is smaller than in the earlier studies; their analysis suggests that the model evolves continuously from two decoupled Ising models (central charge \(c=1\)) to a point in the tricritical Ising class (\(c=0.7\)) at \(g^*\simeq0.54\).
These results connect directly with this notebook. The Ashkin–Teller structure is the \(D_4\) symmetry of the stripe order parameter (Section 2.1) and the two sublattice magnetisations of the \(g\to\infty\) limit (Section 5.2). The difficulty of the problem near \(g=1/2\) — tiny energy scales (Section 4), a degenerate manifold (Section 3.5), first-order or pseudo-first-order behaviour — is what makes the model a demanding test for the unsupervised methods of Labs 019–020.
The results of this notebook and the literature above combine into the phase diagram drawn below. A phase diagram is a map of the control parameters, here the coupling ratio \(g=J_2/J_1\) and the temperature \(T/J_1\), divided into regions with qualitatively different behaviour, the phases, and the lines between them, the phase transitions. The type of a transition is read off from the free energy per spin \(f\) and its derivatives. At a first-order transition a first derivative of \(f\), such as the energy or the order parameter, jumps, and the two phases coexist at the transition temperature; on a finite lattice this shows up as an energy histogram with two peaks, the observation of Kalz et al. [2008]. At a continuous transition the first derivatives are continuous, the order parameter goes to zero continuously, and the correlation length diverges as a power of \(|T-T_c|\) with critical exponents shared by a whole universality class.
The orange dots are the transfer-matrix crossings of Section 8.2 and the blue squares the Monte Carlo Binder crossings of Section 9; the solid lines through them are only a guide to the eye. Three statements are exact and placed exactly: \(T_c=2/\ln(1+\sqrt2)=2.269\,J_1\) at \(g=0\) (Onsager), the asymptote \(T_c\to2.269\,g\,J_1\) for \(g\to\infty\) (two decoupled Ising lattices, Section 5.2), and \(T_c\to0\) at \(g=1/2\), where domain walls cost nothing (Section 4) and where Kalz et al. [2008] find their data consistent with a vanishing transition temperature; the dashed segments connect the computed points to this limit. Below the line on the left the ferromagnet has \(m\neq0\); below the line on the right the stripe phase has \(m_{\rm str}\neq0\); above both lies the paramagnet. On the ferromagnetic side the transition is continuous and in the two-dimensional Ising universality class [Kalz et al. 2008]. On the stripe side, for \(g\) well above \(1/2\), it is continuous with exponents that vary along the line, those of the Ashkin–Teller model introduced in Section 2.1 [Jin, Sen & Sandvik 2012]. Close to \(g=1/2\) (hatched band, \(1/2<g\lesssim0.7\)) its nature is debated: first order according to Kalz et al. [2008, 2011] and Jin et al. [2012, 2013], who place the end of the first-order region at \(g^*=0.67(1)\), while Li and Yang [2021] find at most a much smaller first-order region.

Exercise 1 — single spin flips and mean field
Compute, symbolically and numerically, the energy cost \(\Delta E\) of flipping a single spin in the ferromagnetic ground state and in the stripe ground state as a function of \(J_1,J_2\). Compare with \(T_{\rm MF}\) of Section 6 and explain the relation using \(\Delta E_i=2s_ih_i\).

Solution


Code
L = 8; x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(L), np.arange(L), indexing="ij")
for name, s0 in {"ferromagnet": np.ones((L, L), int), "stripes": (-1) ** x}.items():
    s1 = s0.copy(); s1[3, 3] *= -1                                        # flip one spin
    b0, b1 = bond_sums(s0), bond_sums(s1)
    dE = sp.expand(-J1s * (b1[0] + b1[1] - b0[0] - b0[1]) + J2s * (b1[2] - b0[2]))
    print(f"{name:11s}: Delta E = {dE}   (numerical at g = 0.3: {energy(s1, 0.3) - energy(s0, 0.3):+.2f})")


ferromagnet: Delta E = 8*J_1 - 8*J_2   (numerical at g = 0.3: +5.60)
stripes    : Delta E = 8*J_2   (numerical at g = 0.3: +2.40)


\(\Delta E_{\rm FM}=8J_1-8J_2=2\cdot4(J_1-J_2)\) and \(\Delta E_{\rm str}=8J_2=2\cdot4J_2\): in both cases \(\Delta E=2T_{\rm MF}\). The reason: \(\Delta E_i=2s_ih_i\), and in the perfectly ordered state the local field is \(|h_i|=\mathcal J(\boldsymbol Q)\), which is also \(T_{\rm MF}\). Mean field treats the ordered state as a collection of independent spins in this field. Note that a single flip costs \(8|J_1-J_2|\) or \(8J_2\), which does not vanish at \(g=1/2\) (\(4J_1\)): the soft excitations at \(g=1/2\) are extended domain walls, not single spins (Section 4).



Exercise 2 — odd lattice sizes
Use minplus_torus to compute \(E_0/N\) and the degeneracy on \(4\times5\) and \(5\times5\) tori at \(g=0.75\) and \(g=0.5\). Explain the results.

Solution


Code
for L, M in [(4, 5), (5, 5)]:
    for gv in (0.75, 0.5):
        e0, n0 = minplus_torus(L, M, gv)
        print(f"{L} x {M}, g = {gv}:  E0/N = {e0:+.4f}  (bulk value {min(-2 + 2*gv, -2*gv):+.4f}),  n0 = {n0}  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = {2**L + 2**M - 2})")


4 x 5, g = 0.75:  E0/N = -1.5000  (bulk value -1.5000),  n0 = 2  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 46)
4 x 5, g = 0.5:  E0/N = -1.0000  (bulk value -1.0000),  n0 = 46  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 46)
5 x 5, g = 0.75:  E0/N = -1.3000  (bulk value -1.5000),  n0 = 20  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 62)
5 x 5, g = 0.5:  E0/N = -1.0000  (bulk value -1.0000),  n0 = 62  (2^L + 2^M - 2 = 62)


At \(g=0.75\) stripes need an even period. On \(4\times5\) only the stripes that alternate along the even direction fit: the degeneracy drops from 4 to 2, the energy is unchanged. On \(5\times5\) no stripe state fits, and the ground state must contain a domain wall. The cheapest is one parallel (phase-slip) wall of length 5, energy \(5\,\sigma_\parallel=5\cdot2(2g-1)=5\) at \(g=0.75\), i.e. \(0.2\) per spin above \(-2g\) — exactly the printed difference. Its degeneracy is \(2\) orientations \(\times\) \(5\) positions \(\times\) \(2\) signs \(=20\). At \(g=1/2\) the derivation of Section 3.5 never used the parity of \(L\) or \(M\), and the count \(2^L+2^M-2\) holds for odd sizes as well. Choosing even \(L\) in simulations of this model is not a detail.



Exercise 3 — Binder cumulant limits by sampling
Draw \(10^6\) samples of (a) a Gaussian scalar, (b) a scalar \(\pm1\), (c) a two-dimensional Gaussian vector, (d) a two-dimensional vector of length 1 pointing to one of the four directions \((\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)\). Evaluate \(U_m\) for (a), (b) and \(U_{\rm str}\) for (c), (d), and compare with the limits of Section 9.

Solution


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(7); n = 10**6
U1 = lambda q: 1 - (q**4).mean() / (3 * (q**2).mean()**2)
U2 = lambda q: 2 - (q**4).mean() / (q**2).mean()**2
a = rng.standard_normal(n); b = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], n)
c = np.hypot(rng.standard_normal(n), rng.standard_normal(n))
d = np.ones(n)                                                         # |(+-1, 0)| = |(0, +-1)| = 1
print(f"(a) Gaussian scalar: U_m = {U1(a):+.4f} (expected 0);   (b) +-1: U_m = {U1(b):.4f} (expected 2/3 = {2/3:.4f})")
print(f"(c) 2D Gaussian: U_str = {U2(c):+.4f} (expected 0);   (d) four stripe states: U_str = {U2(d):.4f} (expected 1)")


(a) Gaussian scalar: U_m = +0.0002 (expected 0);   (b) +-1: U_m = 0.6667 (expected 2/3 = 0.6667)
(c) 2D Gaussian: U_str = +0.0006 (expected 0);   (d) four stripe states: U_str = 1.0000 (expected 1)


The finite-sample values deviate from the limits by \(O(n^{-1/2})\). In a simulation the distribution at \(T_c\) is neither Gaussian nor two delta peaks, and the cumulant takes an intermediate, universal value that depends on the universality class and on the boundary conditions.

title: Lab 030: Physics of the 2D XY model and the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
text:
1. Continuous symmetry in two dimensions
We begin by recalling equilibrium statistical mechanics. A configuration \(\boldsymbol\theta\) of a classical system with energy \(H(\boldsymbol\theta)\) occurs at temperature \(T\) with the Boltzmann probability \[
\begin{aligned}
p(\boldsymbol\theta)&=\frac{e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol\theta)}}{Z},\qquad \beta=\frac1T,\\
Z&=\int\! d\boldsymbol\theta\; e^{-\beta H(\boldsymbol\theta)},
\end{aligned}
\] with \(k_B=1\). The free energy \(F=-T\ln Z\) balances energy against entropy, \(F=E-TS\): at low \(T\) the energy wins and the system orders, at high \(T\) the entropy wins and it disorders. A phase transition is a temperature at which \(F/N\) (with \(N\) the number of spins, \(N\to\infty\)) is not an analytic function of \(T\).
In the 2D Ising model (\(s_i=\pm1\)) the energy is invariant under the global flip \(s_i\to-s_i\), yet below \(T_c\) the system picks one of the two ordered states and the magnetisation \(\langle m\rangle\) is non-zero: the symmetry is spontaneously broken. To destroy the order one has to create a domain wall, whose energy grows with its length, and at low \(T\) such walls are too expensive.
The situation changes when the symmetry is continuous. If the spins are planar unit vectors \(\boldsymbol s_i=(\cos\theta_i,\sin\theta_i)\) and the energy depends only on relative angles, there is no domain wall: the direction can rotate gradually over a long distance. Turning the spins by \(2\pi\) gradually across a region of linear size \(\ell\) costs \(\frac J2(2\pi/\ell)^2\) per bond, i.e. an energy \(\propto\ell^{d-2}\) for the whole region: independent of \(\ell\) in two dimensions, whereas an Ising domain wall costs \(\propto\ell^{d-1}\) (Section 3 makes the spin-wave argument precise). These long-wavelength twists, spin waves, are the Goldstone modes of the broken continuous symmetry, and they are so cheap in \(d\le2\) that thermal fluctuations destroy the long-range order at every \(T>0\). Mermin and Wagner (1966) proved this rigorously for the isotropic Heisenberg model; Berezinskii (1971) analysed systems with a continuous symmetry group in one and two dimensions. We derive the effect for the XY model in the spin-wave approximation and check it with Monte Carlo.
The sketch below compares the two cases on a strip of twelve columns. In the Ising model (top) the spins change from up to down across a single column of bonds; every bond on that column is broken and costs \(2J\), so a wall across a region of linear size \(\ell\) costs an energy proportional to \(\ell^{d-1}\). In the XY model (bottom) the angle can instead turn by \(2\pi\) gradually, by \(2\pi/\ell\) from one column to the next. Each bond then costs only about \(\frac J2(2\pi/\ell)^2\), and the twist of a whole region costs an energy proportional to \(\ell^{d-2}\), which in two dimensions does not grow with \(\ell\).


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;
#   satisfied bond: solid blue line, broken (frustrated) bond: dashed purple line marked with a cross.
# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,
# and shown here at a higher screen resolution.
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

NAVY, ORANGE, BLUE, GRAY, PURPLE, GREEN = "#002B5C", "#D35A05", "#005CA7", "#5A6270", "#AA3377", "#228833"
SKETCH_STYLE = {"font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.labelsize": 11, "xtick.labelsize": 10,
                "ytick.labelsize": 10, "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 130, "lines.linewidth": 1.5,
                "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}

def save_sketch(fig, name, extra_dirs=()):
    # PNG copy for the lecture slides: white background, 300 dpi, included at its physical width
    os.makedirs("../beamer/figures", exist_ok=True)
    for d in ("../beamer/figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_spin(ax, x, y, s, r=0.26, sign=False, alpha=1.0, fs=10, lw=1.3):
    # one Ising spin at (x, y): navy disc for s = +1, white disc with orange rim for s = -1 (optionally with "+" / "-")
    face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if s > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x, y), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=lw, alpha=alpha, zorder=4))
    if sign:
        ax.text(x, y, "+" if s > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", alpha=alpha,
                fontsize=fs, fontweight="bold", zorder=5)

def draw_bond(ax, p, q, broken=False, lw=1.5, alpha=1.0, color=None, cross=True):
    # bond between points p and q: solid blue if satisfied, dashed purple with a cross if broken
    c = color or (PURPLE if broken else BLUE)
    ax.plot([p[0], q[0]], [p[1], q[1]], color=c, lw=lw, ls=(0, (2.5, 1.5)) if broken else "-",
            alpha=alpha, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
    if broken and cross:
        ax.plot((p[0] + q[0]) / 2, (p[1] + q[1]) / 2, marker="x", ms=3.5 * lw, mew=lw * 0.9, color=c, alpha=alpha, zorder=3)

def draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.75, color=NAVY, lw=1.3, head=7, dot=True):
    # planar spins: an arrow of fixed length centred on every lattice site (x, y), angle theta[y, x]
    for (y, x), t in np.ndenumerate(theta):
        dx, dy = 0.5 * length * np.cos(t), 0.5 * length * np.sin(t)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + dx, y + dy), xytext=(x - dx, y - dy),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=lw, mutation_scale=head, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
        if dot:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", color=GRAY, ms=1.5, zorder=1)

def plaquette_winding(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (lower-left corner (x, y)), corners traversed counter-clockwise
    wrap = lambda a: (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi           # angle difference mapped to [-pi, pi)
    t1, t2 = theta[:-1, :-1], theta[:-1, 1:]                       # (x, y), (x+1, y)
    t3, t4 = theta[1:, 1:], theta[1:, :-1]                         # (x+1, y+1), (x, y+1)
    return np.rint((wrap(t2 - t1) + wrap(t3 - t2) + wrap(t4 - t3) + wrap(t1 - t4)) / (2 * np.pi)).astype(int)

def draw_vortex_marks(ax, w, r=0.3):
    # vortex (w = +1): navy disc with "+";  antivortex (w = -1): white disc with orange rim and "-"
    for (y, x), v in np.ndenumerate(w):
        if v != 0:
            face, edge, txt = (NAVY, NAVY, "white") if v > 0 else ("white", ORANGE, ORANGE)
            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x + 0.5, y + 0.5), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=1.3, zorder=6, alpha=0.9))
            ax.text(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, "+" if v > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7)

def sketch_wall_versus_spin_wave():
    nx, ny = 12, 3
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.5, 2.9))
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, bottom=0.01, top=0.92, hspace=0.45)
    # (a) Ising: the spins flip abruptly across one column of bonds
    for yy in range(ny):
        for xx in range(nx):
            draw_spin(ax1, xx, yy, 1 if xx < nx // 2 else -1, r=0.3, lw=0.9)
    ax1.plot([nx / 2 - 0.5] * 2, [-0.5, ny - 0.5], color=PURPLE, lw=2.5)
    ax1.set_title(r"(a) Ising: sharp domain wall, $2J$ per broken bond", fontsize=11, color=NAVY, loc="left")
    # (b) XY: the angle turns by 2 pi gradually over ell = nx columns, i.e. by 2 pi / ell per bond
    theta = np.tile(2 * np.pi * np.arange(nx) / nx + np.pi / 2, (ny, 1))
    draw_xy_spins(ax2, theta, length=0.7, lw=1.4, head=8)
    ax2.set_title(r"(b) XY: spin wave, $2\pi$ over $\ell$ sites, $\frac{J}{2}(2\pi/\ell)^2$ per bond", fontsize=11, color=NAVY, loc="left")
    for ax in (ax1, ax2):
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, nx - 0.4); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, ny - 0.4); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    return fig

with plt.rc_context(SKETCH_STYLE):
    fig = sketch_wall_versus_spin_wave()
save_sketch(fig, "sketch_xy_spin_wave.png")
plt.show()





Berezinskii (1971, 1972) and Kosterlitz and Thouless (1973) showed that the 2D XY model nevertheless has two distinct phases, and hence a transition without an order parameter. At low \(T\), correlations decay as a power law of distance (“quasi-long-range order”), and the system resists a twist: it has a non-zero spin stiffness. At high \(T\), correlations decay exponentially and the stiffness vanishes. The transition between them is caused by vortices, points around which the angle winds by \(2\pi\). Below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) vortices exist only in tightly bound vortex–antivortex pairs; above, free vortices proliferate. Kosterlitz (1974) worked out the critical behaviour with the renormalisation group, and Nelson and Kosterlitz (1977) predicted that the stiffness drops discontinuously at \(T_{\rm BKT}\) by a universal amount.
The same physics describes any 2D system whose state is a phase: thin films of superfluid \(^4\)He (the phase of the condensate wave function), thin superconducting films, and planar magnets. The Nelson–Kosterlitz prediction refers directly to superfluid films (title: Universal jump in the superfluid density of two-dimensional superfluids), and Bishop and Reppy (1978) studied the superfluid transition in two-dimensional \(^4\)He films experimentally.
The importance of these ideas was recognised by the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded “with one half to David J. Thouless, and the other half to F. Duncan M. Haldane and J. Michael Kosterlitz for theoretical discoveries of topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter” (nobelprize.org); the BKT transition is the topological phase transition of that citation.
For the notebooks that follow, the lesson is that a learning algorithm looking at snapshots will find whatever varies most between them. For the XY model the obvious candidate, the magnetisation, is a finite-size effect, and the relevant objects, vortices, are invisible in a single spin’s value: they are a property of the angles around a plaquette. Knowing this physics is the only way to judge what an algorithm has found.

section: 2. Model, symmetries and Monte Carlo sampling
text:
2. Model, symmetries and Monte Carlo sampling

2.1 Definition
On an \(L\times L\) square lattice with periodic boundaries (a torus), \(N=L^2\) planar unit vectors \(\boldsymbol s_i=(\cos\theta_i,\sin\theta_i)\), \(\theta_i\in[0,2\pi)\), interact with their nearest neighbours: \[
\begin{aligned}
H(\boldsymbol\theta)&=-J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\boldsymbol s_i\cdot\boldsymbol s_j\\
&=-J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j),\qquad J>0,
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\langle i,j\rangle\) runs over the \(2N\) nearest-neighbour bonds. We set \(J=1\) and \(k_B=1\); the lattice spacing is \(a=1\).
The figure below shows the model on a small patch: every site carries an arrow of unit length at angle \(\theta_i\), measured from the horizontal axis as on the unit circle on the right, and each bond between nearest neighbours contributes \(-J\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)\) to the energy. Parallel neighbours give \(-J\) and antiparallel neighbours \(+J\), while a small relative angle \(\delta\) costs only \(\frac J2\delta^2\) above the minimum; this is why the gradual twists of Section 1 are so cheap.


Code
# Schematic figure; this cell does not depend on any other cell of the notebook.
# Colour convention shared by all sketches of the course:
#   spin s = +1: filled navy disc,   spin s = -1: white disc with an orange rim;

# The figure is drawn at its physical size on a 16:9 slide (5.5 in = full text width) with 10-12 pt text,

    for d in ("../beamer/figures",) + tuple(d for d in extra_dirs if os.path.isdir(d)):
        fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, name), dpi=300, facecolor="white")

def draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.75, color=NAVY, lw=1.3, head=7, dot=True):
    # planar spins: an arrow of fixed length centred on every lattice site (x, y), angle theta[y, x]
    for (y, x), t in np.ndenumerate(theta):
        dx, dy = 0.5 * length * np.cos(t), 0.5 * length * np.sin(t)
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x + dx, y + dy), xytext=(x - dx, y - dy),

def plaquette_winding(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (lower-left corner (x, y)), corners traversed counter-clockwise
    wrap = lambda a: (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi           # angle difference mapped to [-pi, pi)
    t1, t2 = theta[:-1, :-1], theta[:-1, 1:]                       # (x, y), (x+1, y)

def draw_vortex_marks(ax, w, r=0.3):
    # vortex (w = +1): navy disc with "+";  antivortex (w = -1): white disc with orange rim and "-"
    for (y, x), v in np.ndenumerate(w):

            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x + 0.5, y + 0.5), r, fc=face, ec=edge, lw=1.3, zorder=6, alpha=0.9))
            ax.text(x + 0.5, y + 0.5, "+" if v > 0 else "−", color=txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7)

def sketch_xy_model():
    L = 4
    y, x = np.indices((L, L))
    theta = 0.6 + 0.45 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * x / 7 + 0.8) + 0.35 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * y / 6)   # slowly varying angles
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 2.9))
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.43, 1.0]); tx = fig.add_axes([0.45, 0.0, 0.55, 1.0]); tx.axis("off")
    for k in range(L):
        ax.plot([0, L - 1], [k, k], color=GRAY, lw=0.7, alpha=0.35); ax.plot([k, k], [0, L - 1], color=GRAY, lw=0.7, alpha=0.35)

    ax.plot(*zip(i, j), color=BLUE, lw=6, alpha=0.3, solid_capstyle="round")
    draw_xy_spins(ax, theta, length=0.62, lw=1.5, head=9)
    for (px, py), name in [(i, "i"), (j, "j")]:
        t = theta[py, px]
        ax.plot([px, px + 0.45], [py, py], color=GRAY, lw=0.7, ls=":")         # reference direction theta = 0
        arc = np.linspace(0, t, 30)
        ax.plot(px + 0.25 * np.cos(arc), py + 0.25 * np.sin(arc), color=ORANGE, lw=1.3)
        ax.text(px + 0.36 * np.cos(t / 2) + 0.03, py + 0.36 * np.sin(t / 2) - 0.06, rf"$\theta_{name}$", fontsize=11, color=ORANGE)

The energy is invariant under several transformations. The global rotation \(\theta_i\to\theta_i+\alpha\) for all \(i\), with any \(\alpha\), is a continuous symmetry, the rotation part \(U(1)\cong SO(2)\) of the group \(O(2)\); together with the global reflection \(\theta_i\to-\theta_i\) it forms \(O(2)\). The periodicity \(\theta_i\to\theta_i+2\pi\) on any single site looks harmless, but it is what allows vortices (Section 4). Finally there are the lattice symmetries: translations, rotations by \(90^\circ\) and mirror reflections.
Every term of \(H\) is at least \(-J\), so the minimum energy \(E_0=-2JN\) is reached when all spins are parallel, \(\theta_i=\theta_0\). The ground state is not unique: it is a continuous family labelled by \(\theta_0\in[0,2\pi)\) (compare the two ground states of Ising).
The basic observables are the magnetisation vector and the energy per spin, \[
\boldsymbol m=\frac1N\sum_i\boldsymbol s_i,\qquad |\boldsymbol m|=\sqrt{m_x^2+m_y^2},\qquad e=\frac{H}{N}.
\] Because of the rotation symmetry \(\langle\boldsymbol m\rangle=0\) on any finite lattice; the useful quantities are \(\langle|\boldsymbol m|\rangle\) and \(\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle\).
In the code, angles are stored as an array theta of shape (..., L, L), axis -1 is the \(x\) direction (columns) and axis -2 the \(y\) direction (rows). jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) is the right neighbour of every site, so jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) - theta lists the angle differences on all \(N\) horizontal bonds at once (and similarly for the \(N\) vertical bonds). The cell below checks the ground-state energy, the energy of a random state, and the invariance of \(H\) under the global rotation, the reflection and a shift by \(2\pi\) on one site.

TWO_PI = 2 * np.pi

def wrap(a):
    # map angles to the interval [-pi, pi)
    return (a + jnp.pi) % TWO_PI - jnp.pi

def bond_differences(theta):
    # theta: (..., L, L).  Returns dx = theta_{r+x} - theta_r and dy = theta_{r+y} - theta_r, each (..., L, L): one entry per bond
    return jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1) - theta, jnp.roll(theta, -1, -2) - theta

def energy_per_spin(theta):
    # e = H / N = -(J/N) sum over the 2N bonds of cos(theta_i - theta_j);  output shape (...)
    dx, dy = bond_differences(theta)
    return -J * (jnp.cos(dx) + jnp.cos(dy)).mean((-2, -1))

def magnetisation(theta):
    # m = (1/N) sum_i (cos theta_i, sin theta_i);  returns (m_x, m_y), each of shape (...)
    return jnp.cos(theta).mean((-2, -1)), jnp.sin(theta).mean((-2, -1))

2.2 Checkerboard Metropolis updates
To sample the Boltzmann distribution we start from the Metropolis algorithm, which Lab 010 derived for Ising spins and which works for any energy. We propose a new angle for spin \(i\), \(\theta_i'=\theta_i+\delta\,(2u-1)\) with \(u\) uniform in \([0,1)\) and a step width \(\delta\), and accept with probability \(\min\!\left(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E_i}\right)\). The proposal is symmetric, so detailed balance holds. The energy change only involves the four neighbours \(j\) of \(i\) and is expressed through the local field \[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol h_i&=\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)}\boldsymbol s_j=\Big(\sum_j\cos\theta_j,\ \sum_j\sin\theta_j\Big),\\
\Delta E_i&=-J\,\boldsymbol h_i\cdot(\boldsymbol s_i'-\boldsymbol s_i).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since nearest neighbours always have different colours on a chessboard (\((x+y)\bmod 2\)), all spins of one colour can be updated simultaneously: none of them appears in another’s local field. One sweep updates all black sites and then all white sites, i.e. one attempted move per spin. In code we propose new angles for all sites and accept only on the current colour (a mask); this wastes half of the random numbers but keeps the code short.


2.3 Wolff cluster updates
Local moves have a weakness. Near \(T_{\rm BKT}\) the correlation length is comparable with \(L\), and below \(T_{\rm BKT}\) it is infinite. Rotating a large correlated region one spin at a time is slow: the autocorrelation time of Metropolis grows with \(L\), as we measure below.
Wolff’s idea (Wolff 1989) is to turn the XY model into an Ising model for one update. Choose a random direction \(\boldsymbol r=(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi)\) and consider only reflections of spins across the line perpendicular to \(\boldsymbol r\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\boldsymbol s_i\to\boldsymbol s_i-2(\boldsymbol s_i\cdot\boldsymbol r)\,\boldsymbol r\\
\Longleftrightarrow\quad &\theta_i\to\pi+2\varphi-\theta_i .
\end{aligned}
\] Write \(\sigma_i=\boldsymbol s_i\cdot\boldsymbol r=\cos(\theta_i-\varphi)\). If a spin is reflected and its neighbour is not, the bond energy changes by \(2J\sigma_i\sigma_j\); reflecting both leaves it unchanged. With respect to reflections the XY model is therefore an Ising model with bond-dependent couplings \(J\sigma_i\sigma_j\), and the Swendsen–Wang/Wolff construction of Lab 018 applies: 1. pick a random seed site; 2. activate each bond \(\langle i,j\rangle\) with probability \(p_{ij}=1-\exp\!\big(\min(0,\,-2\beta J\sigma_i\sigma_j)\big)\) (only bonds with \(\sigma_i\sigma_j>0\) can be active); 3. reflect the whole cluster of sites connected to the seed by active bonds.
The update satisfies detailed balance and needs no acceptance step (Wolff 1989). Combined with a random \(\varphi\) it is ergodic together with the Metropolis moves.
The cluster search needs some care in JAX, because a sequential “grow the cluster” loop is awkward to vectorise over many chains. We use the fact that the bond variables are independent: drawing all bonds of the lattice first and then taking the connected component of the seed gives exactly the same cluster distribution as growing it bond by bond. The connected components are found as in Lab 018 by label propagation: every site starts with its own index as label and repeatedly takes the smallest label among itself and its bonded neighbours, followed by pointer jumping (a site adopts the label of its label), until no label changes. The price: under vmap every chain waits until the slowest chain has converged, and at low \(T\) the clusters span the lattice and need many iterations. On a CPU this makes one Wolff update much more expensive than one Metropolis sweep (measured in Section 2.6).


2.4 Over-relaxation
A cheap alternative for speeding up the sampling (Creutz 1987; Brown and Woch 1987) is to reflect each spin about its local field. With \(\varphi_i\) the direction of \(\boldsymbol h_i\), \[
\begin{aligned}
&\theta_i\to2\varphi_i-\theta_i\\
\Longrightarrow\quad &\boldsymbol h_i\cdot\boldsymbol s_i\ \text{unchanged},\quad\Delta E_i=0 .
\end{aligned}
\] The move is deterministic, its own inverse, and conserves the energy, so it is accepted with probability \(1\) and leaves the Boltzmann distribution invariant. It does not change the energy, so on its own it is not ergodic (it samples at fixed energy); combined with Metropolis sweeps it is. It moves spins by large angles at no cost; Section 2.6 measures how much this shortens the autocorrelation times. The checkerboard applies as for Metropolis.


Code
def checkerboard(L):
    # (L, L) array with values 0 / 1 = colour (x + y) mod 2
    return (jnp.arange(L)[:, None] + jnp.arange(L)[None, :]) % 2

def local_field(theta):
    # h_i = sum of the 4 neighbour vectors;  returns (h_x, h_y), each of the same shape as theta (..., L, L)
    c, s = jnp.cos(theta), jnp.sin(theta)
    nbrs = ((1, -2), (-1, -2), (1, -1), (-1, -1))          # (shift, axis) for the up / down / left / right neighbours
    return sum(jnp.roll(c, d, ax) for d, ax in nbrs), sum(jnp.roll(s, d, ax) for d, ax in nbrs)

def metropolis_sweep(theta, key, beta, delta):
    # theta: (L, L);  one sweep = black sites, then white sites.  Returns new theta and the acceptance rate.
    colour = checkerboard(theta.shape[-1])
    k_prop, k_acc = jax.random.split(key)
    # every site is updated exactly once per sweep, so one proposal and one acceptance number per site suffice
    new = theta + delta * (2.0 * jax.random.uniform(k_prop, theta.shape) - 1.0)
    u_acc = jax.random.uniform(k_acc, theta.shape)
    n_acc = 0.0
    for c in (0, 1):                                          # Python loop, unrolled by jit
        hx, hy = local_field(theta)
        dE = -J * (hx * (jnp.cos(new) - jnp.cos(theta)) + hy * (jnp.sin(new) - jnp.sin(theta)))
        accept = (u_acc < jnp.exp(-beta * dE)) & (colour == c)
        theta = jnp.where(accept, jnp.mod(new, TWO_PI), theta)
        n_acc = n_acc + accept.sum()
    return theta, n_acc / theta.size

def overrelaxation_sweep(theta):
    # reflect every spin about its local field, black sites then white sites: theta_i -> 2 phi_i - theta_i,
    # with phi_i = atan2(h_y, h_x) the direction of the local field.  The energy is unchanged; no random numbers.
    colour = checkerboard(theta.shape[-1])
    for c in (0, 1):
        hx, hy = local_field(theta)
        theta = jnp.where(colour == c, jnp.mod(2.0 * jnp.arctan2(hy, hx) - theta, TWO_PI), theta)
    return theta

def connected_labels(bond_x, bond_y):
    # bond_x[y, x]: site (y, x) bonded to (y, x+1);  bond_y[y, x]: site (y, x) bonded to (y+1, x);  periodic lattice.
    # Returns (L, L) int labels: two sites have the same label iff they are connected by active bonds.
    L = bond_x.shape[0]
    big = L * L
    bond_xm, bond_ym = jnp.roll(bond_x, 1, 1), jnp.roll(bond_y, 1, 0)        # bonds to the left / lower neighbour
    def body(carry):
        lab, _ = carry
        new = lab
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_x, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 1), big))
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_xm, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 1), big))
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_y, jnp.roll(lab, -1, 0), big))
        new = jnp.minimum(new, jnp.where(bond_ym, jnp.roll(lab, 1, 0), big))
        new = new.ravel()[new]                                                  # pointer jumping
        return new, jnp.any(new != lab)
    lab, _ = lax.while_loop(lambda c: c[1], body, (jnp.arange(big).reshape(L, L), True))
    return lab

def wolff_update(theta, key, beta):
    # one Wolff single-cluster update of theta (L, L).  Returns new theta and the cluster size / N.
    L = theta.shape[-1]
    k_phi, k_x, k_y, k_seed = jax.random.split(key, 4)
    phi = jax.random.uniform(k_phi, (), maxval=TWO_PI)                         # reflection direction r = (cos phi, sin phi)
    sigma = jnp.cos(theta - phi)                                               # sigma_i = s_i . r
    p_x = 1.0 - jnp.exp(jnp.minimum(0.0, -2.0 * beta * J * sigma * jnp.roll(sigma, -1, 1)))
    p_y = 1.0 - jnp.exp(jnp.minimum(0.0, -2.0 * beta * J * sigma * jnp.roll(sigma, -1, 0)))
    bond_x = jax.random.uniform(k_x, theta.shape) < p_x
    bond_y = jax.random.uniform(k_y, theta.shape) < p_y
    lab = connected_labels(bond_x, bond_y)
    seed = jax.random.randint(k_seed, (), 0, L * L)
    in_cluster = lab == lab.ravel()[seed]
    theta = jnp.where(in_cluster, jnp.mod(jnp.pi + 2.0 * phi - theta, TWO_PI), theta)
    return theta, in_cluster.mean()


After every Monte Carlo step (one Metropolis sweep followed by n_or over-relaxation sweeps and n_wolff Wolff updates) we record ten numbers per chain. With \(\Delta^x_r=\theta_{r+\hat x}-\theta_r\) and \(\Delta^y_r=\theta_{r+\hat y}-\theta_r\) the bond angles, these are the bond sums \[
\begin{aligned}
C_x&=\sum_r\cos\Delta^x_r,\quad C_y=\sum_r\cos\Delta^y_r,\\
S_x&=\sum_r\sin\Delta^x_r,\quad S_y=\sum_r\sin\Delta^y_r,\\
E&=-J(C_x+C_y),
\end{aligned}
\] together with the magnetisation \((m_x,m_y)\), the vortex density \(n_v\) (number of plaquettes with non-zero winding number per site, defined in Section 4), the Metropolis acceptance rate and the Wolff cluster size. \(S_x,S_y\) enter the helicity modulus (Section 5).
The function simulate runs many independent chains at once: jax.vmap over chains (each with its own \(\beta\) and random key), lax.scan over Monte Carlo steps, everything compiled by jax.jit. The input theta0 has shape (C, L, L), keys (C, 2), betas (C,); the output time series has shape (C, n_meas, 10) and the stored snapshots (C, n_store, L, L), taken every n_meas // n_store steps.


Code
def vorticity(theta):
    # winding number of every plaquette (Section 4).  Plaquette (y, x) has corners (y,x) -> (y,x+1) -> (y+1,x+1) -> (y+1,x),
    # traversed counter-clockwise (x to the right, y upwards).  Output: int32 array (..., L, L) with values in {-1, 0, +1} (rarely +-2).
    t00 = theta
    t01 = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -1)                    # (y, x+1)
    t11 = jnp.roll(t01, -1, -2)                      # (y+1, x+1)
    t10 = jnp.roll(theta, -1, -2)                    # (y+1, x)
    circ = wrap(t01 - t00) + wrap(t11 - t01) + wrap(t10 - t11) + wrap(t00 - t10)
    return jnp.round(circ / TWO_PI).astype(jnp.int32)

OBS = ["E", "Cx", "Cy", "Sx", "Sy", "mx", "my", "nv", "acc", "cluster"]       # the ten recorded numbers

def measure(theta):
    dx, dy = bond_differences(theta)
    cx, cy = jnp.cos(dx).sum(), jnp.cos(dy).sum()
    sx, sy = jnp.sin(dx).sum(), jnp.sin(dy).sum()
    mx, my = magnetisation(theta)
    nv = (vorticity(theta) != 0).mean()
    return jnp.stack([-J * (cx + cy), cx, cy, sx, sy, mx, my, nv])

@partial(jax.jit, static_argnames=("n_equil", "n_meas", "n_store", "n_wolff", "n_or"))
def simulate(theta0, keys, betas, delta, n_equil, n_meas, n_store, n_wolff, n_or):
    gap = n_meas // n_store
    def one_chain(theta, key, beta):
        def mc_step(carry, _):
            theta, key = carry
            key, k_m, k_w = jax.random.split(key, 3)
            theta, acc = metropolis_sweep(theta, k_m, beta, delta)
            for _ in range(n_or):                                           # n_or over-relaxation sweeps
                theta = overrelaxation_sweep(theta)
            size = 0.0
            for k in jax.random.split(k_w, max(n_wolff, 1))[:n_wolff]:     # n_wolff cluster updates (0 = Metropolis only)
                theta, size = wolff_update(theta, k, beta)
            return (theta, key), jnp.concatenate([measure(theta), jnp.stack([acc, size])])
        carry, _ = lax.scan(mc_step, (theta, key), None, length=n_equil)    # equilibration, measurements discarded
        def block(carry, _):
            carry, series = lax.scan(mc_step, carry, None, length=gap)
            return carry, (series, carry[0])
        carry, (series, snaps) = lax.scan(block, carry, None, length=n_store)
        return series.reshape(n_store * gap, len(OBS)), snaps, carry[0]
    return jax.vmap(one_chain)(theta0, keys, betas)

def run_chains(L, T_list, n_chains, n_equil, n_meas, n_store, n_wolff=0, n_or=0, delta=1.0, seed=0, start="ordered"):
    # n_chains independent chains for every temperature in T_list.
    # Returns series (nT, n_chains, n_meas, 10) and snapshots (nT, n_chains, n_store, L, L), as numpy arrays.
    T_list = np.asarray(T_list, np.float32)
    C = len(T_list) * n_chains
    betas = jnp.asarray(np.repeat(1.0 / T_list, n_chains))
    k_init, k_run = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    if start == "ordered":
        theta0 = jnp.zeros((C, L, L))
    else:
        theta0 = jax.random.uniform(k_init, (C, L, L), maxval=TWO_PI)
    series, snaps, _ = simulate(theta0, jax.random.split(k_run, C), betas, delta, n_equil, n_meas, n_store, n_wolff, n_or)
    series = np.asarray(series).reshape(len(T_list), n_chains, n_meas, len(OBS))
    snaps = np.asarray(snaps).reshape(len(T_list), n_chains, n_store, L, L)
    return series, snaps




2.5 Low- and high-temperature limits
Before trusting the sampler we test it. There is no exact solution of the 2D XY model, but two limits are exact enough to test the code, and the three update schemes must agree with each other.
At low temperature, expanding \(\cos x\approx1-x^2/2\) (Section 3) gives a quadratic energy with \(N-1\) non-zero modes, each carrying \(T/2\) by equipartition, so \(\;e\approx-2J+\tfrac{T}{2}\,\tfrac{N-1}{N}\), with corrections of order \(T^2\). At high temperature the bonds become nearly independent, and for independent bonds \(\langle\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)\rangle=\dfrac{\int_0^{2\pi}\cos x\,e^{\beta J\cos x}dx}{\int_0^{2\pi}e^{\beta J\cos x}dx}=\dfrac{I_1(\beta J)}{I_0(\beta J)}\), with \(I_n\) the modified Bessel functions. This is exact on a lattice without closed loops (for instance an open chain); on the square lattice closed loops of bonds give corrections that become small at high \(T\). So \(e\approx-2J\,I_1(\beta J)/I_0(\beta J)\). Finally, Metropolis alone, Metropolis + over-relaxation and Metropolis + Wolff are all exact algorithms, so at \(T=0.9\) they must give the same averages within errors.

def jackknife(f, chain_means):
    # chain_means: (n_chains, k) per-chain averages;  f maps a (k,) vector of averages to an estimate.
    # Returns (estimate, jackknife error) using leave-one-chain-out averages.
    n = chain_means.shape[0]
    full = f(chain_means.mean(0))
    loo = (chain_means.sum(0)[None, :] - chain_means) / (n - 1)
    vals = np.array([f(v) for v in loo])
    return full, np.sqrt((n - 1) / n * ((vals - vals.mean(0)) ** 2).sum(0))

At high \(T\) the independent-bond formula is close and the remaining difference comes from closed loops of bonds. Next we compare the three update schemes at \(T=0.9\), close to the transition, where sampling is hardest. SCHEMES maps a name to (n_wolff, n_or), the number of Wolff updates and over-relaxation sweeps per Metropolis sweep.


Code
def helicity_from_means(v, beta, N):
    # v = per-chain or pooled averages of (C_x + C_y, S_x^2 + S_y^2);  Section 5 derives Upsilon = [<C> - beta <S^2>] / (2N)
    return (v[0] - beta * v[1]) / (2 * N)

def chain_moments(series):
    # series: (n_chains, n_meas, 10)  ->  per-chain means (n_chains, 9) of the quantities needed below
    E, Cx, Cy, Sx, Sy, mx, my, nv, acc = (series[..., k] for k in range(9))
    m2 = mx**2 + my**2
    cols = [E, E**2, Cx + Cy, Sx**2 + Sy**2, np.sqrt(m2), m2, m2**2, nv, acc]
    return np.stack([c.mean(-1) for c in cols], -1)

MOMENTS = ["E", "E2", "C", "S2", "absm", "m2", "m4", "nv", "acc"]

SCHEMES = {"Metropolis": (0, 0), "Metropolis + over-relaxation": (0, 1), "Metropolis + Wolff": (1, 0)}

2.6 Autocorrelation times and cost
The three schemes agree within the errors in \(e\), \(\Upsilon\) and \(\langle\boldsymbol m^2\rangle\), so they differ only in efficiency, and efficiency is what we measure next. Consecutive Monte Carlo configurations are correlated. For an observable \(A\) with time series \(A_t\), the normalised autocorrelation function and the integrated autocorrelation time are \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho(t)&=\frac{\langle A_sA_{s+t}\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2}{\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2},\\
\tau_{\rm int}&=\frac12+\sum_{t=1}^{W}\rho(t),
\end{aligned}
\] where the window \(W\) is the first \(t\) with \(t\ge6\,\tau_{\rm int}(t)\) (a standard self-consistent cut-off that avoids summing pure noise). A run of \(n\) steps contains about \(n/(2\tau_{\rm int})\) independent measurements. We measure \(\tau_{\rm int}\) of \(|\boldsymbol m|^2\), the slowest common observable, at \(T=0.9\approx T_{\rm BKT}\) for \(L=16\) and \(L=32\), and compare it with the CPU time of one step. The figure of merit is the CPU time per independent sample, \(2\tau_{\rm int}\times\)(time per step).


Code
def tau_int(series):
    # series: (n_chains, n_t).  Autocorrelation averaged over chains, then the self-consistent window.
    a = series - series.mean()
    n_t = a.shape[1]
    f = np.fft.rfft(a, 2 * n_t, axis=1)
    acf = np.fft.irfft(f * np.conj(f), axis=1)[:, :n_t].mean(0)
    rho = acf / acf[0]
    tau = 0.5
    for t in range(1, n_t):
        tau += rho[t]
        if t >= 6 * tau:
            break
    return tau, rho

TAU = {}
n_eq_tau, n_meas_tau = 500, 2500
for L in (16, 32):
    for name, (n_wolff, n_or) in SCHEMES.items():
        run_chains(L, [0.9], 16, 10, 10, 1, n_wolff, n_or, seed=3)                       # compile first, then time
        t0 = time.time()
        ser, _ = run_chains(L, [0.9], 16, n_eq_tau, n_meas_tau, 1, n_wolff, n_or, seed=3)
        dt = (time.time() - t0) / (n_eq_tau + n_meas_tau)                                # seconds per step (16 chains)
        tau, rho = tau_int(ser[0, :, :, 5] ** 2 + ser[0, :, :, 6] ** 2)
        TAU[(L, name)] = (tau, rho, dt)
        print(f"L = {L:2d}, {name:29s}:  tau_int(|m|^2) = {tau:6.1f} steps,  time per step (16 chains) = {1e3 * dt:6.2f} ms,  "
              f"time per independent sample = {2 * tau * dt * 1e3:7.1f} ms")
NUMBERS.update({f"tau_L{L}_{name.replace(' + ', '_').replace(' ', '_')}": round(float(TAU[(L, name)][0]), 1) for (L, name) in TAU})

With Metropolis alone \(\tau_{\rm int}\) roughly triples when \(L\) doubles from 16 to 32: critical slowing down. One over-relaxation sweep per step shortens \(\tau_{\rm int}\) by more than an order of magnitude at a small extra cost per step. The Wolff update gives the shortest \(\tau_{\rm int}\), but the array-based cluster search makes each step several times more expensive, increasingly so with \(L\). Per CPU second, Metropolis + over-relaxation produces the most independent samples, so the production runs below use one Metropolis sweep + one over-relaxation sweep per step.

    L = int(d["L"]); N = L * L
    out = {k: np.zeros((len(d["T"]), 2)) for k in ["u", "c", "ups", "absm", "m2", "nv"]}
    for i, T in enumerate(d["T"]):
        cm = d["chain_moments"][i]

        out["u"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[0] / N, cm)
        out["c"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: beta**2 * (v[1] - v[0] ** 2) / N, cm)
        out["ups"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: helicity_from_means(v[[2, 3]], beta, N), cm)
        out["absm"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[4], cm)
        out["m2"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[5], cm)
        out["nv"][i] = jackknife(lambda v: v[7], cm)
    return out
