class fractions, VAE d = 2:              [0.154 0.111 0.122 0.076 0.09  0.076 0.121 0.077 0.092 0.081]
class fractions, AE d = 2, uniform box:  [0.052 0.476 0.028 0.004 0.011 0.072 0.202 0.117 0.004 0.034]


The \(d=16\) VAE produces every digit with roughly the frequency of the training set: no class is missing (no mode collapse). The \(d=2\) VAE over-produces 0s (15.4%) and under-produces 3s, 5s and 7s (about 7.6% each): in two dimensions the digits are crowded, and the prior does not give each the same area. The classifier is confident about real digits (95.9% above 0.9) far more often than about VAE samples (54.5% for \(d=16\)), because many samples are blurry or lie between two digits. The \(d=16\) autoencoder decoded from a fitted Gaussian is the worst case, at 36.7%. The \(d=2\) autoencoder sampled uniformly over its box scores high, 78.1%: in two dimensions its decoder produces digit-like images almost everywhere. Uniform sampling of the box is nevertheless not a model of the data: it over-produces the digits whose codes are spread over a large area of the plane (47.6% are 1s, see the printed class fractions), and it has no probability distribution attached.
As an exercise, sort the 10 000 VAE samples by the classifier confidence and show the 20 least confident ones. Identify the pairs of digits they lie between, and compare with the largest off-diagonal entries of the confusion matrix.

title: Lab 024: Variational and conditional autoencoders
text:
6. The conditional VAE
A VAE draws some digit. Often we want to choose what to generate: the digit 7, or, in physics, a spin configuration at temperature \(T\). If a label \(\mathbf c\) is known for every training image, it can be given to both networks as an extra input [K. Sohn, H. Lee, X. Yan, Learning Structured Output Representation using Deep Conditional Generative Models, NeurIPS 2015, proceedings]. The encoder becomes \(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)=\mathcal N\big(\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x,\mathbf c),\mathrm{diag}\,\boldsymbol\sigma^2_\phi(\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\big)\), whose input is the concatenation \([\mathbf x,\mathbf c]\in\mathbb R^{784+10}\), and the decoder becomes \(p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\), whose input is \([\mathbf z,\mathbf c]\in\mathbb R^{d+10}\). The prior stays \(p(\mathbf z)=\mathcal N(0,I)\), the same for every \(\mathbf c\). Generation then means choosing \(\mathbf c\), drawing \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) and decoding \(\sigma(G_\theta(\mathbf z,\mathbf c))\).
The model is now a model of the conditional distribution, \[p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf c)=\int p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\,p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z ,\] and the derivation of Section 3.2 goes through with \(\mathbf c\) carried along as a fixed parameter. Bayes’ rule at fixed \(\mathbf c\) reads \(p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf c)=p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z,\mathbf c)p(\mathbf z)/p_\theta(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\); taking the logarithm, inserting \(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\) and averaging over it gives the conditioned ELBO, \[\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf c)=\underbrace{\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)}\big[\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\big]-\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big)}_{\mathrm{ELBO}(\theta,\phi;\,\mathbf x,\mathbf c)}+\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\,\|\,p_\theta(\mathbf z|\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\big)}_{\ge 0}.\] The loss is again BCE plus the closed-form KL divergence, now computed from \((\boldsymbol\mu,\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2)=\) encoder\(([\mathbf x,\mathbf c])\) and logits \(=\) decoder\(([\mathbf z,\mathbf c])\), and the training data are pairs \((\mathbf x_i,\mathbf c_i)\). Sohn et al. also allow a learned, \(\mathbf c\)-dependent prior \(p_\theta(\mathbf z|\mathbf c)\); the fixed \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) used here is the simplest choice and lets us sample \(\mathbf z\) the same way for every \(\mathbf c\).
The shapes are \(\mathbf x\): \((B,784)\); \(\mathbf c\): \((B,10)\); encoder input \([\mathbf x,\mathbf c]\): \((B,794)\); \(\boldsymbol\mu,\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2,\mathbf z\): \((B,d)\); decoder input \([\mathbf z,\mathbf c]\): \((B,d+10)\); logits: \((B,784)\).
Here \(\mathbf c\) is the one-hot vector of the digit, \(c_j=\delta_{j,y}\). A single number \(y\in\{0,\dots,9\}\) would impose an order and a distance on the classes, as if 3 were between 2 and 4. Since \(\mathbf c\) already tells the decoder which digit to draw, the KL term pushes \(\mathbf z\) to carry only what \(\mathbf c\) does not say: the style of the handwriting.
The VAE class of Section 3 already supports all this: VAE(d, cond=10) provides model.encode(x, c) and model.decode(z, c), and vae_loss receives the minibatch (x, c). We train a cVAE with \(d=8\) (20 epochs) and, to draw its latent plane, one with \(d=2\) (10 epochs).


Code
_m = VAE(8, cond=10, rngs=nnx.Rngs(0))
_mu, _lv = _m.encode(Xtr_d[:5], Ctr_d[:5])
assert Ctr_d.shape == (60000, 10) and _mu.shape == (5, 8)
assert _m.decode(_mu, Ctr_d[:5]).shape == (5, 784)
print("one-hot condition of the first training image (label", int(ytr[0]), "):", np.asarray(Ctr_d[0]).astype(int))

t0 = time.time()
print("cVAE, d = 8"); cvae, h_cvae = train(VAE(8, cond=10, rngs=nnx.Rngs(6)), vae_loss, (Xtr_d, Ctr_d), epochs=EPOCHS_VAE, seed=6)
print("cVAE, d = 2"); cvae2, _ = train(VAE(2, cond=10, rngs=nnx.Rngs(7)), vae_loss, (Xtr_d, Ctr_d), epochs=10, seed=7)
nums["cvae_train_seconds"] = time.time() - t0
Cte_d = jax.nn.one_hot(jnp.asarray(yte), 10)
_, aux = nnx.jit(vae_loss)(cvae, (Xte_d, Cte_d), jax.random.key(8))
nums["cvae8_test"] = {k: float(v) for k, v in aux.items()}
print("cVAE d = 8, test, per image:", {k: round(v, 1) for k, v in nums["cvae8_test"].items()})
cvae_enc = nnx.jit(lambda m, x, c: m.encode(x, c))
cvae_dec = nnx.jit(lambda m, z, c: jax.nn.sigmoid(m.decode(z, c)))

Digits on demand
The first test of the cVAE is whether the condition and the latent vector play the roles we intended. Each row of the figure uses one condition \(\mathbf c\), the digits 0 to 9. Each column uses one random \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), the same in every row.


Code
zc = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(14), (10, 8))
rows = [np.asarray(cvae_dec(cvae, zc, jax.nn.one_hot(jnp.full(10, dgt), 10))) for dgt in range(10)]
show_grid(np.concatenate(rows), 10, 10, "gen_cvae_mnist.png", size=0.55,
          row_labels=[f"$c={d}$" for d in range(10)], fontsize=9)





Along a column the digit changes and the style stays: slant, stroke width and size are carried by \(\mathbf z\), the identity by \(\mathbf c\).


Style transfer
The same separation lets us transfer the handwriting of a real digit to other digits. We encode a real test digit with its own label, \(\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x,\mathbf c_y)\), then decode this one \(\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu\) with every condition \(\mathbf c=0,\dots,9\): the same handwriting, all ten digits.


Code
picks = [first_of(2), first_of(7, 3), first_of(4, 2), first_of(0, 5)]
rows = []
for k in picks:
    mu, _ = cvae_enc(cvae, Xte_d[k:k + 1], Cte_d[k:k + 1])
    out = np.asarray(cvae_dec(cvae, jnp.repeat(mu, 10, 0), jnp.eye(10)))
    rows.append(np.concatenate([Xte[k:k + 1], np.ones((1, 784)) * 0, out]))
show_grid(np.concatenate(rows), len(picks), 12, "gen_cvae_style.png", size=0.6)







The latent plane of a cVAE
If \(\mathbf z\) really carries only style, the digit identity should no longer be visible in the latent plane. We repeat the test of Section 4 for a cVAE with \(d=2\): the right panel shows the means \(\boldsymbol\mu_\phi(\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\) of the test digits, coloured by the digit, and the left panel the VAE with \(d=2\) for comparison. A simple number quantifies the difference: we predict the digit from the nearest class mean in the latent plane and report how often this prediction is correct.


Code
mu_c2 = in_chunks(lambda x, c: cvae_enc(cvae2, x, c)[0], Xte_d, Cte_d)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.3))
for a, Z, title in [(axs[0], mu2_te, "VAE: $\\boldsymbol{\\mu}_\\phi(\\mathbf{x})$"),
                    (axs[1], mu_c2, "cVAE: $\\boldsymbol{\\mu}_\\phi(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{c})$")]:
    for d in range(10):
        m = yte == d
        a.scatter(Z[m, 0], Z[m, 1], s=1.5, color=cmap10(d), label=str(d), rasterized=True)
    for r in (1, 2, 3): a.plot(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t), "k:", lw=0.8)
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xlim(-4, 4); a.set_ylim(-4, 4); a.set_xlabel("$z_1$"); a.set_ylabel("$z_2$"); a.set_title(title)
axs[1].legend(markerscale=6, fontsize=8, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5))
plt.tight_layout(); save(fig, "gen_cvae_latent.png"); plt.show()

# how much does z tell about the digit? nearest-class-mean accuracy in the latent plane
def centroid_acc(Z, y):
    cent = np.stack([Z[y == d].mean(0) for d in range(10)])
    return float((((Z[:, None] - cent[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1) == y).mean())
nums["latent_centroid_acc_vae2"], nums["latent_centroid_acc_cvae2"] = centroid_acc(mu2_te, yte), centroid_acc(mu_c2, yte)
print(f"digit predicted from the nearest class mean in the latent plane: VAE {nums['latent_centroid_acc_vae2']:.3f}, "
      f"cVAE {nums['latent_centroid_acc_cvae2']:.3f} (chance 0.1)")

zg2 = jnp.asarray([[a, b] for b in np.linspace(2, -2, 7) for a in np.linspace(-2, 2, 7)], dtype=jnp.float32)
show_grid(np.asarray(cvae_dec(cvae2, zg2, jax.nn.one_hot(jnp.full(49, 7), 10))), 7, 7, "gen_cvae2_grid7.png", size=0.5)

In the VAE the digits form separate regions of the plane, and the nearest class mean predicts the digit correctly in 73% of the cases. In the cVAE all digits share the same disc, and the position of a digit in the latent plane says little about which digit it is: the nearest-class-mean prediction is correct in 18% of the cases, close to the chance level of 10%. The latent plane of the cVAE is a map of style alone: decoding a grid of \(\mathbf z\) with \(\mathbf c=7\) gives sevens that differ in slant and width.


Confusion matrix of requested digits
The classifier of Section 5 now tests whether the cVAE draws what we ask for. For every requested digit \(a\) we generate 1000 images with \(\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) and \(\mathbf c=\) one-hot\((a)\), and let the classifier label them. The confusion matrix now has one row per requested digit \(a\) and one column per digit \(b\) assigned by the classifier, \[C_{ab}=\frac{\#\{\text{samples generated with }\mathbf c=a\text{ assigned to }b\}}{1000}.\]

title: Lab 024: Variational and conditional autoencoders
text:
From autoencoders to conditional generation
An autoencoder learns a latent space but not a distribution on it, which is why random latent vectors decode to non-digits. Maximum likelihood is the principle for fitting a distribution \(p_\theta\) to data; for a latent-variable model \(p_\theta(\mathbf x)=\int p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)p(\mathbf z)d\mathbf z\) the likelihood cannot be computed, and the VAE maximises instead the lower bound \(\mathrm{ELBO}=\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)-\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)\), made trainable by the reparametrisation trick. The KL term shapes the latent space into the prior \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), so that sampling, interpolation and traversals work, although individual axes need not have a meaning. A classifier trained on real data then serves as a referee for synthetic data through confusion matrices, class distributions and confidence. Finally, a conditional VAE adds a known label \(\mathbf c\) to encoder and decoder: \(\mathbf c\) selects what is generated, and \(\mathbf z\) carries the rest. Lab 025 applies this machinery to spin configurations.

title: Lab 025: Synthetic spin configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
1. Hamiltonian, Boltzmann distribution and observables
We start by recalling what a “correct” sample of a spin model is. A classical spin model assigns an energy \(H(\mathbf s)\) to every configuration \(\mathbf s=(s_1,\dots,s_N)\), \(s_i=\pm1\), on an \(L\times L\) lattice with periodic boundaries (\(N=L^2\)): \[
\text{Ising: } H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j,\qquad
J_1\text{–}J_2:\ H=-J_1\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j+J_2\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}s_is_j ,
\] with \(\langle ij\rangle\) nearest neighbours and \(\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle\) diagonal neighbours; we set \(J=J_1=1\) and \(k_B=1\). In thermal equilibrium at temperature \(T\) (inverse temperature \(\beta=1/T\)) a configuration occurs with the Boltzmann probability \[
p(\mathbf s)=\frac{e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}}{Z},\qquad Z=\sum_{\mathbf s}e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)} .
\] At low \(T\) the low-energy, ordered configurations dominate; at high \(T\) all configurations become nearly equally likely and the system is disordered.
Every observable we use is an average over this distribution: for a quantity \(O(\mathbf s)\) of a single configuration, \[
\langle O\rangle=\frac1Z\sum_{\mathbf s}O(\mathbf s)\,e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)} .
\] The partition function also generates the thermodynamics: the energy per spin is the first derivative of \(\ln Z\) with respect to \(\beta\), and the specific heat per spin is the second derivative, which equals the variance of the energy, \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle e\rangle&=\frac{\langle H\rangle}{N}=-\frac1N\,\frac{\partial\ln Z}{\partial\beta},\\
c&=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\,\frac{\partial^2\ln Z}{\partial\beta^2}=\frac{\beta^2}{N}\big(\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2\big)
=N\beta^2\big(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\big).
\end{aligned}
\] The sums run over all \(2^N\) configurations and cannot be performed for \(N=900\) or \(N=1024\). Monte Carlo instead draws \(n\) configurations \(\mathbf s^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf s^{(n)}\) with probability \(p(\mathbf s)\) at each temperature, and every average \(\langle O\rangle\) is estimated by the plain sample mean \(\overline{O}=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n O(\mathbf s^{(k)})\). A generator is judged by computing exactly the same sample means over its own configurations. The table lists each observable in both forms: the definition through the Boltzmann distribution, and the estimator that the functions ising_observables and j1j2_observables below compute. Here \(e_k=H(\mathbf s^{(k)})/N\) and \(m_k=\frac1N\sum_i s_i^{(k)}\) are the energy and magnetisation per spin of sample \(k\), \(\overline{x}\) is the mean over the \(n\) samples, and on a finite lattice without a field \(\langle m\rangle=0\) by the symmetry \(\mathbf s\to-\mathbf s\), which is why \(|m|\) is used.

All variances are the population variances (division by \(n\)), as computed by numpy.var.
For the 2D Ising model the transition temperature is known exactly from Onsager’s solution: \(T_c=2/\ln(1+\sqrt2)\approx2.269\).

title: Lab 025: Synthetic spin configurations from a conditional VAE
section: 2. The conditional evidence lower bound for spins
text:
2. The conditional evidence lower bound for spins
Next we recall the generator. A configuration \(\mathbf s=(s_1,\dots,s_N)\), \(s_i=\pm1\), is stored as bits \(b_i=(s_i+1)/2\in\{0,1\}\), and the condition is \(c\), with \(c=T\) for the Ising model and \(c=(g,T)\) for the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model. The cVAE consists of a prior \(p(\mathbf z)=\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbb 1)\) over a latent vector \(\mathbf z\in\mathbb R^{d}\); a decoder \(p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid\mathbf z,c)=\prod_{i=1}^N \sigma(\ell_i)^{b_i}\,\big(1-\sigma(\ell_i)\big)^{1-b_i}\), which outputs one logit \(\ell_i(\mathbf z,c)\) per site, with \(\sigma(\ell)=1/(1+e^{-\ell})\); and an encoder \(q_\phi(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf s,c)=\mathcal N\big(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf s,c),\mathrm{diag}\,\boldsymbol\sigma^2(\mathbf s,c)\big)\).
Training should make the log-likelihood \(\log p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid c)\) of the Monte Carlo configurations large, but this quantity is an integral over all latent vectors and cannot be computed. We therefore maximise a quantity that can be computed and is never larger: the evidence lower bound (ELBO). “Evidence” is the traditional name of the log-likelihood of the data, \(\log p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid c)\), and the ELBO is a lower bound on it; the derivation is given in full in Lab 024. For every training configuration \[
\log p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid c)\;\ge\;\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf s,c)}\big[\log p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid\mathbf z,c)\big]\;-\;
\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf s,c)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big)\;=\;\mathrm{ELBO},
\] where the Bernoulli reconstruction term and the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between two Gaussians take the closed forms \[
\log p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid\mathbf z,c)=\sum_{i=1}^N\Big[b_i\log\sigma(\ell_i)+(1-b_i)\log\big(1-\sigma(\ell_i)\big)\Big],\qquad
\mathrm{KL}=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{d}\big(\sigma_j^2+\mu_j^2-1-\log\sigma_j^2\big).
\] Here \(p(\mathbf z)=\mathcal N(0,\mathbb 1)\); in Section 3.4 we will also use a prior that depends on the condition, \(p_\psi(\mathbf z\mid c)\), and the KL term is then taken with respect to it. We minimise \(-\mathrm{ELBO}\) averaged over the data, sampling \(\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\epsilon\) with \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\mathbb 1)\) (the reparametrisation trick). To generate a configuration at a condition \(c\) we draw \(\mathbf z\) from the prior, compute the logits and draw every spin from its Bernoulli distribution. Alternatively, we can take the most likely configuration \(\hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}\,\ell_i\).
This structure already tells us which tests will be hard. The generator defines a model distribution \(p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid c)=\int d\mathbf z\,p(\mathbf z)\,p_\theta(\mathbf s\mid\mathbf z,c)\) that should approximate the Boltzmann distribution \(p(\mathbf s)=e^{-\beta H(\mathbf s)}/Z\). At fixed \(\mathbf z\), however, the decoder is a product over sites, the same structure as a mean-field ansatz: \(\langle s_i\rangle_{\mathbf z}=\tanh(\ell_i/2)\) and \[
\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\mathbf z}=\tanh(\ell_i/2)\tanh(\ell_j/2)\quad (i\neq j),\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(s_i,s_j)=\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathbf z}\big(\tanh(\ell_i/2),\tanh(\ell_j/2)\big).
\] All correlations between spins must therefore be carried by the few latent variables \(\mathbf z\). The energy \(H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\) is a sum of nearest-neighbour correlations, and a site-independent Bernoulli draw breaks bonds at random. This is why the energy, the specific heat and \(G(r)\) are the sharp tests in this lab.

def unpack_spins(packed, L):
    '''Packed bits (..., L, ceil(L/8)) uint8  ->  spins (..., L, L) int8 with values -1, +1.'''
    bits = np.unpackbits(packed, axis=-1, count=L)       # (..., L, L) in {0, 1}

text:
3. The 2D Ising model

3.1 Monte Carlo data
The file ising_L30.npz holds 256 Swendsen–Wang configurations at each of 37 temperatures, \(T\in[1.5,3.5]\), sampled more densely near \(T_c\). At every temperature we split them into three sets. The 128 configurations of S_train are the training set both of the generator and of the evaluator networks. The remaining configurations form two independent held-out real sets, S_A and S_B, of 64 snapshots each. S_A is the reference for every test, while the difference between S_A and S_B measures the statistical noise of a 64-snapshot estimate; we call it the real-vs-real baseline. All arrays have the shape (n_T, n, L, L), that is (temperatures, snapshots, rows, columns).


Code
data = np.load(f"{DATA}/ising_L30.npz")
L = int(data["L"]); N = L * L
order = np.argsort(data["T"])
T_grid = data["T"][order]                                  # (37,)
S_all = unpack_spins(data["configs"], L)[order]            # (37, 256, 30, 30) int8
n_T, n_per_T = S_all.shape[:2]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
perm = rng.permutation(n_per_T)                            # the same random split at every temperature
S_train = S_all[:, perm[:128]]                             # (37, 128, 30, 30)
S_A = S_all[:, perm[128:192]]                              # (37, 64, 30, 30)  held-out reference
S_B = S_all[:, perm[192:]]                                 # (37, 64, 30, 30)  second held-out set (noise level)
assert S_train.shape == (n_T, 128, L, L) and S_A.shape == S_B.shape == (n_T, 64, L, L)
i_c = int(np.argmin(np.abs(T_grid - TC)))                  # grid temperature closest to T_c
print(f"{n_T} temperatures, T from {T_grid[0]} to {T_grid[-1]}; closest to T_c = {TC:.4f}: T = {T_grid[i_c]}")
print(f"per temperature: {S_train.shape[1]} training, {S_A.shape[1]} + {S_B.shape[1]} held-out real configurations")


37 temperatures, T from 1.5 to 3.5; closest to T_c = 2.2692: T = 2.26
per temperature: 128 training, 64 + 64 held-out real configurations




3.2 Observables fixed by the Hamiltonian
We now turn the observables of Section 1 into formulas for a finite set of snapshots. For one snapshot, with each nearest-neighbour bond counted once (right and down neighbour, periodic boundaries), \[
e=\frac{H}{N}=-\frac1N\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\in[-2,2],\qquad m=\frac1N\sum_i s_i .
\] For a set of snapshots at one temperature (\(k_B=J=1\)) we compute \[
\langle e\rangle,\quad \langle|m|\rangle,\quad c=\frac{N}{T^2}\big(\langle e^2\rangle-\langle e\rangle^2\big),\quad
\chi=\frac{N}{T}\big(\langle m^2\rangle-\langle|m|\rangle^2\big),\quad U_4=1-\frac{\langle m^4\rangle}{3\langle m^2\rangle^2},
\] together with the correlation function along the lattice axes, \(G(r)=\langle s_{\mathbf x}\,s_{\mathbf x+r\hat{\mathbf e}}\rangle\), averaged over \(\mathbf x\), both axes and the snapshots, for \(r=0,\dots,L/2\).
The function ising_observables(S, T) takes S of shape (n_T, n, L, L) and T of shape (n_T,). It returns the per-temperature averages (shape (n_T,)), the per-snapshot \(e\) and \(m\) (shape (n_T, n)) and \(G\) (shape (n_T, L/2+1)). The cell ends with two configurations whose values we know exactly: the all-up state must give \(e=-2\), \(m=1\), and the chessboard state \(e=+2\), \(m=0\).


Code
def ising_observables(S, T):
    '''Observables of the 2D Ising model (J = 1) for snapshots S (n_T, n, L, L) at temperatures T (n_T,).'''
    s = S.astype(np.float32)
    n_sites = s.shape[-1] * s.shape[-2]
    # each bond once: right neighbour (axis -1) and down neighbour (axis -2); np.roll implements periodic boundaries
    e = -(s * np.roll(s, 1, axis=-1) + s * np.roll(s, 1, axis=-2)).mean(axis=(-1, -2))     # (n_T, n)
    m = s.mean(axis=(-1, -2))                                                              # (n_T, n)
    T = np.asarray(T, np.float64)
    obs = {"e": e.mean(1),
           "m": np.abs(m).mean(1),
           "c": n_sites * e.var(1) / T**2,
           "chi": n_sites * ((m**2).mean(1) - np.abs(m).mean(1) ** 2) / T,
           "U4": 1.0 - (m**4).mean(1) / (3.0 * (m**2).mean(1) ** 2),
           "e_samples": e, "m_samples": m}
    # G(r): average of s_x s_{x+r} over sites, both axes and snapshots -> (n_T, L/2 + 1)
    obs["G"] = np.stack([0.5 * ((s * np.roll(s, r, -1)).mean((-1, -2, -3)) + (s * np.roll(s, r, -2)).mean((-1, -2, -3)))
                         for r in range(s.shape[-1] // 2 + 1)], axis=1)
    return obs

# sanity checks on configurations whose answers we know
up = np.ones((1, 1, L, L), np.int8)
chess = np.where((np.arange(L)[:, None] + np.arange(L)[None, :]) % 2 == 0, 1, -1).astype(np.int8)[None, None]
with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):                                          # U4 = 0/0 for the chessboard (m = 0)
    o_up, o_chess = ising_observables(up, [1.0]), ising_observables(chess, [1.0])
assert np.isclose(o_up["e"][0], -2) and np.isclose(o_up["m"][0], 1)          # ground state: every bond satisfied
assert np.isclose(o_chess["e"][0], 2) and np.isclose(o_chess["m"][0], 0)     # chessboard: every bond broken
print("checks passed: all-up e = -2, m = 1;  chessboard e = +2, m = 0")


checks passed: all-up e = -2, m = 1;  chessboard e = +2, m = 0


Averages can agree while the distributions differ, so we also need a distance between distributions. For two samples \(x_1..x_n\) and \(y_1..y_n\) of equal size, the 1D Wasserstein-1 distance is the mean absolute difference of the sorted values, \[
W_1=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\big|x_{(k)}-y_{(k)}\big| ,
\] which is the average distance one has to move probability mass to turn one histogram into the other, measured in units of \(e\) or \(m\).
A raw difference between a synthetic and a real estimate means little without knowing how large the difference between two real sets would be. For an observable \(O(T)\) we therefore compare the synthetic estimate with S_A and express the result in noise units, normalising by the real-vs-real difference: \[
R_O=\frac{\mathrm{mean}_T\,|O_{\rm syn}(T)-O_A(T)|}{\mathrm{mean}_T\,|O_B(T)-O_A(T)|}.
\] A value \(R_O\approx 1\) means that the synthetic set is as close to S_A as an independent Monte Carlo set of the same size; \(R_O\gg1\) signals a real discrepancy. The next cell checks the \(W_1\) implementation on a shifted sample and prints the real-vs-real noise levels that enter the denominators.


Code
def wasserstein1(x, y):
    '''1D Wasserstein-1 distance between equal-size samples along the last axis: mean |sorted(x) - sorted(y)|.'''
    assert x.shape == y.shape
    return np.abs(np.sort(x, axis=-1) - np.sort(y, axis=-1)).mean(axis=-1)

def noise_ratio(O_syn, O_A, O_B):
    '''R = mean_T |O_syn - O_A| / mean_T |O_B - O_A|  (works for averages and for W1 distances: pass W1(syn,A), 0, W1(B,A)).'''
    return float(np.mean(np.abs(O_syn - O_A)) / np.mean(np.abs(O_B - O_A)))

x = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=1000)
assert np.isclose(wasserstein1(x, x + 0.3), 0.3)            # a rigid shift by 0.3 costs exactly 0.3
print("check passed: W1(x, x + 0.3) =", round(float(wasserstein1(x, x + 0.3)), 6))

3.3 Evaluator networks trained on real simulations
The first family of tests asks what a network that has only ever seen real Monte Carlo data thinks of the synthetic snapshots. We train two small convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on S_train only. Both consist of two \(3\times3\) convolutions with periodic (CIRCULAR) padding, a \(2\times2\) max pooling between them, global average pooling (so that the network sees local patterns, not positions) and one hidden dense layer. The temperature regressor outputs an estimate \(\hat T\), is trained with the loss \((\hat T-T)^2\) and uses all 37 temperatures. The phase classifier is trained only far from the transition, on \(T\le1.8\) (ordered, label 0) and \(T\ge2.8\) (disordered, label 1), with the cross-entropy loss; its output \(p_1\) is the probability of “disordered”, and \(\max(p_0,p_1)\) is its confidence (Lecture 4). Near the transition the classifier becomes uncertain, so the minimum of the confidence as a function of \(T\) marks the transition it sees.
One generic trainer is used for every network of the lab. One epoch is a single jit-compiled jax.lax.scan over minibatches, optimised with Adam and a cosine-decaying learning rate. The data arrays are passed as arguments rather than captured as constants, and the spins stay int8 and are converted to float32 per minibatch, which keeps the memory small. On the real held-out sets the regressor reaches a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of about 0.12, and the confidence minimum lies at \(T=2.28\) for both S_A and S_B, next to \(T_c=2.269\); these are the baselines for the synthetic data.

def train_model(model, loss_fn, data, epochs, batch, lr, seed, callback=None, every=0):
    '''Minibatch training of an nnx model.
    loss_fn(model, batch_data, key) -> (scalar loss, aux vector);  data: tuple of arrays with the same leading dimension.
    Returns the per-epoch mean of aux, shape (epochs, len(aux)). callback(model, epoch) is called every `every` epochs and after the last one.'''
    n = len(data[0]); n_batches = n // batch
    schedule = optax.cosine_decay_schedule(lr, decay_steps=epochs * n_batches, alpha=0.05)
    opt = nnx.Optimizer(model, optax.adam(schedule), wrt=nnx.Param)
    graphdef, state = nnx.split((model, opt))              # pure pytree state -> usable inside jax.lax.scan
    data = tuple(jnp.asarray(a) for a in data)

    @jax.jit
    def run_epoch(state, data, key):
        k_perm, k_steps = jax.random.split(key)
        idx = jax.random.permutation(k_perm, n)[: n_batches * batch].reshape(n_batches, batch)   # (n_batches, batch)
        def step(state, inputs):
            batch_idx, k = inputs
            model, opt = nnx.merge(graphdef, state)
            (loss, aux), grads = nnx.value_and_grad(loss_fn, has_aux=True)(model, tuple(a[batch_idx] for a in data), k)
            opt.update(model, grads)
            return nnx.state((model, opt)), aux
        state, aux = jax.lax.scan(step, state, (idx, jax.random.split(k_steps, n_batches)))
        return state, aux.mean(axis=0)

    key, history = jax.random.key(seed), []
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        key, k = jax.random.split(key)
        state, aux = run_epoch(state, data, k)
        history.append(np.asarray(aux))
        if callback is not None and ((epoch + 1) % every == 0 or epoch + 1 == epochs):
            nnx.update((model, opt), state)
            callback(model, epoch + 1)
    nnx.update((model, opt), state)                        # write the trained parameters back into `model`
    return np.array(history)

class CNN(nnx.Module):
    '''(B, L, L) spins -> (B, n_out). Two 3x3 periodic convolutions, max pooling, global average pooling, dense head.'''
    def __init__(self, n_out, *, rngs):
        self.conv1 = nnx.Conv(1, 8, (3, 3), padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)
        self.conv2 = nnx.Conv(8, 16, (3, 3), padding="CIRCULAR", rngs=rngs)
        self.hidden = nnx.Linear(16, 32, rngs=rngs)
        self.out = nnx.Linear(32, n_out, rngs=rngs)
    def __call__(self, x):
        h = nnx.relu(self.conv1(x[..., None]))                           # (B, L, L, 8): add a channel axis
        h = nnx.max_pool(h, (2, 2), strides=(2, 2))                      # (B, L/2, L/2, 8)
        h = nnx.relu(self.conv2(h)).mean(axis=(1, 2))                    # (B, 16): global average pooling
        return self.out(nnx.relu(self.hidden(h)))

@nnx.jit
def cnn_forward(model, x):
    return model(x.astype(jnp.float32))

def predict(model, S, batch=4096):
    '''Apply a CNN to snapshots S (..., L, L); returns (..., n_out).'''
    flat = S.reshape(-1, *S.shape[-2:])
    out = np.concatenate([np.asarray(cnn_forward(model, jnp.asarray(flat[i:i + batch]))) for i in range(0, len(flat), batch)])
    return out.reshape(*S.shape[:-2], -1)

def mse_loss(model, batch, key):
    x, y = batch
    loss = jnp.mean((model(x.astype(jnp.float32))[:, 0] - y) ** 2)
    return loss, jnp.stack([loss])

def xent_loss(model, batch, key):
    x, y = batch
    logits = model(x.astype(jnp.float32))
    loss = optax.softmax_cross_entropy_with_integer_labels(logits, y).mean()
    return loss, jnp.stack([loss, (logits.argmax(-1) == y).mean()])

3.4 The conditional VAE
The generator has a dense encoder and decoder. The spins are flattened, so x has shape (B, N), and the condition c has shape (B, 1) with \(c=T-2.5\): \[
\text{encoder: } [\mathbf s, c]\;\xrightarrow{\;N+1\to512\to256\;}\;(\boldsymbol\mu,\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^{d}\times\mathbb R^{d},\qquad
\text{decoder: } [\mathbf z, c]\;\xrightarrow{\;d+1\to256\to512\to N\;}\;\boldsymbol\ell ,
\] with ReLU activations and latent dimension \(d=16\). We train three variants, each of which adds one physics-motivated ingredient to the previous one.
The first variant, called cVAE, is the model of Lab 024 with the prior \(p(\mathbf z)=\mathcal N(0,\mathbb 1)\), trained on the raw data.
The second variant, cVAE+Z2, uses the symmetry of the Hamiltonian. The Ising Hamiltonian is invariant under the global flip \(\mathbf s\to-\mathbf s\), so below \(T_c\) the data consist of two mirror-image families (\(m\approx\pm|m|\)) that the generator would have to place separately in the Gaussian latent space; prior samples that fall between them decode to mixtures of the two. We impose the symmetry by construction instead: every training snapshot is replaced by its representative with \(m\ge0\), and every generated snapshot is flipped with probability 1/2, so that \(p(\mathbf s)=\tfrac12\big[p_+(\mathbf s)+p_+(-\mathbf s)\big]\) holds exactly.
The third variant, cVAE+Z2+p(z|T), adds a conditional prior \(p_\psi(\mathbf z\mid c)=\mathcal N\big(\boldsymbol\mu_\psi(c),\mathrm{diag}\,\boldsymbol\sigma^2_\psi(c)\big)\), computed by a small network \(c\xrightarrow{1\to64\to}(\boldsymbol\mu_\psi,\log\boldsymbol\sigma_\psi^2)\) (the prior network of Sohn, Lee and Yan). The reason is that the encoder sees the configuration, and a configuration itself reveals its temperature: it is ordered or disordered, with large or small domains. The encoded snapshots of different temperatures therefore occupy different regions of \(\mathbf z\)-space. With the fixed prior \(\mathcal N(0,\mathbb 1)\), generation at temperature \(T\) draws \(\mathbf z\) from all these regions and produces a mixture of temperatures; with \(p_\psi(\mathbf z|T)\) it draws from the region that belongs to \(T\). The KL term becomes \[
\mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p_\psi\big)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d\Big[\log\frac{\sigma_{\psi,j}^2}{\sigma_j^2}+\frac{\sigma_j^2+(\mu_j-\mu_{\psi,j})^2}{\sigma_{\psi,j}^2}-1\Big],
\] which reduces to the formula of Section 2 for \(\boldsymbol\mu_\psi=0\), \(\boldsymbol\sigma_\psi=1\). The cell below checks the Bernoulli negative log-likelihood and compares this closed-form KL with a Monte Carlo estimate (1.2077 against 1.2124).


Code
class CVAE(nnx.Module):
    '''Dense conditional VAE with a Bernoulli decoder: x (B, N) spins +-1, c (B, n_cond).
    conditional_prior=False: p(z) = N(0, 1);  True: p(z|c) = N(mu_psi(c), sigma_psi(c)^2) from a small prior network.'''
    def __init__(self, n_sites, n_cond, latent=16, hidden=512, conditional_prior=False, *, rngs):
        self.enc1 = nnx.Linear(n_sites + n_cond, hidden, rngs=rngs)
        self.enc2 = nnx.Linear(hidden, 256, rngs=rngs)
        self.enc_mu = nnx.Linear(256, latent, rngs=rngs)
        self.enc_logvar = nnx.Linear(256, latent, rngs=rngs)
        self.dec1 = nnx.Linear(latent + n_cond, 256, rngs=rngs)
        self.dec2 = nnx.Linear(256, hidden, rngs=rngs)
        self.dec3 = nnx.Linear(hidden, n_sites, rngs=rngs)
        self.conditional_prior, self.latent = conditional_prior, latent
        if conditional_prior:
            self.pri1 = nnx.Linear(n_cond, 64, rngs=rngs)
            self.pri_mu = nnx.Linear(64, latent, rngs=rngs)
            self.pri_logvar = nnx.Linear(64, latent, rngs=rngs)
    def encode(self, x, c):
        h = nnx.relu(self.enc2(nnx.relu(self.enc1(jnp.concatenate([x, c], axis=-1)))))
        return self.enc_mu(h), self.enc_logvar(h)                          # (B, d), (B, d)
    def decode(self, z, c):
        h = nnx.relu(self.dec2(nnx.relu(self.dec1(jnp.concatenate([z, c], axis=-1)))))
        return self.dec3(h)                                                # (B, N) logits l_i
    def prior(self, c):
        '''Mean and log-variance of p(z|c), each (B, d); zeros (standard normal) without a prior network.'''
        if not self.conditional_prior:
            zeros = jnp.zeros((c.shape[0], self.latent))
            return zeros, zeros
        h = nnx.tanh(self.pri1(c))
        return self.pri_mu(h), self.pri_logvar(h)

def gaussian_kl(mu_q, logvar_q, mu_p, logvar_p):
    '''KL( N(mu_q, e^logvar_q) || N(mu_p, e^logvar_p) ) per dimension (diagonal Gaussians).'''
    return 0.5 * (logvar_p - logvar_q + (jnp.exp(logvar_q) + (mu_q - mu_p) ** 2) / jnp.exp(logvar_p) - 1.0)

def cvae_terms(model, x, c, key):
    '''Per-configuration terms of -ELBO: reconstruction -log p(s|z,c), shape (B,), and KL per latent dimension, shape (B, d).'''
    mu, logvar = model.encode(x, c)
    z = mu + jnp.exp(0.5 * logvar) * jax.random.normal(key, mu.shape)     # reparametrisation: one z per configuration
    logits = model.decode(z, c)
    bits = (x + 1.0) / 2.0                                                 # s = +-1  ->  b = 1, 0
    rec = optax.sigmoid_binary_cross_entropy(logits, bits).sum(-1)        # -sum_i [b log s(l) + (1-b) log(1-s(l))]
    kl = gaussian_kl(mu, logvar, *model.prior(c))                         # closed form, per dimension
    return rec, kl

def cvae_loss(model, batch, key):
    x, c = batch
    rec, kl = cvae_terms(model, x.astype(jnp.float32), c, key)
    loss = (rec + kl.sum(-1)).mean()
    return loss, jnp.stack([loss, rec.mean(), kl.sum(-1).mean()])

Before generating anything we monitor the health of the training. During training we record the training \(-\)ELBO per epoch and, every 5 epochs, the \(-\)ELBO on the held-out real data S_A + S_B. A held-out value that rises while the training value falls signals overfitting: with 128 snapshots per temperature and \(\sim1.2\times10^6\) parameters this starts after a few tens of epochs, so we train for 40 epochs.
After training we look at the KL per latent dimension on held-out data. A dimension with \(\mathrm{KL}_j\approx0\) is ignored by the decoder (an inactive unit); if all of them are inactive, the model has collapsed to \(p(\mathbf s|c)\) without latent structure (posterior collapse). We also report the fraction of spins that the decoder reproduces from \(\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf s,c)\) with \(\hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}\,\ell_i\). def canonical(S):
    '''Z2 representative: flip every snapshot with m < 0 (the last two axes are the lattice).'''
    sign = np.where(S.sum(axis=(-1, -2), keepdims=True) >= 0, 1, -1).astype(np.int8)
    return S * sign

cond_I = lambda T: (np.asarray(T, np.float32) - 2.5)[..., None]       # (..., 1): the condition fed to the networks

@nnx.jit
def cvae_eval(model, x, c, key):
    '''Held-out terms: reconstruction (B,), KL per dimension (B, d), and the fraction of spins reproduced by sign(l) at z = mu.'''
    rec, kl = cvae_terms(model, x, c, key)
    mu, _ = model.encode(x, c)
    acc = (jnp.sign(model.decode(mu, c)) == x).mean(-1)
    return rec, kl, acc

def held_out_terms(model, X, C, key, batch=4096):
    '''cvae_eval in batches over X (n, N) int8 and C (n, n_cond); returns three concatenated numpy arrays.'''
    parts = [cvae_eval(model, jnp.asarray(X[i:i + batch], jnp.float32), jnp.asarray(C[i:i + batch]), jax.random.fold_in(key, i))
             for i in range(0, len(X), batch)]
    return [np.concatenate([np.asarray(p[j]) for p in parts]) for j in range(3)]

def fit_cvae(symmetric, conditional_prior, epochs=40, seed=0):
    '''Train a cVAE on S_train; monitor -ELBO on the held-out S_test. Returns model, training history, held-out curve.'''
    S_tr, S_ho = (canonical(S_train), canonical(S_test)) if symmetric else (S_train, S_test)
    X = S_tr.reshape(-1, N)                                            # int8 (37*128, N)
    C = cond_I(np.repeat(T_grid, S_tr.shape[1]))                       # (37*128, 1)
    model = CVAE(N, 1, conditional_prior=conditional_prior, rngs=nnx.Rngs(seed))

    hist = train_model(model, cvae_loss, (X, C), epochs=epochs, batch=128, lr=1e-3, seed=seed, callback=monitor, every=5)
    return model, hist, np.array(curve)

3.5 Synthetic data at the same conditions
With the three generators trained, each of them produces 64 configurations at every one of the 37 temperatures, the same number as in S_A and S_B, using Bernoulli sampling. For the best model we also keep the most likely configuration \(\hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}\,\ell_i\) obtained from the same latent vectors, to see what happens when the sampling noise of the decoder is removed. The figure compares snapshots of all sets side by side.


Code
@nnx.jit
def decoder_logits(model, z, c):
    return model.decode(z, c)

def generate(model, cond, n_per_cond, key, side, symmetric=False, batch=8192):
    '''n_per_cond configurations at every condition row of cond (K, n_cond); z ~ p(z|c).
    Returns two int8 arrays (K, n_per_cond, side, side): Bernoulli samples and most likely configurations (same z).'''
    c_all = np.repeat(np.asarray(cond, np.float32), n_per_cond, axis=0)          # (K * n, n_cond)
    bern, ml = [], []
    for i in range(0, len(c_all), batch):
        k_z, k_s, k_f = jax.random.split(jax.random.fold_in(key, i), 3)
        c = jnp.asarray(c_all[i:i + batch])
        mu_p, logvar_p = model.prior(c)                                          # (b, d) each; zeros for N(0, 1)
        z = mu_p + jnp.exp(0.5 * logvar_p) * jax.random.normal(k_z, mu_p.shape)  # z ~ p(z|c)
        logits = decoder_logits(model, z, c)                                     # (b, side*side)
        s_b = jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(k_s, jax.nn.sigmoid(logits)), 1, -1)   # independent Bernoulli spins
        s_m = jnp.where(logits > 0, 1, -1)                                        # most likely configuration
        if symmetric:                                                             # global flip with probability 1/2
            flip = jnp.where(jax.random.bernoulli(k_f, 0.5, (len(c), 1)), -1, 1)
            s_b, s_m = s_b * flip, s_m * flip
        bern.append(np.asarray(s_b, np.int8)); ml.append(np.asarray(s_m, np.int8))
    shape = (len(cond), n_per_cond, side, side)
    return np.concatenate(bern).reshape(shape), np.concatenate(ml).reshape(shape)

3.8 Two-sample test and memorisation
The physics tests check selected observables; a classifier two-sample test (C2ST) checks the distribution as a whole. If two sets come from the same distribution, no classifier can tell them apart better than chance. At three temperatures we train a fresh small CNN to separate real from synthetic snapshots (balanced classes, 75% for training, 25% held out) and report the held-out accuracy: 0.5 means indistinguishable, 1.0 means trivially separable. As a sanity check, real (S_train) against real (S_A+S_B) must give \(\approx0.5\).
A generator that copies its training set would pass every physics test, so we must also exclude memorisation. For every synthetic and every held-out real snapshot we compute the normalised Hamming distance to the nearest training snapshot at the same \(T\), minimised over the global flip: \[
d_{\rm NN}(\mathbf s)=\min_{\mathbf t\in\text{train}}\ \frac{1-|\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf t|/N}{2}\in[0,\tfrac12].
\] Real held-out snapshots are new draws from the Boltzmann distribution, so their \(d_{\rm NN}\) is the reference; a synthetic \(d_{\rm NN}\) much smaller than the real one would mean copying.


Code
def c2st(X1, X2, seed, epochs=25):
    '''Held-out accuracy of a CNN trained to separate X1 (n1, L, L) from X2 (n2, L, L).
    Both classes are cut to n = min(n1, n2) and split 75 / 25 *within each class* (stratified): with a plain random split a
    class that is over-represented in training is under-represented in the test set, which biases the accuracy below 0.5.'''
    n = min(len(X1), len(X2)); n_tr = int(0.75 * n)
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    p1, p2 = r.permutation(len(X1))[:n], r.permutation(len(X2))[:n]
    X_tr = np.concatenate([X1[p1[:n_tr]], X2[p2[:n_tr]]]); y_tr = np.repeat(np.array([0, 1], np.int32), n_tr)
    X_te = np.concatenate([X1[p1[n_tr:]], X2[p2[n_tr:]]]); y_te = np.repeat(np.array([0, 1], np.int32), n - n_tr)
    model = CNN(2, rngs=nnx.Rngs(seed))
    train_model(model, xent_loss, (X_tr, y_tr), epochs=epochs, batch=32, lr=3e-3, seed=seed)
    pred = predict(model, X_te).argmax(-1)
    return float((pred == y_te).mean()), len(y_te)

def nn_hamming(Q, R):
    '''Q (nq, L, L), R (nr, L, L) spins -> (nq,) normalised Hamming distance to the nearest R, minimised over the global flip.'''
    q = Q.reshape(len(Q), -1).astype(np.float32); r = R.reshape(len(R), -1).astype(np.float32)
    overlap = q @ r.T / q.shape[1]                                     # (nq, nr) in [-1, 1]
    return ((1.0 - np.abs(overlap)) / 2.0).min(axis=1)                 # |overlap|: the flipped copy counts as the same

3.9 Pattern-level and Hamiltonian-level tests
Taken together, the tests of this section draw a consistent picture. The training health is similar for the three models: the held-out \(-\)ELBO is close, all latent units are active and about 80% of the spins are reproduced from \(\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu\). The ELBO alone therefore does not tell which model generates the right physics.
The plain cVAE, asked for a fixed \(T\), produces a mixture of temperatures. Its \(\langle|m|\rangle\) is far too small below \(T_c\) and too large above, the regressor reads temperatures that depend only weakly on the requested one, and below \(T_c\) a large fraction of the snapshots are mixtures of the two ordered states. Imposing the \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry removes part of these mixtures, but the temperature is still not followed. Only with the conditional prior does the generator follow the temperature: \(\langle|m|\rangle\), \(\chi\), \(P(m)\) and the regressor below \(T_c\) are now close to the Monte Carlo values, within a few noise units.
The local tests nevertheless fail. The energy \(\langle e\rangle\) is too high around and above \(T_c\), by tens of noise units; the specific heat is several times to more than ten times too large; and \(P(e)\) is far too broad. The reason is the one anticipated in Section 2: given \(\mathbf z\) the spins are drawn independently, and every spin whose logit is not saturated breaks its bonds at random. Taking the most likely configuration \(\hat s_i=\mathrm{sign}\,\ell_i\) removes that noise and over-smooths instead: \(\langle e\rangle\) is too low, the domains are large and compact, \(G(r)\) is too large at all distances and the regressor reads temperatures far too low.
The C2ST separates every synthetic set from the Monte Carlo data, clearly so near and above \(T_c\), while real against real gives 0.5. The generator does not memorise: the nearest-neighbour distances of the best model to the training set are those of new Monte Carlo snapshots.
The lesson of the Ising model is that global, pattern-level quantities (\(\langle|m|\rangle\), the regressor, the classifier) are more forgiving than local, Hamiltonian-level ones (\(\langle e\rangle\), \(c\), \(P(e)\)). A generator that passes only the first kind of test merely looks right.

title: Lab 025: Synthetic spin configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
4. The \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model
We now move to a model with a richer phase diagram, \[
H=-J_1\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j+J_2\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}s_is_j,\qquad g=J_2/J_1,\quad J_1=1 ,
\] which is a ferromagnet for \(g<1/2\) and forms stripes for \(g>1/2\) (Lab 018). For every snapshot we compute \(|m|\), the stripe order parameter \(m_{\rm str}=\sqrt{m_{(\pi,0)}^2+m_{(0,\pi)}^2}\) with \(m_{(\pi,0)}=\frac1N\sum_{x,y}(-1)^x s_{x,y}\), and the energy per spin \(e=-\frac1{2N}\sum_i s_i h_i\) with the local field \(h_i=\sum_{\rm nn}s_j-g\sum_{\rm nnn}s_j\); per grid point we compute \(c=N\,\mathrm{Var}(e)/T^2\).
The condition is now \(c=(g,T)\), and this model lets us ask a new question: can the generator produce correct configurations at conditions it has never seen? At every grid point the 100 snapshots are split into training (60), S_A (20) and S_B (20). The cVAE is trained only at every second \(g\) and every second \(T\), a quarter of the grid that we call “seen”, and generates at every grid point, so three quarters of the conditions were never seen in training. The phase classifier, in contrast, is trained on real training snapshots at all points.


Code
dj = np.load(f"{DATA}/j1j2_L32.npz")
LJ = int(dj["L"]); NJ = LJ * LJ
g_grid = dj["g"]; oT = np.argsort(dj["T"]); TJ = dj["T"][oT]
SJ = unpack_spins(dj["configs"], LJ)[:, oT]                          # (nG, nT, 100, L, L) int8
nG, nT, nS = SJ.shape[:3]
pj = np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(nS)
J_train, J_A, J_B = SJ[:, :, pj[:60]], SJ[:, :, pj[60:80]], SJ[:, :, pj[80:100]]
seen = np.zeros((nG, nT), bool); seen[::2, ::2] = True               # conditions used to train the generator
print(f"grid {nG} g x {nT} T, g in [{g_grid[0]}, {g_grid[-1]}], T in [{TJ[0]:.2f}, {TJ[-1]:.2f}], {nS} snapshots per point")
print(f"split per point: {J_train.shape[2]} training, {J_A.shape[2]} + {J_B.shape[2]} held-out;  "
      f"seen conditions: {seen.sum()} of {seen.size}")

The function j1j2_observables(S) takes S of shape (nG, nT, n, L, L) and returns per-snapshot arrays of shape (nG, nT, n): \(|m|\), \(m_{\rm str}\), \(e\) and the stripe orientation, which is \(+1\) if \(|m_{(\pi,0)}|>|m_{(0,\pi)}|\) (the spins alternate along \(x\)) and \(-1\) otherwise. The loop runs over \(g\) to keep the memory small. The cell first checks the energy formula on a ferromagnet and on a perfect stripe state at \(g=0.75\), where the exact energies are \(-0.5\) and \(-1.5\).


Code
def j1j2_observables(S):
    '''Per-snapshot |m|, m_str, e and stripe orientation for S (nG, nT, n, L, L); outputs (nG, nT, n).'''
    phase_x = np.where(np.arange(LJ) % 2 == 0, 1.0, -1.0)[None, :]       # (1, L): (-1)^x along the column index
    phase_y = phase_x.T                                                   # (L, 1): (-1)^y along the row index
    out = {k: np.zeros(S.shape[:3], np.float32) for k in ["m", "m_str", "e", "orient"]}
    for a in range(S.shape[0]):
        s = S[a].astype(np.float32)                                       # (nT, n, L, L)
        nn = sum(np.roll(s, sh, ax) for sh in (1, -1) for ax in (-1, -2))                                 # 4 nearest neighbours
        nnn = sum(np.roll(np.roll(s, sy, -2), sx, -1) for sy in (1, -1) for sx in (1, -1))                # 4 diagonal neighbours
        out["e"][a] = -0.5 * (s * (nn - g_grid[a] * nnn)).mean((-1, -2))   # each bond appears twice in sum_i s_i h_i
        m_pi0, m_0pi = (s * phase_x).mean((-1, -2)), (s * phase_y).mean((-1, -2))
        out["m"][a] = np.abs(s.mean((-1, -2)))
        out["m_str"][a] = np.sqrt(m_pi0**2 + m_0pi**2)
        out["orient"][a] = np.where(np.abs(m_pi0) > np.abs(m_0pi), 1.0, -1.0)
    return out

def j1j2_maps(o):
    '''Grid maps (nG, nT) of <|m|>, <m_str>, <e>, c from per-snapshot observables.'''
    return {"m": o["m"].mean(-1), "m_str": o["m_str"].mean(-1), "e": o["e"].mean(-1), "c": NJ * o["e"].var(-1) / TJ[None, :] ** 2}

# sanity check: ground-state energies e_FM = -2 + 2g and e_stripe = -2g on a single site of the grid
iG = int(np.argmin(np.abs(g_grid - 0.75)))
fm = np.ones((1, 1, 1, LJ, LJ), np.int8)
stripes = np.broadcast_to(np.where(np.arange(LJ) % 2 == 0, 1, -1).astype(np.int8), (LJ, LJ))[None, None, None]
for nm, S0, e_exact, ms in [("ferromagnet", fm, -2 + 2 * g_grid[iG], 0.0), ("stripes", stripes, -2 * g_grid[iG], 1.0)]:
    o0 = j1j2_observables(np.broadcast_to(S0, (nG, 1, 1, LJ, LJ)))
    assert np.isclose(o0["e"][iG, 0, 0], e_exact) and np.isclose(o0["m_str"][iG, 0, 0], ms)
    print(f"check passed at g = {g_grid[iG]:.3f}: {nm} e = {o0['e'][iG, 0, 0]:.3f} (exact {e_exact:.3f}), m_str = {o0['m_str'][iG, 0, 0]:.0f}")

t0 = time.time()
O_A, O_B, O_tr = j1j2_observables(J_A), j1j2_observables(J_B), j1j2_observables(J_train)
M_A, M_B, M_tr = j1j2_maps(O_A), j1j2_maps(O_B), j1j2_maps(O_tr)
print(f"real observables computed in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

check passed at g = 0.750: stripes e = -1.500 (exact -1.500), m_str = 1


real observables computed in 48 s


As in the Ising case, we first need an evaluator that has only seen real data. Here it is a three-class CNN that distinguishes the ferromagnet, the stripe phase and the paramagnet. The labels come from the order parameters of the real training snapshots at each grid point: ferromagnet if \(\langle|m|\rangle>0.5\), stripes if \(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle>0.5\), paramagnet if both are below 0.2. Points in between are not used for training, and 5 snapshots per labelled point enter the training set. Applied to the two real held-out sets, the classifier gives the same majority phase for S_A and S_B at 99.7% of the grid points, which is the real-vs-real baseline.


Code
N_PER_POINT = 5 if nG * nT > 3000 else 10                           # about 30 000 training snapshots for either grid
label = np.full((nG, nT), -1)
label[M_tr["m"] > 0.5] = 0; label[M_tr["m_str"] > 0.5] = 1; label[(M_tr["m"] < 0.2) & (M_tr["m_str"] < 0.2)] = 2
gi, ti = np.where(label >= 0)
X_ph = J_train[gi, ti, :N_PER_POINT].reshape(-1, LJ, LJ)             # (n_labelled * N_PER_POINT, L, L)
y_ph = np.repeat(label[gi, ti], N_PER_POINT).astype(np.int32)
t0 = time.time()
phase_clf = CNN(3, rngs=nnx.Rngs(3))
h_ph = train_model(phase_clf, xent_loss, (X_ph, y_ph), epochs=4, batch=128, lr=2e-3, seed=3)
print(f"phase classifier: {len(y_ph)} training snapshots, {np.bincount(y_ph)} per class (FM, stripes, PM), "
      f"trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s, training accuracy {h_ph[-1, 1]:.3f}")

def phase_map(S):
    '''Majority vote of the classifier at every grid point: (nG, nT) in {0, 1, 2}.'''
    return predict(phase_clf, S).argmax(-1)                          # (nG, nT, n) votes
def majority(votes):
    return np.apply_along_axis(lambda v: np.bincount(v, minlength=3).argmax(), -1, votes)

PH_A, PH_B = majority(phase_map(J_A)), majority(phase_map(J_B))
agree_AB = float((PH_A == PH_B).mean())
print(f"real-vs-real: majority phase of S_A and S_B agree at {100 * agree_AB:.1f}% of the grid points")
NUMBERS.update(j1j2_phase_agree_AB=round(agree_AB, 3))

real-vs-real: majority phase of S_A and S_B agree at 99.7% of the grid points


The cVAE for the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model has the same dense architecture with \(N=1024\) and a two-component condition \(c=\big(2(g-\tfrac12),\,(T-2)/2\big)\), latent dimension 16, and both ingredients of the best Ising model: the \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry imposed by construction (the global flip leaves \(H\) invariant for every \(g\)) and a conditional prior \(p_\psi(\mathbf z\mid g,T)\). The training set consists of the 60 training snapshots at the seen grid points. To see whether the model generalises, the held-out \(-\)ELBO is evaluated on S_A separately at seen and at unseen grid points; the two values (476.5 and 481.7) are close to each other and to the training value 476.0.

GG, TT = np.meshgrid(g_grid, TJ, indexing="ij")                       # (nG, nT) coordinates of every grid point

parts = [cvae_eval(cvae_J, jnp.asarray(x_ho[i:i + 4096]), jnp.asarray(c_ho[i:i + 4096]), jax.random.key(i)) for i in range(0, len(x_ho), 4096)]

print(f"cVAE (J1-J2): {len(X_J)} training snapshots, {12} epochs, {t_J:.0f} s;  -ELBO training {h_J[-1, 0]:.1f};  "
      f"held-out at seen points {nelbo_ho[seen].mean():.1f}, at unseen points {nelbo_ho[~seen].mean():.1f};  "

4.1 Interpolation of the phase diagram
The phase classifier trained on real data assigns the synthetic snapshots to the same phase as the Monte Carlo snapshots at 95.4% of the grid points, compared with 99.7% for real against real, and it does so equally at seen and at unseen \((g,T)\): the generator interpolates the phase diagram. The phase boundary of the synthetic data is smeared, and near \(g=1/2\) and close to the transition lines the two maps differ. The order parameters \(\langle|m|\rangle\) and \(\langle m_{\rm str}\rangle\) are reproduced within a few noise units, and the two stripe orientations are generated with equal frequency, as in the Monte Carlo data.
The energy fails as in the Ising case. In the paramagnet the synthetic \(\langle e\rangle\approx0\), the value for independent spins, while the Monte Carlo energy shows the short-range correlations of the paramagnet; the specific heat is wrong by orders of magnitude. The most likely configurations are ordered almost everywhere, so the classifier sees ferromagnets or stripes deep in the paramagnet and agrees with S_A at only 35% of the grid points.

The numbers support a clear conclusion. A cVAE trained on Monte Carlo data reproduces what the networks trained on real data look at: the phase, the order parameter and its distribution, and the position of the transition; for the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) model it does so also at conditions it has never seen. Two ingredients were needed for this, and both come from physics: the \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry of \(H\) imposed by construction, and a prior that depends on the condition, so that \(\mathbf z\) is drawn from the region of latent space that belongs to the requested temperature.
The cVAE does not reproduce what the Hamiltonian measures locally: the energy, its fluctuations (the specific heat) and \(P(e)\). Given \(\mathbf z\) the decoder is a product over sites, a mean-field-like distribution, and nearest-neighbour correlations beyond what the 16 latent variables carry are lost. A classifier two-sample test detects this at every temperature. Synthetic configurations can therefore be useful for questions about the phase, but they are not samples of \(e^{-\beta H}/Z\) and cannot replace Monte Carlo for thermodynamics.

Exercises

Increase the latent dimension from 16 to 64. Which tests improve? Does the energy?
Replace the dense decoder by a convolutional one. The spins are still independent given \(\mathbf z\): what changes, and what cannot?
Train the \(J_1\)–\(J_2\) cVAE without the \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry and without the conditional prior and repeat the phase and stripe-orientation tests.
